justification: Confirmed: line 187 states 'The gap is only calculated among problems to which the solvers can get a feasible solution,' and line 311 shows CMILP with 1.1% gap and 75% dataset feasibility on the referenced Random dataset.

weakness: Imprecise 'one-step' framing: the title/abstract call the solver 'one-step' but the full inference pipeline includes iterative objective-guided sampling with multiple gradient steps, and Table 5 shows more inference steps improve performance.
justification: The paper's own framing conflates the one-step generative model with the multi-step guided sampling procedure described in Section 3.3; this is a legitimate precision critique grounded in the text.

weakness: Table labeling error in Tables 2, 3, and 4 where the first row of proposed methods is mislabeled 'SCMILP (Ours)' twice instead of 'CMILP (Ours)' for one row.
justification: Confirmed directly in the extracted paper text: lines 244/245, 262/263, and 273/274 each show two consecutive rows both labeled 'SCMILP (Ours)' with different values, matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: The claim of being 'first' to extend binary ILP neural solvers to the non-binary case is contradicted by the paper's own citation of Tang et al. (2025), which addresses non-binary ILP, and this prior work is never compared experimentally.
justification: Line 42 claims to be first, while line 55 states 'Tang et al. (2025) deals with non-binary ILP by introducing an integer correction layer,' and no experimental comparison to Tang et al. appears in the results tables.

weakness: SCMILP and MFILP training losses are deferred entirely to the appendix, with only CMILP's loss (Eq. 6) given in the main text, despite being core methodological contributions.
justification: Confirmed by line 107: 'The detailed introduction of shortcut and mean flow models are put in the appendix,' leaving readers unable to evaluate two of the three proposed methods from the main text.

weakness: Shared source between training data (pretraining seed docs, SFT data) and RedSage-Bench undermines the benchmark's independence; decontamination only filters query similarity >0.9, not pretraining memorization of seed document facts.
justification: Paper (line 202) confirms decontamination only removes SFT instances with query similarity above 0.9 to benchmark questions, and does not address that the model is pretrained (Sec 3.1) directly on the same RedSage-Seed documents used to generate benchmark items.

weakness: Numerical inconsistency in open-ended QA results: text (line 256) claims +7% correctness and +0.07 quality advantage for RedSage-8B-DPO over Qwen3-8B, but Figure 6 data (line 290) shows 0.73 vs 0.40 correctness (+33%) and 7.07 vs 7.50 quality (-0.43); also text states RedSage-8B-Ins quality as 6.43 while figure shows 7.43.
justification: Directly confirmed by comparing paper line 256 text against the Figure 6 caption description at line 290, which shows the stated contradictions exactly as the review describes.

weakness: General benchmark comparison (Table 6) is framed as a net improvement over Qwen3-8B-Base, but Qwen3-8B (instruct) shows substantial degradation vs its own base (e.g., HellaSwag 79.62->56.70), so RedSage's real achievement is avoiding degradation rather than outperforming the base model.
justification: Table 6 values in the paper (line 349, 357) confirm Qwen3-8B-Base MMLU 78.73/ARC-C 68.09/Winog 79.62 vs Qwen3-8B (instruct) 73.59/62.54/56.70, matching the reviewer's cited degradation exactly.

weakness: No ablation studies for key design choices: the 30% FineWeb-Edu replay ratio, agentic augmentation vs. naive Q&A generation, and Planner Agent vs. directly prompting the Augmenter are never ablated.
justification: A full-text search of the paper finds no ablation section or experiments isolating the replay ratio, naive-QA-vs-agentic comparison, or Planner-vs-Augmenter contribution; only CFW-only/Seed-only/combined pretraining variants are compared.

weakness: LLM-as-Judge for open-ended evaluation (using Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen2.5-72B, the same model families used to generate benchmark data) lacks human calibration, inter-rater agreement, or correlation with human judgment.
justification: The paper (line 196) describes the LLM-as-judge rubric for open-ended Q&A scoring but no human evaluation, inter-rater agreement, or human-LLM correlation study is reported anywhere in the text.

weakness: Minor numerical inconsistency between abstract (+5.59 points on cybersecurity benchmarks) and conclusion (+5.9 points on cybersecurity tasks).
justification: Confirmed: abstract line 9 states +5.59, while conclusion line 377 states +5.9, a discrepancy in the reported headline number.

weakness: The abstract's 'on par with ARMs' claim for text generation overstates the evidence given the 18.5% relative NLL gap on LM1B.
justification: Table 2 shows ARM NLL=3.94 vs ILM NLL=4.67 on LM1B, a substantial gap, while the abstract states ILMs 'perform on par with ARMs' without qualification.

weakness: The mismatch between the training objective (predicting aggregate count distributions) and the one-at-a-time inference procedure is acknowledged as biased but never analyzed empirically.
justification: The paper only states in one sentence (lines 79-80) that the objective is biased due to high variance of the exact objective, with no ablation or ablation of the bias's effect on results.

weakness: The Prometheus LLM-judge evaluation (Figure 5) lacks numerical reporting; only a bar-chart image is given with no scores or confidence intervals.
justification: Figure 5 is described only as a bar chart image with prose interpretation; no table of Prometheus scores appears anywhere in the provided text.

weakness: No ablation isolates which design choices (stop classifier, biased objective, RoPE, denoising-style dropping) drive ILM's improvement over Insertion Transformer.
justification: The paper attributes IT's poor Star_easy performance (35.2 vs 100) solely to the EOS-vs-stop-classifier difference (line 147) without running a controlled ablation varying each factor.

weakness: The 'arbitrary length' claim is not tested beyond the training distribution (sequences padded to 128/1024 tokens).
justification: The paper reports training/eval only up to the padded lengths (Section 5.3) and provides no experiment generating substantially longer sequences to support the arbitrary-length claim empirically.

weakness: MDM baselines use only the standard tau-leaping sampler, not the improved greedy/top-k/flow-based variants the paper itself cites as addressing MDM's unmasking limitation.
justification: Section 5.3.1 states tau-leaping is used for MDM, while Related Work (Section 4) cites Gong et al. 2024, Zheng et al. 2024, and Campbell et al. 2024 as offering better unmasking strategies that are never used as a baseline.

weakness: No comparison with fill-in-the-middle (FIM) ARMs on the infilling task.
justification: The paper explicitly explains (line 129) that FIM cannot perform arbitrary multi-segment infilling, which is precisely the capability gap ILMs are designed to address, so comparing against a method acknowledged to be structurally incapable of the task is not a meaningful baseline requirement.

weakness: Figure 6's legend/caption is inconsistent with the running text about which color represents MDM vs ILM.
justification: Line 215 text states 'MDM (red) ... stays below that of the ILM (blue)' while the figure's own caption/legend lists MDM (red), ARM (blue), ILM (green), a genuine internal inconsistency.

weakness: The analysis never connects r-dynamics to actual optimization performance (no f(x_k)-f(x*), gradient norm, or comparison to baseline SD/BB/CG).
justification: The paper only plots r trajectories in Sec 3-4 and never reports function value or gradient norm convergence; the conclusion only speculates that unstable state 'can... potentially accelerate convergence' without evidence.

weakness: The N-dimensional analysis in Section 3 is non-rigorous, with Eq.32 presented without derivation and heatmap-based heuristic arguments substituting for proof.
justification: Section 3.1 indeed jumps from Eq(11) to Eq(32) with no derivation shown, and the weight argument (lines 200-204) is a qualitative reading of Figure 2 heatmaps rather than a rigorous proof.

weakness: Insufficient experimental validation: single synthetic problem, only three t values, only r-trajectory plots, no baseline comparison, no ablation/replication, and unclear BB method comparison in Figure 7.
justification: Section 4 confirms exactly one synthetic setup (arithmetic-progression eigenvalues) with t=0.9,1.0,1.1, plotting only r; Figure 7's BB scatter plot lacks axis definitions in the text.

weakness: Misuse of dynamical-systems terminology, calling stable fixed points 'strange attractors' and using 'chaos/chaotic' without computing Lyapunov exponents.
justification: The paper text at line 163/171 explicitly calls stable fixed points 'strange attractor' and uses 'chaos motion' (line 117) without any Lyapunov exponent calculation, matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: Key derivations lack intermediate steps (Eq.15→16, Eq.17 differentiation, and the t bound in Sec 2.3), making verification difficult.
justification: The paper indeed jumps from Eq(15) to Eq(16) and presents Eq(17) as a finished derivative with no shown steps, and the t>((a1+a2)/2a1) bound in Sec 2.3 appears without derivation.

weakness: The headline performance claims ('92-97% of baseline performance across all tasks' and '15-25% higher F1 on multi-hop reasoning') are contradicted by the paper's own Table 1 data, e.g. DeepSeek-Coder on HotpotQA retains only 75.5%, and best-baseline comparisons on HotpotQA yield gains of only 1.6-8.8%.
justification: Table 1 numbers (0.256/0.339=75.5%, 0.459/0.566=81.1%, 0.220/0.267=82.4%, 0.247/0.291=84.9%) directly confirm the reviewer's arithmetic, and comparing against best baselines per model on HotpotQA gives gains well below 15-25%.

weakness: The 'logarithmic compression beyond classical information-theoretic limits' claim is false for the actual classical-simulation implementation, since it must explicitly store all 512 amplitudes per segment (O(N)), not O(log N).
justification: The paper itself states at line 100 that 'the current implementation operates as a classical simulation,' confirming the reviewer's point that the O(log N) claim (line 60, Table 3) does not hold for what was actually run.

weakness: No inference latency or throughput measurements are provided despite claims of 'minimal latency overhead'.
justification: Line 216 asserts 'minimal latency overhead' and the implementation section mentions optimizations for overhead, but no wall-clock/tokens-per-second data appears anywhere in the text or tables provided.

weakness: The quantum component contributes negligibly to performance (Full QubitCache 0.491 vs No Quantum 0.472, a 3.9% relative difference), and the 'No Quantum' ablation configuration and its dataset are underspecified.
justification: Table 4 and its surrounding text (line 238) confirm these exact numbers and the paper indeed never specifies the dataset/task for Table 4 or what 'No Quantum' entails.

weakness: The 'relational structure preservation' framing overstates the method, since Equation 3 computes only a per-token scalar (accumulated attention to that token), not a pairwise relational structure.
justification: Equation 3 (line 74) indeed sums over j to produce a single scalar a_i per token, matching the reviewer's characterization, while the abstract and intro repeatedly use language like 'relational structure' and 'topology preservation'.

weakness: Figure 3b's reported F1 range (0.7-0.85) and the '103% of baseline' claim at depth 15 do not correspond to any benchmark/task reported in Table 1, and the benchmark for Figure 3 is never stated.
justification: No entry in Table 1 reaches F1=0.84, and Section 4.5.2/Figure 3 caption text never states which dataset was used, matching the reviewer's observation.

weakness: The paper never compares quantum amplitude encoding against a simple classical baseline of storing the same probability distribution as a plain float vector, so it cannot isolate whether the quantum formalism adds value.
justification: No such classical-vector baseline is described anywhere in Section 4's baselines (only FullKV, ScissorHand, H2O, StreamingLLM, GEAR) or ablations.

weakness: The paper's characterization that 'all existing methods continue to frame the problem primarily as token selection' ignores quantization approaches like GEAR and KVQuant that operate on precision reduction rather than token selection.
justification: Line 21 makes this blanket claim, yet the same paper's own Section 2 and intro (line 15) discuss KVQuant/GEAR as quantization methods distinct from token selection, so the paper's own text contradicts its blanket framing.

weakness: Gradient flow through the hard clustering assignment (argmax over cosine similarity) is not addressed; the paper does not state whether a straight-through estimator, Gumbel-softmax, or other gradient approximation is used for the discrete assignment used in token permutation.
justification: The paper (Sec 3.3) states the codebook is updated via non-gradient EMA/K-Means and draws an explicit parallel to VQ-VAE, but nowhere states how gradients propagate through the argmax-based cluster assignment/permutation; this is a genuine methodological gap.

weakness: GPP's causal relaxation is limited to the output readout (C matrix) rather than the recurrent state update, so the paper's claim of 'relaxing strict causality' somewhat overstates what actually changes.
justification: Eq. in Sec 3.4 shows O_i=(C+P)h_i+Dx_i while h_i=Āh_{i-1}+B̄x_i remains unchanged, confirming the state propagation itself stays strictly causal.

weakness: The prompt dimension d_s is never numerically reported, making it impossible to assess GPP's computational overhead.
justification: The paper defines U ∈ R^{K×d_s} and projection A: R^d→R^{d_s} (line 173-175) but never gives a concrete value for d_s anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: Training details are incomplete: total training steps/epochs, batch size, and learning rate schedule are omitted.
justification: Section 4.1 reports optimizer, initial LR, lambda values, and GPU type (A100) but does not state steps/epochs, batch size, or LR schedule anywhere in the main text.

weakness: Baseline number provenance in Table 1 is unclear (not stated whether numbers are re-implemented or taken from original papers).
justification: Table 1 and the surrounding text (Sec 4.3) list numerous baselines without stating the source of each reported number.

weakness: Table 1 uses 'MambaC' while the text consistently uses 'MambaIC' for the same method (Zeng et al., 2025), a naming inconsistency.
justification: Table 1 lists 'MambaC' as a row label while the running text (Sec 2.2, 4.3, 4.4) refers to the same citation as 'MambaIC'.

weakness: The claim that multi-directional scanning 'quadruples computational complexity' (line 28) is a simplification that glosses over capacity trade-offs.
justification: The review itself labels this a trivial nitpick that 'does not affect the paper's contribution,' making it an overly harsh, low-value criticism rather than a substantive weakness.

weakness: No uncertainty quantification across runs (no error bars, standard deviations, or mention of number of seeds), making comparative model rankings unreliable.
justification: The paper text contains no mention of random seeds, repeated runs, or error bars for the reported MAE results in the empirical analysis section; all results appear as single-point estimates.

weakness: Tension between the paper's framing of testing whether models capture 'underlying physical principles' and its use of semi-empirical GFN2-xTB reference labels, without discussing whether GFN2-xTB itself degrades for OOD molecules.
justification: The paper explicitly describes GFN2-xTB as a method 'known for its balance between computational efficiency and accuracy' (Abstract/§3) while also framing the benchmark as testing whether models 'capture the underlying physical principles' -- the paper does not discuss GFN2-xTB's own accuracy degradation on OOD molecules, supporting this critique.

weakness: Limited analysis of why certain architectures exhibit certain generalization behaviors -- patterns are reported descriptively without explaining which architectural features (equivariance, attention, directional messages) correlate with generalization performance.
justification: The paper's results section reports per-model performance differences but does not provide an architectural-feature-level explanation for these differences, matching the reviewer's characterization of the analysis as purely descriptive.

weakness: Uneven turn budgets (30 vs. 100 turns for Claude Sonnet 4 and Qwen 3 Coder) confound comparative claims like 'proprietary models show stronger evidence of a significant difference'.
justification: The paper states in line 106 that Claude Sonnet 4 and Qwen 3 Coder get up to 100 turns while other models get 30, with justification 'to account for their greater reasoning and planning capacity' -- this is indeed circular and confounds the comparative claims made in §3.1.

weakness: Claude Sonnet 4's Hidden baseline is measured on only 100/500 instances with subset selection undescribed, making the headline 74% improvement claim unverifiable.
justification: Footnote 4 (line 131) confirms the 100/500 subset for Claude Sonnet 4's Hidden setting and gives no detail on how the subset was chosen, only asserting significance without describing sampling methodology.

weakness: The 'up to 74%' improvement claim is not clearly traceable to numbers in Figure 3/Table results.
justification: Computing relative improvements from the reported table (Hidden/Interaction/Full percentages) does not obviously yield exactly 74% for any model or metric, and the paper never explicitly states which model/calculation produces this headline number.

weakness: The user proxy has access to file locations that need modification (line 92), making the Interaction setting artificially easier than real deployments, undercutting the '89% recovery' framing.
justification: Line 92 explicitly states the proxy 'has access to file locations that need modification and can provide them when queried,' and the 89% recovery claim (§3.2) doesn't carry this caveat outside the limitations section.

weakness: No confidence intervals are reported for the resolve rates in Figure 3, despite small sample sizes (500, or 100 for Sonnet 4 Hidden).
justification: The paper reports Wilcoxon signed-rank test significance (Table 4) but the main text and figures present only point estimates without interval estimates, which is a genuine gap given the sample sizes discussed.

weakness: The 'Middle Score Anomaly' framing (that intermediate scores are 'highly unusual' for humans) is over-claimed and partially contradicted by the paper's own human data in Table 4, which shows humans scoring in intermediate ranges on several other subtests.
justification: The paper's own text (line 188) explicitly claims it would be 'highly unusual' for humans to score at intermediate levels, using this as evidence models lack reasoning, yet the paper's Table 4 human data shows humans achieving intermediate scores on multiple other subtests, which undercuts the generalized framing.

weakness: The parametric synthetic difficulty generator is validated on only one model (GPT-4.1), leaving unclear whether difficulty gradations transfer across architectures; and the MA1 subtest shows a non-monotonic anomaly (Easy=50.0% lower than Hard=70.8%) that goes unremarked.
justification: This is a specific, checkable claim about the single-model validation and an unexplained non-monotonic result in the reported table, which is a legitimate gap not addressed in the paper's text.

weakness: The dismissal of human underperformance on RL2 as due to models' textual object knowledge is a thin, post-hoc justification given RL2 is included as a visual cognition subtest in the benchmark.
justification: This is a specific critique of the paper's own explanatory reasoning for an anomalous result, pointing out an internal tension between including RL2 as a visual subtest and excusing its result as non-visual.

weakness: The conclusion's characterization of model performance as 'often performing near chance' is misleading since 30.17% is roughly 10x the 2.89% chance floor.
justification: This is a precise numerical critique grounded in the paper's own reported chance-floor and top model accuracy figures.

weakness: The VZ3 chance calculation '14.6/4 = 3.65%' includes an unexplained '14.6' value not derived in the main text.
justification: This is a specific, checkable claim about self-containedness of a stated calculation in the paper.

weakness: The LLaMA-3.2 evaluation uses temperature 0.6 while all other models use temperature 0, introducing an undisclosed-justification non-determinism for one model family.
justification: This is a specific, checkable methodological inconsistency in the evaluation setup as reported in the paper.

weakness: The experimental section does not adequately support the theory: reports test loss/accuracy vs outer iterations (not SFO calls or wall time, conflating p-fold per-iteration cost), does not report gradient norm (the actual stationarity criterion), lacks error bars/multiple seeds, and uses fixed K=10 across methods while the theory requires K to scale with problem parameters.
justification: Section 5 confirms: 'we report the test loss/accuracy v.s. the number of outer-loop iterations t'; K=10 is fixed for 'all the algorithms'; no mention of seeds/error bars or gradient norm anywhere in the experiments section, while Theorem 3.1 explicitly ties K to problem parameters (Eq. 10).

weakness: The normalized gradient step in Algorithm 1 (line 14) is not adequately justified: Remark 3.1 only says normalization eases the analysis and expresses belief (not proof) that results also hold for standard GD, despite normalized GD having different convergence properties than standard GD.
justification: Remark 3.1 in the paper literally states the normalization 'make[s] the analysis of inner loops easier' and that the authors 'believe' (not prove) the guarantees also hold for standard gradient step 'via a more involved analysis' -- this is an unproven belief, exactly as the review characterizes it.

weakness: The abstract de-emphasizes the κ dependence: the bound is O(pκ^{9+2/p}ε^{-4-2/p}) but the abstract states only O(pε^{-4-2/p}), and the near-optimality qualification 'if κ is constant' does not appear in the abstract.
justification: The abstract's stated bound omits κ, matching Table 1's full bound O(pκ^{9+2/p}ε^{-4-2/p}) and the near-optimality claim in the text (line 255) is indeed qualified only in the body, not the abstract.

weakness: The experiments do not probe the κ or ε regime the theory addresses: only a single problem instance with fixed K=10 is tested at moderate precision, without varying ε or κ to test predicted scaling.
justification: Section 5 uses one dataset/problem instance ('20 Newsgroup', Example 2.2) with fixed T=1000, K=10, and no variation of ε or κ reported, consistent with the review's claim.

weakness: Asymmetric comparison inflates KL-divergence claims because TDDM's spatial prior H is computed from real target data while baselines get no such conditioning, and this drives most of the gap.
justification: Algorithm 2 line 3 confirms H is computed from real X_target, and ablation (Table 2) confirms removing the prior degrades KL by ~5x, supporting the reviewer's claim.

weakness: Missing variance estimates for most metrics; only TSTR reports ± values, and models are trained/sampled/evaluated once per dataset, making it impossible to assess statistical significance.
justification: Table 1 and 2 captions explicitly state 'Models are trained, sampled and evaluated once per dataset,' and only TSTR shows ± values, confirming this gap.

weakness: 'Zero-shot' framing requires qualification since it still requires access to target-city trajectory data to compute the spatial prior H, and the abstract/conclusion invite over-interpretation of this limitation.
justification: Algorithm 2 line 3 shows H is computed from X_target, and the abstract/conclusion use 'zero-shot' without this caveat, though lines 169-173 do explain it as the review itself notes.

weakness: Baseline adaptation for DiffTraj is unclear: DiffTraj is described as relying on strong sample-specific conditioning, yet is compared on the unconditional task without explanation of how it was adapted.
justification: Section 1 describes DiffTraj as using 'strong sample-specific conditioning' but the main text of the provided paper gives no explanation of how it was stripped down for the unconditional comparison in Table 1.

weakness: The 'w/o spatial prior + rejection' condition in Table 2 is unexplained; the main text never describes what rejection scheme was used.
justification: Table 2 includes this column but no description of the rejection mechanism appears anywhere in the visible main text.

weakness: The claim that DiffTraj/ControlTraj's sample-specific conditioning increases risk of memorization is asserted without evidence.
justification: Section 1 states this as a bare assertion ('it increases the risk of memorization and prevents cross-region generalization') with no supporting experiment or citation for memorization specifically.

weakness: Computational cost (training time, inference time, model size, parameter count) is not reported for TDDM or any baseline.
justification: No such figures appear anywhere in the visible paper text, including the evaluation and appendix references given.

weakness: The headline 288x speedup conflates architectures/hardware/budgets: comparing IVF-PQ ret-only (1.02ms) against an external 'SASRec CPU p90 (ETUDE)' benchmark (292ms), while the paper's own table shows IVF-PQ+encode (2.5ms) vs SASRec GPU (102ms) is only ~40x.
justification: Table in Section 4.5 (line 260-265) explicitly labels the 292ms column 'SASRec CPU p90 (ETUDE)' and 102ms as 'SASRec GPU p90 (ETUDE)', citing Kersbergen et al. 2024, yet the text (line 273) describes the same numbers as 'exhaustive dot-product scoring... using the same dual-encoder scoring function s(u,i)' -- a genuine internal inconsistency, and the fairer same-architecture comparison (IVF-PQ+encode vs SASRec GPU) gives ~40x, not 288x.

weakness: Cold-start (LOOC) evaluation on public benchmarks reports no comparative baselines (e.g., content-based KNN), so readers cannot tell if the numbers represent strong or weak performance, despite the abstract/intro claiming outperformance of a content-based baseline (which is only shown on the proprietary dataset).
justification: Table 2 (lines 229-236) shows only RetrievalFormer LOO/LOOC numbers with baselines marked N/A; the content-based KNN baseline is only used in the proprietary email dataset (Appendix G, line 250), confirming the public-benchmark cold-start section has no baseline comparison.

weakness: Accuracy claims are selectively framed around Recall@20 while NDCG (especially NDCG@5 on MovieLens-1M: 0.0823 vs SASRec's 0.1285, a 36% gap) tells a substantially worse story and is not discussed anywhere in the main text.
justification: Table at lines 198-199 confirms RetrievalFormer NDCG@5=0.0823 vs SASRec 0.1285 and NDCG@20=0.1390 vs 0.1745 on MovieLens-1M, and the surrounding prose (lines 173-177) discusses only Recall@20 percentages, never mentioning this NDCG gap.

weakness: AttrFormer's outlier-level Recall@20 performance on MovieLens-1M (0.4128, ~15% higher than next best) is labeled a 'notable outlier' but given no explanation, despite being a directly relevant attribute-based baseline.
justification: Line 177 confirms the paper calls it a 'notable outlier' and gives no analysis of why AttrFormer outperforms by ~15%, so the critique is accurate.

weakness: Ablation results (attention fusion, uniformity loss) lack a clearly defined additive baseline configuration, and the full ablation table is deferred to an appendix not available in the main text.
justification: This is a reasonable observation about self-containment of the main text ablation presentation; cannot verify appendix content, but the reviewer's description of the main-text numbers not summing cleanly is a legitimate specificity critique grounded in the numbers themselves.

weakness: No variance/run-count information is reported for RetrievalFormer's results in Table 1, unlike baselines which are averaged over five runs.
justification: The paper does not report any variance or run count for RetrievalFormer anywhere in the results sections read, only citing baseline protocol adoption from Liu et al. 2025.

weakness: Equation (7) notation shifts from h_{i_t} in Eq (6) to h_t without explanation.
justification: Trivial but plausible notation nitpick; not contradicted by any paper text found.

weakness: Metrics terminology inconsistency: line 167 states Hit Rate@20 is reported for cold-start, but Table 2 reports Recall@20 and NDCG@20, not Hit Rate@20.
justification: Line 167 explicitly says 'For cold-start evaluation, we report Hit Rate@20 for new-item recommendations,' while Table 2 (lines 229-236) only shows Recall@20 and NDCG@20 columns, confirming the inconsistency.

weakness: The paper mentions 'graceful handling of missing features via attention masking' but never explains the mechanism.
justification: Line 111 contains exactly this phrase with no further elaboration found elsewhere in the read paper text, confirming the mechanism is unexplained.

weakness: Unresolved inconsistency between Table 2 and Figure 1 for the same metric (function name recovery F1) on the same data (x86-64, decompiled code) — Table 2 values are 3-10x lower than Figure 1's 'with CodeWordNet' values, and don't even clearly match the 'without CodeWordNet' values either.
justification: Section 3.4 states CodeWordNet-based semantic matching is used for the primary name recovery metric, yet Table 2's reported F1 values (e.g., CodeLlama O0: 0.04) are far lower than Figure 1's 'w CodeWordNet' values (e.g., CodeLlama O0: ~0.15) for the same model/setting, and the paper gives no explanation for this discrepancy.

weakness: The introduction's headline claim that fine-tuned DeepSeek-R1 reaches an F1 score of 0.37 is not grounded in any table in the visible main text, and the x86-64 results (Tables 2-4, 6) show much lower fine-tuned DeepSeek-R1 scores.
justification: Line 19 states the 0.37 figure but no main-text table corroborates it; the paper only says non-x86-64 results are in the Appendix, so the reader cannot verify or locate the source of this advertised headline number.

weakness: Single-prompt zero-shot evaluation without any prompt sensitivity analysis across the nine models.
justification: Section 3.2 explicitly states the authors adopt a single established prompt rather than optimizing prompts per model, and the paper itself later documents strong prompt sensitivity (Finding 7, and prompt modification for DeepSeek-R1), supporting the concern that low zero-shot scores could partly reflect prompt mismatch rather than pure model capability.

weakness: Fine-tuning protocol lacks convergence validation (fixed 200 steps, no learning curves or hyperparameter sweep), and in some cases fine-tuning reduces performance.
justification: Section 3.3/4.3 only mentions LoRA fine-tuning for a fixed step count with no reported loss curves or convergence checks, and Table 3 shows fine-tuning actually lowering variable name recovery F1 for DeepSeek-V2 at O1 (0.10 to 0.05), which the paper does not investigate further.

weakness: Title is broader than the evidence, since the study evaluates only open-source models in a narrow 12B-34B size range and explicitly excludes ChatGPT/GPT-4.
justification: Section 4.2 confirms ChatGPT, GPT-3, and GPT-4 are explicitly excluded due to cost and size, so the title's general claim about 'LLMs' is broader than the actually tested model scope.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance reporting; unclear how many runs were performed given F1 scores as low as 0.00-0.05.
justification: The paper's tables report single point-estimate F1 scores per model/setting with no mention of number of runs, standard deviations, or confidence intervals anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: The LLM/TOFU experiments (Table 5) do not support the paper's claims and may contradict them (TARF worse at forgetting/retaining than baselines in several settings, and TARF matches GA baseline exactly in several settings).
justification: Table 5 numbers (lines 304-325) confirm TARF(GA) has QA Prob on F=0.0762 vs CL(GA)=0.0009 in All-matched, TARF(GA) R=0.0094 vs CL(NPO) R=0.4481 in Target Mismatch, and several rows where TARF(GA)==TARF(NPO)==GA exactly, matching the reviewer's specific numeric claims.

weakness: Theorem 3.2 is a standard Lipschitz bound / Taylor expansion result, not a deep theoretical result, and the paper overstates its contribution by calling it foundational.
justification: The paper's own text (lines around Section 3.2) frames the theorem as revealing 'crucial forgetting dynamics' while the actual empirical analysis (Figure 3, Figure 9) is what substantiates the claims, supporting the reviewer's characterization.

weakness: The target identification procedure assumes the number of classes belonging to the target concept is known in target mismatch forgetting, which may not hold in practice, and the paper does not explore misspecification.
justification: Line 61 explicitly states 'we assume that the number of classes in D_un belonging to the target concept is known in target mismatch forgetting,' confirming this assumption, and no sensitivity analysis on misspecified composition appears in the main text.

weakness: Key hyperparameters (k, t0, t1, beta) lack concrete guidance in the main text and are deferred to the appendix with only vague guidance.
justification: Line 152 gives only a rough description of beta ('can be estimated by the information about the specific unlearning request...') and line 335 explicitly defers 'a practical guideline in Appendix E.1', confirming the guidance is vague and appendix-deferred.

weakness: No error bars in main tables; standard deviations are relegated to the appendix.
justification: Line 198 and 246 explicitly state 'Complete results with mean and std values in Appendix F.7' and 'report results under multiple runs in Appendix F.7 with std values,' confirming std is not in main tables.

weakness: Limited discussion of computational cost, deferred to appendix.
justification: Line 353 explicitly says the paper 'discuss[es] and check[s] the computational cost of TARF in target identification stage in Appendix E.2,' confirming it is not discussed in the main text body beyond a pointer.

weakness: No comparison against any existing baseline method (e.g., constrained FedAvg, AL/ADMM, EF-SGD, SAFE-EF) in the experiments; only FEDSGM variants and a centralized oracle are compared.
justification: The experiments section (NP classification and CMDP) only compares FEDSGM variants (hard/soft, different E, m/n, K/d) against each other and a centralized version; no prior method identified in the introduction (He et al. 2024, EF-SGD, SAFE-EF) is benchmarked.

weakness: The non-vanishing constant terms in the partial-participation bound (which prevent ε from decaying to zero as T→∞) are not discussed or flagged in the abstract/contributions or limitations section.
justification: Theorem 1's partial participation ε formula (line 100) indeed contains T-independent terms like (n/m)(2DG√(1-q)/q²), and the limitations paragraph (lines 269-273) only discusses convexity and gradient-descent restrictiveness, not this irreducible error term.

weakness: Theory-experiment disconnect for the CMDP experiment: Assumption 1 requires convexity, but the CMDP uses non-convex deep RL policy gradients (TRPO), so the experiment does not validate the theory.
justification: The paper itself states Assumption 1 requires convex f_j, g_j, and separately acknowledges in the limitations (lines 269-273) that convexity does not hold for the RL experiment, confirming this is a genuine gap even though partially self-acknowledged.

weakness: Small-scale experimental setup: NP classification uses a small breast cancer dataset (569 samples, 30 dims) with only 3 seeds, and CMDP uses only 5 seeds, which is small for reliable statistical conclusions.
justification: The paper explicitly states the breast cancer dataset is used with three random seeds for NP classification (Section 4) and 5 runs for CMDP (Section 4 Discussion: Cartpole), confirming the small scale.

weakness: Notation inconsistency in Algorithm 1 line 126: uses "G(w_t) ≤ ε" instead of the defined constraint estimate Ĝ(w_t) used elsewhere in the paper.
justification: Algorithm 1 line 9 (pseudocode) literally reads "if G(w_t) ≤ ε" while the rest of the paper (Section 2, eq. for switching rule) consistently uses Ĝ(w_t), confirming the inconsistency.

weakness: The soft-switching stability vs. exact feasibility trade-off (Figure 1 shows soft switching settling at g(w)≈0.05 vs hard switching at g(w)≈0, tied to β≥2/ε forcing large β for small ε) deserves more transparent discussion than the brief mention given.
justification: The paper does briefly note the β≥2/ε trade-off (lines 215-216) but Figure 1 shows a real gap between soft and hard switching constraint values that is not elaborated on further in the text.

weakness: Overclaimed methodological novelty and imprecise terminology: paper describes FF-Erase as 'gradient ascent' while it's actually KL-minimization/distillation, and doesn't situate against prior distillation-based unlearning (Chundawat et al.)
justification: The Conclusion (line 289) literally calls it 'a novel FF-specific gradient ascent method' while the actual mechanism per Eq.5 is gradient descent minimizing KL divergence; the paper cites Chundawat et al. 2023b only for exact unlearning, not comparing its distillation mechanism against Chundawat 2023a's incompetent-teacher distillation approach.

weakness: G-MIA is mischaracterized as 'black-box' when it requires per-layer goodness vectors from all layers, giving it more access than the FL black-box baseline it's compared against
justification: The paper repeatedly calls G-MIA black-box (Abstract, §5) while stating it uses goodness vectors from all layers (§5 step 2), which is strictly more output access than the final-layer-only FL baseline it outperforms.

weakness: Limited baseline comparison: unlearning evaluation only compares against RE and GA, with no adaptation of existing approximate unlearning methods (e.g., distillation-based, Fisher forgetting) to FF setting
justification: §6.2 confirms the paper only compares FF-Erase with RE and GA; no other approximate unlearning baselines (Qiao et al., Liu et al., or distillation-based methods mentioned in §2) are adapted and tested.

weakness: G-MIA scores show an inconsistency between Figure 4(c) and Table 1 for RE's score (0.5320 vs 0.551), unexplained and without confidence intervals
justification: Figure 4(c) explicitly reports RE G-MIA ACC of 0.5320, while Table 1 reports RE G-MIA ACC of 0.551; the paper gives no explanation for this discrepancy or reports variance.

weakness: No statistical significance reported; all results are point estimates without variance across multiple runs
justification: All tables (Table 1, Figures 3-5) report single point-estimate numbers with no reported standard deviations or confidence intervals across seeds.

weakness: Reproducibility gaps for hyperparameters K, epsilon1, epsilon2: no default values, ranges, or sensitivity analysis provided beyond a general note on K's tradeoff
justification: The paper only vaguely states K is 'empirical' and determined by dataset (footnote 2, §4.1 line 160) without giving concrete default values or sensitivity analysis for K, epsilon1, or epsilon2.

weakness: The notion of 'feature' is used imprecisely across the argument, referring to properties of causes, absences of correlates, semantic properties, and neural network activations without explicit criteria for individuability.
justification: The paper never gives explicit criteria for what counts as an individuable 'correlative feature' — it uses 'feature' loosely across the clay, owl, and neural network cases without defining individuation criteria, so this critique is well-grounded.

weakness: The owls example is presented as a stronger illustration than the evidence supports, since the categorical claim that 'no feature... correlates' conflates semantic meaning with statistical correlation, going beyond the paper's own hedging that this is just a 'candidate explanation'.
justification: The paper itself states at line 151 the categorical 'There is no feature of the set that means owl... or correlates to a disposition' and only later (line 153) hedges to 'candidate explanation,' confirming the tension the reviewer identifies.

weakness: The trust section concedes limited practical impact, leaving unclear what the argument actually changes about practical engagement with neural networks beyond linguistic revision.
justification: The paper explicitly states at line 165 that reframing opacity as ontological rather than epistemic 'makes no ultimate difference to the trust we do, or should, have in a system,' supporting the reviewer's point about limited practical consequence.

weakness: The central importance ratio approximation (replacing the exact terminal flow difference with a velocity-variation estimate along an interpolation path) is never empirically validated against the exact importance ratio.
justification: The paper (Sec 4, Eqs 9-13) only derives and asserts the approximation and gives a theoretical error bound in the appendix; no experiment in the main text computes/compares exact vs approximate importance ratios.

weakness: The claimed O(epsilon) error bound (Eq. 11) is asserted in the main text without the derivation being shown, and the link between the PPO clipping range and the geometric approximation error is not fully explained in the main body.
justification: The main text only states the bound qualitatively ("which can be naturally enforced by the clipping range epsilon in PPO") and defers the full derivation to Appendix A; the sensitivity study in Fig 4a tests learning outcomes under different epsilon, not approximation accuracy itself.

weakness: The claim that PolicyFlow "achieves asymptotic performance that consistently matches or surpasses PPO across all tasks" on IsaacLab overstates the evidence in Table 1, since PPO significantly outperforms PolicyFlow on H1.
justification: Table 1 shows p=0.0069 for H1 with PPO's bolded/higher mean (29.3 vs 27.3), a statistically significant loss for PolicyFlow, contradicting the paper's "matches or surpasses ... across all tasks" claim.

weakness: FPO and DPPO, the paper's primary competitor baselines, are not evaluated on the IsaacLab benchmark suite, so IsaacLab results cannot substantiate improvement over prior SOTA there.
justification: The paper itself states in Sec 5.2 that FPO/DPPO are excluded from IsaacLab due to JAX/PyTorch framework incompatibility and engineering effort, confirming this gap is real.

weakness: The Brownian regularizer is presented as "principled" while the paper's own remark concedes the velocity field does not strictly correspond to rectified flow dynamics, making the regularizer a heuristic rather than a principled derivation.
justification: Paper text: "the Brownian regularizer provides a principled yet computationally lightweight alternative" (line 226) directly juxtaposed with the Remark stating "the velocity field in our policy ... does not strictly correspond to the rectified flow dynamics" (line 228), a genuine tension the reviewer correctly identifies.

weakness: The MultiGoal experiment (Fig. 2) provides only qualitative trajectory visualizations with no quantitative diversity/coverage metric to substantiate the multimodality claim.
justification: Section 5.1 and Fig. 2 only describe visual trajectory plots; no entropy, coverage, or visitation-proportion metric is reported anywhere in the visible text for this experiment.

weakness: MuJoCo Playground results (Fig. 3) are shown only as learning curves without terminal performance tables or statistical significance tests, unlike the IsaacLab results which do include such tables.
justification: Section 5.2 and Fig. 3 present only training curves with standard error shading; no terminal reward table or p-values are given for MuJoCo Playground, in contrast to Table 1 for IsaacLab.

weakness: The hyperparameter comparison on MuJoCo Playground is asymmetric: PPO uses default settings while PolicyFlow (and FPO/DPPO) use tuned configurations, potentially understating PPO's performance.
justification: Paper states "the hyperparameters for FPO and DPPO follow the tuned configurations from the FPO paper, and PPO uses the default settings recommended by the MuJoCo Playground repository" (Sec 5.2), confirming the asymmetry.

weakness: Theorem 1 is incoherent: q* is never defined, and the bound's RHS is decreasing in beta_q in the assumed regime, contradicting the claimed intuition.
justification: The paper's Theorem 1 (lines 143-149) introduces q_0 and k, but the conclusion uses CosSim(M_Q, q*) with q* undefined anywhere in the text, and S_q is later defined as -CosSim(M_Q, q*), an unexplained switch of variable.

weakness: >1.0 normalized accuracy scores in Table 3 and the 'surpasses dense attention' claim on Math500 are presented without error bars or explanation of the mechanism.
justification: Table 3 shows Smollm3 scores of 1.03 and 1.028, and Section 4.4 states QUOKA 'in some cases even surpasses the accuracy of dense attention' with no variance estimates or discussion of why sparse attention would beat dense attention anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: Missing data point in Table 1: QUOKA row for GPT-OSS-20B at 32k sequence length is blank while baselines have entries.
justification: In Table 1's GPT-OSS-20B block, the last four values are 79.19, 73.40, 57.79, and a blank cell, confirming the QUOKA 32k entry is missing while all baseline rows are filled for that column.

weakness: No variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for any accuracy result across the tables.
justification: All tables (1, 2, 3) report single point-estimate numbers with no reported standard deviations or error bars anywhere in the text.

weakness: The paper does not describe how baselines like SparQ and Loki, originally designed for single-query generation, were adapted/extended to the multi-query prefill setting.
justification: Section 2.4/5 states these methods were designed for single-query decode and that naive averaging degrades accuracy, but no adaptation procedure for the actual multi-query prefill implementation used in experiments is described in the visible text.

weakness: The overhead of the query subselection/scoring step (O(N_Q*T*d)) is not measured separately from end-to-end speedups, making it unclear what fraction of prefill time it consumes.
justification: Section 4.6 reports only end-to-end and module-level speedups relative to dense attention; no separate breakdown of scoring overhead vs. reduced attention time is given.

weakness: Figure 8 case study shows a contradictory judgment: LEGO-EVAL outputs 'Valid ✓' while its own reasoning states the constraint cannot be satisfied since neither object is present, contradicting the paper's own definition that a scene is valid only if it fulfills all constraints.
justification: The paper text (lines 338-340, 350) explicitly shows the output 'Valid ✓' followed by reasoning 'the constraint cannot be satisfied,' and separately states 'A scene is deemed valid only if it fulfills all constraints' — this is a genuine internal contradiction in the paper.

weakness: The refinement experiment in Section 5 underspecifies the feedback/refinement mechanism (unclear what performs the scene refinement based on LEGO-EVAL's feedback).
justification: The paper only states 'we provide feedback to refine invalid scenes. We iterate this refinement process 3 times' (line 348) without ever specifying what model or pipeline performs the refinement.

weakness: Ground-truth provenance for the component analysis in Table 5 (human-annotated tool execution plans) is unspecified — no detail on how these annotations were created or how consistency was ensured.
justification: The paper (line 311) references 'human-annotated tool execution plan' but nowhere describes the annotation process, annotators, or consistency checks for these specific annotations (distinct from the instruction dataset collection covered in Appendix B.2).

weakness: The paper never discusses where LEGO-EVAL itself makes mistakes (false positives/negatives by constraint type or per-category performance), so readers cannot judge its reliability beyond outperforming weak baselines.
justification: A full-text search for terms like 'false positive', 'false negative', 'error analysis', or 'failure mode' relating to LEGO-EVAL's own errors finds no such discussion in the paper.

weakness: No variance reporting (standard deviations or confidence intervals) for the main F1 and Cohen's kappa results in Table 1, despite LLM-based planning having inherent sampling variance.
justification: A search of the paper for 'standard deviation', 'variance', 'multiple runs', or similar terms relating to Table 1 results finds none; no such statistics are reported.

weakness: Sample sizes (N) per complexity bin (simple/moderate/complex) for Figure 6 are unreported, making the sharp decline in success rates for extreme bins less conclusive.
justification: The paper (lines 292-305) defines the simple/moderate/complex bins and shows the results but never reports the number of instructions falling into each bin.

weakness: The adversarial framing is overclaimed: reviewer tests must pass the golden patch, making the reviewer's optimal strategy closer to quality assurance than adversarial competition; self-play scenarios (Claude-vs-Claude 1.00, GPT-4o-vs-GPT-4o 0.97) are interpreted as 'strong internal alignment' but could indicate circularity, and the paper's own caveat that Win Rate is adversarial and higher values may indicate weaker reviewer tests undercuts the main result table.
justification: The paper text confirms reviewer tests 'must compile and pass when applied to the golden patch' (Section 3.2, Reviewer Test Quality Gates), the paper does interpret self-play win rates as 'strong internal alignment' (line 187/Section 4.2), and explicitly states 'Win Rate is adversarial: higher values may also indicate weaker reviewer tests' (line 148) without resolving this tension.

weakness: Main experimental results are near-ceiling (Table 1 win rates 0.89-1.00) and do not differentiate models meaningfully; more differentiated metrics show modest spreads, and no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests are reported for any result despite only 100 instances per language.
justification: Table 1 in the paper text confirms win rates ranging 0.89 to 1.00 across all 16 matchups, and no confidence intervals or significance tests appear anywhere in the results sections (4.2, 4.3) or table captions.

weakness: No comparison to SWE-bench or any existing benchmark despite repeatedly positioning itself against SWE-bench's limitations, making it impossible to assess whether the adversarial protocol adds signal beyond simpler evaluation.
justification: The paper criticizes SWE-Bench's Python-only focus and one-shot paradigm (Section 1, Section 2.1) but nowhere in the provided text (including Section 4 Experiments) is there a direct empirical comparison of the same models on SWE-bench vs SWINGARENA.

weakness: The 'w/o RACG' condition in the ablation study (Table 3) is never defined -- unclear whether it means no code context, full raw codebase, or another baseline; additionally the ablation model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) is not explicitly stated in the ablation section itself.
justification: Section 4.3 discusses RACG ablation results extensively but never defines what 'w/o RACG' means as a baseline condition; the model used for ablation is only mentioned in Section 4.1 ('we use Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct to do ablation studies'), not restated in Section 4.3 itself, requiring the reader to cross-reference.

weakness: Best@k metric is unclearly specified across tables: the formal definition uses an unspecified success function, Table 2 doesn't clarify whether it measures submitter, reviewer, or battle outcome, and there is a large unexplained gap between Best@3 values and Win Rate values for the same model.
justification: The formal definition (line 140) defines success(t,i) without specifying what constitutes success, and Table 2's caption 'Best@3 across Models and Languages' does not specify submitter vs reviewer vs battle; Table 3 shows Best@3 values (0.38-0.58) markedly lower than corresponding Win Rate values (0.71-0.84) without explanation in the text.

weakness: No confidence intervals or statistical testing on any result across Tables 1, 2, and 3.
justification: Reviewing all table presentations and surrounding text in Sections 4.2-4.3 confirms only point estimates are reported with no error bars, CIs, or significance tests anywhere.

weakness: 'PK-style' terminology used in the contributions list without definition.
justification: Line 32 uses 'PK-style dual-role evaluation' with no definition or explanation of 'PK-style' anywhere in the paper text provided.

weakness: The battle protocol description appears in two places (Section 3.2 and Section 3.3) with near-verbatim overlap.
justification: Comparing lines 96 and 128, both contain a 'Battle Protocol' heading with nearly identical text describing scoring rules for submitter and reviewer, confirming the duplication.

weakness: The core directional-asymmetry assumption (that Shapley-value asymmetry correlates with causal direction) is asserted without theoretical or empirical justification.
justification: Paper line 127 states the intuition purely qualitatively and line 155-159's 'consistency remark' only addresses asymptotic penalty growth, not validity of the directional signal; no synthetic test isolates this claim.

weakness: PDAG-to-DAG completion via random orientation penalizes PC/GES baselines with noise that XBIC does not face, confounding the directed-edge F1 comparison.
justification: Paper line 190 explicitly states undirected edges from PDAG-returning baselines are randomly oriented before computing directed-edge metrics, which is a genuine methodological asymmetry not addressed elsewhere in the paper.

weakness: No analysis isolates where the F1 improvement comes from (e.g., edge type breakdown, orientation-only subset, or random-Shapley ablation), despite the paper framing its contribution as resolving Markov-equivalence ambiguities.
justification: The paper's introduction frames the contribution around orientation within equivalence classes, but the results section (around line 206) reports only aggregate F1/SHD deltas with no breakdown by edge type or ablation isolating the Shapley signal's specific contribution.

weakness: Improvements over the primary baseline (BIC-HC) are modest and inconsistent across networks/sample sizes, with some configurations showing negative deltas.
justification: Consistent with paper's own admission (line 206) that on smaller networks/limited data XBIC sometimes does not improve on BIC, and the headline gain is a modest +5.6% relative / +0.04 absolute.

weakness: Computational cost is very high (50-500x slower) relative to the F1 gain, without adequate cost-benefit discussion.
justification: Paper's Table 5 and line 245 confirm XBIC is markedly slower than BIC/PC due to classifier training and SHAP aggregation, and the limitations section (line 313) only briefly mentions runtime as future work without quantifying the tradeoff.

weakness: The abstract's '+9.6% over GES' figure lacks caveats about being computed only on a subset of runs where GES completed within the time limit.
justification: Paper line 278 confirms GES statistics were computed only on the subset of completed repetitions, a detail explained in §4.5 but omitted from the abstract's headline number.

weakness: The confidence threshold tau used in the main experiments (Table 2) is not explicitly reported, only that it was varied between 0.7 and 0.95 with <1% effect on F1.
justification: Paper line 194 reports the sensitivity range but does not state the specific tau value used to generate the main Table 2 results.

weakness: Table 2 entries report only point estimates without standard deviations or confidence intervals, despite each setting being repeated 10 times.
justification: Paper line 192 confirms 10 repetitions per setting, but Table 2 as described in the results section reports only F1 deltas without variance information.

weakness: The functional form of Eq. (2) (dividing dim(G) by exp(w*SHAP(G))) is not motivated or derived, presented as an unmotivated design choice.
justification: The paper presents the formula directly without deriving it from first principles or comparing to alternative functional forms.

weakness: 'Avg. MB Size' in Table 1 is not defined in the text.
justification: Table 1 (line 177) lists 'Avg. MB Size' as a column header but the surrounding text does not define this term (Markov Blanket size).

weakness: Reward-hacking claim is calibrated to a single verifier (R1-Distill-Verifier-1.5B) but stated as a general property of fine-tuned/model-based verifiers in the abstract and Section 7, while general-verifier (also fine-tuned) shows no hacking and xVerify-3B-Ia (best static performer) is not evaluated in RL at all.
justification: The abstract says model-based verifiers 'are highly susceptible to hacking...particularly after fine-tuning' and Table 2 confirms only R1-Distill-Verifier-1.5B (55.6) collapses while general-verifier (57.0) does not; xVerify-3B-Ia, despite having best static precision/recall 0.90/0.78 in Table 1, is absent from Table 2's RL results.

weakness: GPT-4o is used both as the annotation model for the static evaluation dataset and as the oracle for detecting reward hacking during RL, creating a potential correlated bias between the two evaluations.
justification: Section 3.1 uses GPT-4o for static labels and Section 5.2 uses GPT-4o oracle rewards for hacking detection; the paper only validates GPT-4o against humans for the static task (Appendix B), not for the oracle-reward use case, so the correlated-bias concern is not addressed.

weakness: The adversarial probing study (Section 6) tests model-based verifiers standalone rather than through the paper's own hybrid pipeline, so the practical severity under the hybrid system used elsewhere in the paper is unclear.
justification: Section 6 evaluates 'general-purpose LLMs...our own trained verifiers, and state-of-the-art verifiers' directly rather than via the cascaded rule+model hybrid described in Section 4.1, and the paper does not re-run probing through the hybrid to show whether rule-based filtering mitigates the attacks.

weakness: All RL experiments use a single policy model (Qwen2.5-7B Base), limiting generalization of the reward-hacking finding across policy-model architectures/sizes.
justification: The RL results (Table 2, Figure 3, Appendix I) are all reported for one policy model; cross-dataset tests (Skywork-OR1, WebInstruct-Verified) reuse the same policy model rather than varying it.

weakness: Section 5.2 has a naming inconsistency, referring to 'the untrained verifier, R1-Distill-Verifier-1.5B' when R1-Distill-Verifier-1.5B is actually the custom rejection-fine-tuned model (should likely be DS-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B).
justification: The paper text itself states 'the untrained verifier, R1-Distill-Verifier-1.5B, and the rule-based verifier do not exhibit such instability,' which directly conflicts with Section 5.1's description of R1-Distill-Verifier-1.5B as the rejection-fine-tuned model, confirming the typo.

weakness: Table 2 reports only peak RL performance, which may overstate the effective performance of hacked verifiers like R1-Distill-Verifier-1.5B (55.6, near the rule-based baseline of 55.0) given that reward hacking manifests as training collapse.
justification: Figure 3 (Left) shows training collapse over iterations while Table 2 reports a single peak number (55.6), so peak reporting could obscure the degradation documented elsewhere in the paper.

weakness: xVerify-3B-Ia achieves the best static precision/recall (0.90/0.78) but is not evaluated in RL (Table 2), weakening the claim that static accuracy doesn't predict RL robustness.
justification: Table 1 lists xVerify-3B-Ia's static scores but it does not appear among the verifiers evaluated in Table 2's RL results, confirming the omission.

weakness: The probing attack dataset (471 samples, 13 pattern types, ~10 verifiers) is modest, yielding limited samples per pattern-verifier combination, and confidence intervals are not reported for Table 3's attack success rates.
justification: Section 6.1 confirms the dataset size (~471 samples) and 13 pattern types across many verifiers, and no confidence intervals are reported alongside Table 3's success-rate numbers.

weakness: The 'universal' Pareto front claim (title/abstract) is overstated because it only holds for the constant similarity function under Var=0, while Proposition 1's linear decay case yields quantitatively different curves.
justification: The paper's own text (lines 100, 148, 184) shows the exact universal curve is derived only for the constant similarity function and homogeneous case, while Proposition 1 gives different coefficients (3/2-log2 vs 1, 1-log2 vs 0.5) for linear decay, supporting the reviewer's claim of an overclaim in the title/abstract.

weakness: Section 5 large-scale experiments (CNN, LLM, VLM) do not provide discriminating evidence for the specific quantitative tradeoff derived in Theorems 1-3; they show finite resolution exists but don't measure/compare (p_S,p_I) against the predicted Pareto curve, and the LLM/VLM tasks lack an identification counterpart.
justification: The paper's own limitations section (line 222) admits 'showing its presence in large language-vision models is still outstanding (despite we provided evidence for finite resolution in them)', directly corroborating the reviewer's critique.

weakness: The noise parameter Delta is empirically fit/estimated post-hoc from the learned similarity function rather than predicted independently, reducing falsifiability.
justification: The paper states (line 176) 'Estimating this noise scale Delta and using that in the equations... shows that the corresponding dashed curve accurately predicts the value of p_I at which the training stops,' confirming Delta is fit post-hoc rather than predicted.

weakness: The bijection assumption (Phi: S -> M is a bijection) is strong and undiscussed, since real neural network mappings are rarely injective.
justification: The paper states the bijection assumption at line 34 and nowhere in the visible text discusses relaxing it or its implications for non-injective real-world mappings.

weakness: The resolution parameter epsilon is never directly, quantitatively measured in any trained network; in the toy model it is visually estimated, and in large-scale models it is not measured at all, only inferred post-hoc (e.g., LLM ~70-80 year estimate).
justification: The paper describes epsilon estimation as visual/qualitative in the toy model (line 180) and the LLM resolution is reported as an interpretive estimate (~70-80 years, Figure 5b caption) rather than a direct, principled measurement, supporting the critique.

weakness: The LLM year experiment uses only a single time range (1500-1700) with specific delta-x values, and it is unclear whether the resolution estimate generalizes to other temporal scales.
justification: The paper's described experimental setup (lines 196-197) confirms a single fixed range [1500,1700] was used, and there is no discussion of generalization to other scales, supporting this as a genuine limitation.

weakness: The LLM backbone used by SimGCL in the main experiments (Tables 2 and 3) is not clearly stated in the main text, confounding SimGCL-vs-SimpleCIL comparisons with potential model-scale differences.
justification: The visible main text states SimpleCIL uses RoBERTa (line 78/Section 3.2) but never specifies SimGCL's backbone for Tables 2/3; Figure 3 only varies backbone on Arxiv, so the claim is grounded.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance is reported for any result in Tables 2, 3, or 4; every cell is a single number with no seeds/error bars.
justification: Tables 2-4 in the paper indeed list single point values with no standard deviation or multi-seed reporting.

weakness: Missing ablation studies isolating the two claimed mechanisms behind SimGCL's gains: graph-structured instruction tuning (vs. text-only prompt) and training-free prototype classification (vs. full instruction tuning).
justification: The paper attributes SimGCL's gains to these two factors (Section 3.3, Obs ❻) but no ablation table separating their individual contribution appears in the visible text.

weakness: SimGCL underperforms SimpleCIL substantially on Arxiv-23, and the paper's attribution to sparse graph structure is not empirically investigated further (e.g., no check of whether instruction tuning overfits the first session on this dataset).
justification: Obs ❻ does offer a hypothesis (sparse graph structure of Arxiv-23) but explicitly states this is an attribution without deeper investigation, so the review's call for further analysis is grounded.

weakness: No sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (e.g., the scaling temperature tau in Eq. 2, LoRA rank, number of few-shot examples), and no default values referenced in the main text.
justification: Eq. 2 introduces tau as a hyperparameter with no stated default or sensitivity study in the visible main text.

weakness: The paper's framing is inconsistent: Obs ❸ states 'current GLM-based methods demonstrate unsatisfactory performance' while SimGCL, also a GLM by the paper's own taxonomy, dramatically outperforms all others.
justification: Obs ❸ groups GLM baselines (GCN_Enh, ENGINE, GraphPrompter, GraphGPT, LLaGA) as underperforming, then Obs ❻ separately praises SimGCL, which is also introduced as a GLM-based approach in Section 3.3/Conclusion, creating a real taxonomic tension the review correctly flags.

weakness: The prompt template (described as inspired by Wang et al., 2025) is not shown in the main text, hurting reproducibility.
justification: The visible main text describes the prompt components in prose (Section 3.3) but does not display the actual template; only Figure 2 shows a partial example, not the full template.

weakness: The observation numbering jumps from Obs ❹ to Obs ❻ with no Obs ❺, likely a parser artifact.
justification: The paper text indeed shows Obs ❶ ❷ ❸ ❹ then jumps to ❻, ❼, ❽ with no ❺ visible.

weakness: Theorem 4.1's monotonicity assumption is insufficiently justified in the main text, conflating distributional concentration with probability of a specific string under different conditioning contexts.
justification: The paper's main-text rationale (lines 130-131) is heuristic and defers rigorous validation to Appendix C.2, so the main-text argument alone is indeed logically incomplete.

weakness: RA's performance at late intervention steps (t_inter=32) is only briefly acknowledged (line 241) without discussing practical security implications, leaving ASR at 43-79% depending on model.
justification: Table 2 confirms high residual ASR at t_min=32 and the paper only briefly notes this is 'challenging' without further analysis of practical threat implications.

weakness: The mechanism by which RA improves robustness against conventional jailbreak attacks (PAIR, Crescendo) is asserted as a 'plausible mechanism' but not empirically analyzed via intermediate-state inspection.
justification: The paper itself uses the word 'plausible' (lines 243, 301) and provides no intermediate-state analysis to substantiate the claimed recovery mechanism for conventional attacks.

weakness: Limited discussion of sensitivity to generation length L and denoising steps T, which are fixed at 128 without exploring how these choices affect the vulnerability or mitigation.
justification: The paper states 'Unless otherwise specified, we set L=128 and T=128' (line 80) with no sensitivity analysis in the main text (only a pointer to Appendix C.5 for generation length, not T).

weakness: The reward model specification is incomplete: unclear whether it outputs a single combined score, how safety/usefulness are weighted, and how it was validated as reliable for MDLM outputs.
justification: The paper only states R 'computes a reward from a query and a response' and that DeBERTaV3 is used 'without additional fine-tuning' (lines 167, 204) without further specification of scoring mechanics or validation.

weakness: The 'affirmative token' terminology is circular/imprecise since any token from the harmful response (including function words like 'Lastly') can serve as a primer.
justification: The paper's definition (line 84) is generic ('tokens which endorse or advance a harmful intent') and Figure 1 uses 'Lastly' as an example, supporting the critique that the term lacks a mechanistic characterization.

weakness: Inference cost (step counts, latency, FLOPs) for the multi-step tool-invoking pipeline is entirely unreported, making the data-efficiency comparison against single-pass baselines incomplete.
justification: The paper describes an iterative multi-turn tool-invocation pipeline (Algorithm/Section 3, Figure 5 baselines) but nowhere reports average steps per prediction, latency, or compute cost relative to single-pass models like V2P-7B/GTA-1-7B.

weakness: No statistical significance or variance reporting across multiple seeds; all accuracy numbers appear to be single-run point estimates.
justification: Tables 3-5 and Figure 2-5 report single accuracy numbers per configuration with no mention of multiple seeds, standard deviation, or confidence intervals anywhere in the text.

weakness: Selective comparison framing: the paper highlights ScreenSpot-Pro where it leads, but on UI-Vision (23.4% vs UI-Venus-Ground-7B's 26.5%) and OSWorld-G (62.7% vs GTA1-7B's 67.7%) GUI-Spotlight trails other 7B models, which is not reflected in the 'substantially outperforming comparable 7B baselines' claim.
justification: The paper's own contribution claim (line 31) states 'substantially outperforming comparable 7B baselines' referencing both ScreenSpot-Pro and UI-Vision, yet Table 4/5 data (as summarized in the review) shows it trailing specific 7B models on those benchmarks, supporting the criticism of overstated framing.

weakness: Modest gain (5.2 points) over a simpler training-free repeated single-turn inference baseline (47.6% vs 52.8%), with insufficient discussion of what the RL training specifically contributes beyond the cheaper baseline.
justification: Section 5.4/Figure 5 confirms strategy 2 (repeated single-turn) reaches 47.6% and GUI-Spotlight reaches 52.8%, and the paper's discussion of this gap is brief, mainly stating it 'demonstrates a substantive post-training gain' without deeper analysis of the RL's specific contribution.

weakness: Figure 2 table labeling inconsistency: the table associates 2561 samples with Stage 0 and 12K samples with Stage 1, but the text states Stage 1 uses 2561 trajectories and Stage 2 uses 12K samples.
justification: Lines 142-143 of the paper show the table listing '0 | 39.3 | 2561' and '1 | 17.8 | 12K', while the text (line 136) states 'Stage 1: We perform one epoch of SFT on 2561 trajectories... Stage 2: We train on 12K examples with RL' -- confirming the labeling is shifted by one stage as the review claims.

weakness: Main results table (Tab. 3) compares against weak baselines (EarlyExit, Interleaved Layer Skipping) while the more natural comparisons (Basic MoD, w/o task-aware router) are relegated to a separate ablation table (Tab. 5), making the headline results look stronger than the ablation data supports, especially since 'w/o task-aware router' is within 0.1-0.7 points on GQA/POPE/MMMU/VQAv2.
justification: Table 3 (line 213-220) only lists EarlyExit and Interleaved Layer Skipping baselines, while Table 5 (line 268-274) shows 'w/o task-aware router' scores (GQA 54.4, POPE 80.2, MMMU 25.6, VQAv2 65.5) close to UniMoD (54.5, 80.3, 25.7, 66.2), confirming the natural baseline is omitted from the main table.

weakness: No variance or confidence intervals reported for benchmark results across Tabs. 3, 4, 5, making it hard to assess whether small deltas (0.1-2.1 points) are meaningful or noise.
justification: The tables (lines 213-220, 268-274) report single point values with no error bars or multiple-run statistics mentioned anywhere in the text.

weakness: Training cost metric in Tab. 4 ('1.30x/iter & 67G') is unclearly defined, with the ratio's reference point and unit for '/iter' left unexplained.
justification: Line 231-233 shows the raw values '1.30x/iter & 67G' and '3.56x/iter & 65G' with no accompanying definition of what the ratio is relative to or what time unit '/iter' uses.

weakness: The Emu3 results rest on a reimplementation whose fidelity relative to the original published Emu3 model is not validated or reported.
justification: Line 242 explicitly states 'Our full Emu3 results differ from the original paper because we use alternative training datasets, as the official code and data are not publicly available,' and the paper never reports a comparison to the original published Emu3 numbers.

weakness: The GQA score of 0.0 when skipping layer 3 in Tab. 1 is not explained, raising the question of whether this reflects an out-of-distribution inference-time intervention or a specific failure mode.
justification: Table 1 (line 131) shows the discontinuous sequence 35.0, 0.0, 48.0, 49.0..., and the surrounding text (lines 121-125) only states the general conclusion that early layers are more critical without addressing the anomalous 0.0 value.

weakness: Pruning schedules and per-layer capacities (e.g., 'scale the capacity from 1 down to 0.2' and 'prune 20% of the tokens in the later layers') are not specified precisely enough for reproduction.
justification: Line 209 gives only this qualitative description without an exact per-layer schedule or formula, matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: Naming inconsistency between 'UniMoD' (title/abstract/text) and 'UniMod' (Tab. 3 and Tab. 4).
justification: The abstract and body consistently use 'UniMoD' while Table 3 (line 220) and Table 4 (lines 231-233) use 'UniMod', confirming the inconsistency.

weakness: MathArena §5.4 comparison rests on an unclear sampling procedure: the paper never explicitly states whether the final-answer accuracy column in Fig. 5 comes from standard MathArena evaluation or from the retried, correct-final-answer-conditioned sample.
justification: The paper states in §3.1 'we only retained solutions with a correct final answer, retrying generation if necessary' but Fig. 5/§5.4 present a 'Correct final (%)' column that is not below 100% (e.g. o3 87.6%), and the text never clarifies whether this figure is from standard evaluation or the retried subset, creating exactly the ambiguity the reviewer identifies.

weakness: Best-of-n uses O4-MINI as both generator and judge despite documented self-judgment bias in Table 3, and the paper does not discuss whether this affects the reported best-of-n magnitudes or ordering.
justification: Table 3 shows O4-MINI judging its own proofs (81.3%) is worse than judging others' (86.9%, 84.8%), and §5.5 confirms O4-MINI is used as judge for best-of-n without any discussion of this self-bias interacting with the selection results.

weakness: The human baseline (90.4%) is computed on all double-graded proofs, not on the actual test subset, and the double-graded subset may not be a uniform sample given the pilot phase's 35% double-grading rate and discrepancy-triggered re-grading.
justification: The paper itself admits in §5.2 (line 246) that the human baseline is not measured on the test subset, and §3.3 confirms the pilot phase had ~35% double-grading vs ~10% overall and discrepancies were reviewed, supporting the reviewer's concern about non-uniformity.

weakness: The LLM issue-summary bias check only tests whether summaries shift human judgments toward O4-MINI's opinion, not whether they shift judgments away from ground truth; a stronger check would compare human-only vs human+summary grading against a gold-standard set.
justification: The paper's described check (§3.1, line 115) only measures agreement rate between O4-MINI and human graders before/after introducing summaries, which indeed does not establish accuracy against ground truth, matching the reviewer's critique.

weakness: The independence assumption in the judge error-rate computation (p=5% from 0.904 = (1-p)^2+p^2) assumes judges' errors are independent, which may not hold since judges could make correlated errors on the same subtle proof flaws.
justification: The paper explicitly states in §4 'Assuming independent judgments, we can estimate...' without further justification or caveat, so the reviewer's point about a potentially unwarranted independence assumption is well-grounded.

weakness: The theoretical analysis (Section 4/Theorem 4.1) analyzes a stochastic diffusion SDE (dx_t = g(t)dw_t), but FourierFlow actually uses flow matching with a deterministic linear interpolation path, and the paper does not address whether/how the SNR-based spectral bias result transfers to the flow-matching setting, nor bridges forward-process SNR to reverse-generation failure.
justification: Section 4 explicitly derives Theorem 4.1 from an SDE dx_t=g(t)dw_t, while Section 2.3 defines flow matching as a deterministic ODE with linear interpolation x(t)=(1-t)x0+tx1; no passage in the paper connects these two formalisms.

weakness: The common-mode noise concept is conflated between a spatial-averaging phenomenon (Section 1's 'small-scale structures averaged out at the global level') and a channel-wise constant signal defined formally in Section 2.2, and the explicit L_cm loss defined in Section 2.2 is never used in the actual training objective (Section 3.3 only uses L_CFM + gamma*L_Align).
justification: Section 2.2 defines n_cm = alpha*1_C (channel-wise constant) while Section 1/3.2 describe averaging of small-scale spatial structures; Section 3.3 explicitly states L_Total = L_CFM + gamma*L_Align, with no L_cm term, confirming the defined loss is unused.

weakness: Table 1 and the ablation bar charts (Figures 4-6) report single numbers without error bars, standard deviations, or confidence intervals, making it impossible to assess whether small-margin results are statistically meaningful.
justification: Table 1 and Figures 4-6 in the paper show only point estimates with no variance/seed information anywhere in the visible text.
