justification: Paper explicitly frames itself around 'solving complex, multi-step problems' (line 13) and 'solve more difficult tasks that require scaling inference-time computation' (line 312), yet only evaluates perplexity, LAMBADA, HellaSwag, BLiMP, PIQA, none of which are multi-step reasoning tasks, and the paper itself admits this gap in limitations (line 322).

weakness: Parameter-matched and FLOPs-matched claims in Table 1 are stated without supporting evidence (no parameter counts, FLOPs measurements, or wall-clock comparisons).
justification: Table 1 caption asserts 'parameter-matched' and 'roughly FLOPs-matched' but the paper text nowhere gives actual parameter counts or FLOPs numbers to substantiate this.

weakness: Overstated characterization of zero-shot results ('across most zero-shot evaluations, our approach outperforms baselines') when BLiMP underperforms Copy baselines in most settings.
justification: Table 1 shows Thoughtbubbles trails Copy-3/Copy-5 on BLiMP in most rows (e.g., 78.8 vs 80.5 at 319M OWT, 67.4 vs 73.3 at 772M peS2o), confirming the overstatement, though paper does note this in one sentence (lines 220-223).

weakness: Gradient flow through the hard top-k operation is not specified (straight-through estimator, REINFORCE, soft relaxation, etc.).
justification: Equations 4-6 define a hard top-k selection but the methods section never states how gradients propagate through it; only a vague mention of a 'top-K gradient bottleneck' appears in limitations without describing the training mechanism.

weakness: The Copy-3/Copy-5 baseline is a weak/naive instantiation of non-adaptive parallel computation, only copying and taking rightmost residual, not maintaining parallel streams throughout all layers.
justification: The paper itself calls it 'naive' (line 169) and describes it as simply copying the input residual and taking the rightmost for decoding, supporting the reviewer's characterization.

weakness: No error bars, confidence intervals, or variance measures reported given modest gains.
justification: Table 1 and the text present only single point estimates for perplexity and zero-shot scores with no reported variance or statistical testing anywhere in the paper.

weakness: The BLiMP negative result is under-analyzed, dismissed with a single sentence despite being systematic.
justification: Lines 220-223 give only one sentence of speculative explanation ('pruned dynamic parallel computation may not be as helpful for syntax matches') without further investigation despite BLiMP underperformance appearing in most configurations.

weakness: Basic statistics about fork allocation (fraction of tokens forked, forks per token, variation across layers) are missing.
justification: Figure 5 only shows an aggregated entropy-vs-fork-count heatmap; the paper text nowhere reports fraction of tokens forked, mean forks per token, or per-layer allocation statistics.

weakness: The entropy-computation 'concave parabolic relationship' in Figure 5 is asserted without statistical support (no curve fit, regression, or correlation reported), and the post-hoc explanation is speculative.
justification: Section 5's discussion of the concave relationship (lines 262-266) is qualitative description with a speculative explanation ('edges of clauses or coreferences') and no reported statistical test or fit metric.

weakness: The headline claim "consistently outperforms all baselines" is contradicted — EmbodiedMAE RGB ties SPA RGB at 73.0% average on MetaWorld, and xArm RGB-only is only 'comparable' per the paper's own caption.
justification: Table 1 shows EmbodiedMAE RGB average of 73.0 identical to SPA RGB 73.0, and Figure 8 caption text explicitly says 'comparable performance to SOTA baselines' on xArm RGB-only, directly contradicting the 'consistently outperforms all baselines' claim in Finding 1.

weakness: No statistical significance or variance reported (no error bars, std, CIs, multiple seeds); real-world tasks use only 10 trials.
justification: The paper reports only single point success-rate numbers throughout Table 1, Figure 6, Figure 8 with no variance/seed information, and Figure 8 caption confirms 'Each task is evaluated across 10 trials.'

weakness: LIBERO results are shown only as learning curves (Figure 6) with no table of final numerical success rates in the main text.
justification: Section 3.3 explicitly states 'We report learning curves on LIBERO in Figure 6' with no accompanying table of final LIBERO success rates in the main body.

weakness: No ablation isolating multi-modal pre-training contribution from dataset/DINOv2-initialization effects (no single-modal RGB-only MAE trained on DROID-3D).
justification: The ablations in Section 3.5 cover masking ratio, feature alignment, loss ratio, and policy model, but nowhere is a DROID-3D-trained RGB-only MAE baseline reported to isolate multi-modal gains from data/init effects.

weakness: Depth quality comparison in Figure 2 is only qualitative, with no quantitative metrics.
justification: Figure 2 and its caption present only visual/qualitative comparisons (Low-Quality, Inconsistent labels) with no numerical accuracy or temporal-consistency metrics reported anywhere in the text.

weakness: Computational cost of pre-training (GPU-hours) is underreported, though data processing time is given.
justification: The paper states 'nearly 500 hours of processing time' for DROID-3D construction (Section 2.1) but no GPU-hours or compute cost figure is given anywhere for the actual EmbodiedMAE pre-training/distillation.

weakness: Inconsistency between claiming the Giant model is trained 'from scratch' (line 85) while the encoder is initialized from DINOv2 pre-trained weights (line 71).
justification: Section 2.2 states the ViT is initialized directly from DINOv2 pre-trained weights, while Section 2.4 says the Giant model is trained 'from scratch,' a direct textual inconsistency.

weakness: MRH receives disproportionate structural weight relative to its empirical support (occupies whole section, title, abstract but main-text evidence is thin, deferred to appendix figure)
justification: The paper itself states 'Empirical evidences' section cites only Fig. 26 for the three MRH tests, and the abstract/title/Section 6 do foreground MRH prominently, supporting the imbalance claim.

weakness: The claim that concept geometry is only weakly shaped by co-activation is not properly supported and is undercut by the paper's own math (Footnote 1 shows a mathematical floor on the correlation, but the actual correlation value is never reported)
justification: Footnote 1 in the paper indeed proves the correlation is 'guaranteed to be positive' as a mathematical artifact, yet the main text only says the correlation is 'weak' without giving a numeric value or comparing to this floor.

weakness: The SAE's sparsity prior conflates the tool with the object of study; no control (e.g., SAE trained on random features) is run to check whether observed geometric departures are DINOv2-specific or SAE artifacts
justification: The paper acknowledges 'stepping beyond the SAE lens' but nowhere in the provided text is a random-feature control SAE experiment described.

weakness: The alignment score, the quantitative backbone of Section 3's task-recruitment analysis, is fully deferred to Appendix C.1 with no summary definition in the main text
justification: The paper explicitly states 'the precise definition and its theoretical justification are deferred to Appendix C.1' without giving even a brief in-text summary.

weakness: Reconstruction fidelity (R^2 > 88%) is reported without specifying whether it is training or held-out data
justification: The paper states 'Training with Adam for 50 epochs yields R^2 > 88% reconstruction fidelity' with no mention of a train/test split for this metric.

weakness: No comparison to simpler decomposition methods (PCA, NMF, ICA) for the same analyses to determine if the SAE provides unique insight
justification: The paper uses PCA only for a separate per-image token visualization (Figure 5/Section 5), not as a comparative baseline against the SAE-based task-recruitment or geometry analyses of Sections 3-4.

weakness: Variance across SAE training seeds is not reported for key geometric patterns (coherence, spectral decay, task alignment)
justification: The paper cites the stable SAE method for reproducibility but the provided text contains no seed-variance ablation for these metrics.

weakness: The generative consistency loss (L_GC) is framed as attenuating hallucination, but Eq. 14/16 shows the regularization loss pulls the 3DGS render toward the diffusion output precisely in the highest-discrepancy regions, which would propagate hallucinated content rather than suppress it.
justification: The paper's own equations (14)-(16) define M_r as marking pixels with the largest gap between I_p and diffusion output, and L_reg pulls I_p toward that diffusion output in exactly those regions, which is inconsistent with the stated goal of suppressing hallucination (Section 3.2.2, lines 153-154, 173-175).

weakness: The CPG module's training protocol (training data, loss function, optimizer, learning rate, number of epochs, or whether it is pre-trained externally) is not specified in the main paper text.
justification: Section 3.1.1 describes the CPG architecture (FPS, DGCNN, Transformer encoder-decoder, FoldingNet) in detail but the visible main text never states how this network is trained, and no such details are given in the reproducibility statement either.

weakness: Table 3 (Shiny dataset) omits several baseline methods that appear in Tables 1 and 2 (e.g., CAT3D, BinoGS, ReconFusion, IPSM, MuRF, DNGaussian, ReconX) without explanation.
justification: Comparing Table 3 to Tables 1 and 2 in the paper confirms the Shiny table only includes RegNeRF, FreeNeRF, SparseNeRF, 3DGS, FSGS and GenCoGS, with no stated reason for the reduced baseline set.

weakness: None of the main tables report standard deviations or per-scene breakdowns, so small reported improvements (e.g., +0.003 SSIM) could be within noise.
justification: Tables 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6 in the paper report only point estimates with no variance or per-scene statistics, so the reviewer's concern about noise on small margins is grounded in what is actually shown.

weakness: The GCGO phase only runs for the last 1,000 of 5,000 iterations (m=4,000), and the paper does not discuss sensitivity to this choice or whether a longer GCGO phase would increase hallucination.
justification: Section 4 states m=4,000 out of 5,000 total iterations, and no ablation or discussion of varying m appears in the visible main text.

weakness: The perturbed camera trajectory's 'see-saw effect' between covering unobserved regions and triggering hallucination is acknowledged by the authors but only addressed with a single fixed hyperparameter (A=2.0), leaving the method potentially brittle across scenes with varying unobserved area.
justification: The paper itself states in Section 4.3 that A=2.0 is set as 'a balanced trade-off in our experiments' based on Figure 8, with no per-scene adaptation or robustness analysis provided, supporting the reviewer's brittleness concern.

weakness: Figure 3 reports implausible correlation coefficients (Pearson r=1.00, Spearman ρ=1.00) while describing 'realistic scatter', with insufficient precision/data disclosure, undermining the correlation evidence for the geometry-performance claim.
justification: The paper's Figure 3 caption text (line 228/232) explicitly reports r=1.00 and ρ=1.00 for multiple panels alongside claims of 'realistic scatter' and no disclosure of data point counts or higher precision, exactly as the reviewer describes.

weakness: No variance estimates for the primary classification results in Table 1, unlike Table 2 which reports ± intervals.
justification: Table 1 (lines 151-166) reports only point estimates for MTIL/X-TAIL, while Table 2 (lines 170-180) reports mean ± std, confirming the inconsistency the reviewer identifies.

weakness: Potential circularity in the geometry→performance correlation, since the sweep in Figure 3 varies settings that directly change the optimization objective, so drift and performance drop are consequences of the same intervention rather than drift causing the drop.
justification: The paper's own description (lines 222-224) confirms the sweep varies certificate size, EMAs, invariance strength, whitening, pairing, LoRA capacity/LR, and loss terms — the same interventions that change both geometry and the training objective, supporting the reviewer's causal-confound concern.

weakness: Zero-shot PD metric is mentioned in the evaluation protocol but missing from the main results tables (Tables 1 and 2), appearing only in the prompt invariance stress test.
justification: Line 147 states PD is reported per protocol, but Tables 1 and 2 (lines 151-180) contain no PD column; PD appears only in Figure 4 discussion (lines 234-240), confirming the reviewer's observation.

weakness: No discussion of limitations in the conclusion (Section 5).
justification: The Conclusion section (lines 244-246) is truncated/brief and contains no limitations discussion, matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: Inflated claims inconsistent with evidence: abstract says 'comparable' but intro/discussion say 'outperforms', while SEVA beats ARSS on SSIM and FID.
justification: Paper text (lines 88, 281) says 'out-performs current state-of-the-art methods' while Table 1 shows SEVA has better SSIM (0.670 vs 0.624) and FID (46.98 vs 47.60 on Re10K, 33.16 vs 47.76 on ACID), supporting the mixed-results critique.

weakness: Camera autoencoder is not ablated against simpler conditioning mechanisms.
justification: Section 4.3 only contains ablations on token order permutation and tokenization strategy (video vs VQ); no ablation removes or simplifies the camera autoencoder.

weakness: Error accumulation analysis (Figure 6) excludes SEVA, the strongest competitor, undermining the 'better than all baselines' claim.
justification: Figure 6's legend lists LVSM, MotionCtrl, Ours, RayZer, ViewCrafter but not SEVA, even though SEVA is the closest competitor in Table 1.

weakness: Zero-shot DL3DV comparison excludes SEVA, so it only compares against weaker baselines.
justification: Table 1 caption confirms SEVA, ViewCrafter, and RayZer results on DL3DV are not reported since DL3DV was in SEVA's training data, leaving only MotionCtrl, LVSM as comparisons (plus ViewCrafter/RayZer excluded too, but SEVA absence is the key gap noted).

weakness: VidTok tokenizer training status (frozen vs fine-tuned) is unspecified.
justification: Section 3.2.1/4.1 states 'We apply VidTok (Tang et al., 2024) as our video tokenizer' without ever stating whether it is frozen or fine-tuned during ARSS training.

weakness: Notation issues in Eq. 5 (d used for two different things, o undefined) and Eq. 7 (missing target argument in CE).
justification: Eq. 5 text literally states 'd is the normalized camera ray direction, d is the momentum term' (duplicate use of d) and o is never defined; Eq. 7 shows CE with only one bracketed argument unlike Eq. 3's two arguments.

weakness: Parallel decoding claim is unsupported by any experiments or latency measurements.
justification: Section 3.2.3 states 'randomly shuffle tokens... allows parallel decoding' citing prior work, but no experiment or latency result anywhere in the paper substantiates this for ARSS.

weakness: Tokenizer ablation (Table 3) conflates tokenization type (video vs image) with quantization method (FSQ vs VQ), so it's unclear which change drives the improvement.
justification: Table 3 only compares 'VQ' (VQ image tokenizer) vs 'ours' (video tokenizer with FSQ), varying both dimensions simultaneously with no isolated ablation.

weakness: No inference speed or latency reported for the sequential 4096-token AR generation.
justification: The paper reports training details (Section 4.1) but nowhere reports inference runtime or latency measurements for the AR sampling process.

weakness: The training protocol evaluates offline compression on expert (Rand vs NE) data, not true online RL, despite paper's introduction framing about online learning potential.
justification: The paper's intro claims potential for online learning, but Section 3.3 confirms GOEI is trained on pre-generated fixed Rand vs NE games and only mentions the interactive-learning gap briefly in the final discussion paragraph, supporting the review's point.

weakness: No evaluation of whether compressed states generalize across opponents other than NE.
justification: The paper only trains and tests against Rand vs NE (Section 3.3); no experiments against π_k or other opponents are reported, so this gap is real.

weakness: The Q-learning baseline is not informative because it is trained on the same offline pre-generated data rather than online interaction, making the comparison staged in GOEI's favor.
justification: Section 3.3 confirms both GOEI and Q-learning are trained on the same 300,000 pre-generated games, so the criticism about comparability is grounded in the paper's stated methodology.

weakness: The NE state count comparison (GOEI vs NE effective state numbers) is not apples-to-apples since they use different groupings (transition dynamics vs. equal expected reward), and the round-4 discrepancy (408 vs 69) is not discussed.
justification: The paper defines NE states via equal expected reward (lines 142-174) while GOEI states are defined via the state reduction model p(s_t|o_t) satisfying transition/reward prediction (Eq. 4); the paper does not address the round-4 discrepancy, supporting this critique.

weakness: The abstract's claim of "all possible observations (15,542)" is misleading because the actual full observation space is 28,477, and 15,542 is only the subset reachable under Rand vs NE play.
justification: Section 2.1 states the number of possible observations is 28,477 while Section 3.3 states only 15,542 are reachable under Rand vs NE; the abstract's wording could mislead readers, and this is explicitly confirmed by the paper's own numbers.

weakness: Metric-reliability tension: the paper argues standard metrics misreport success but main results (Tables 1-2) rely on these same metrics, and LaaJ evaluation is confined to a single setting (TOFU 10%, Llama 3.1 8B).
justification: Confirmed by paper: Fig 4c LaaJ evaluation is explicitly limited to TOFU 10% with Llama 3.1 8B (line 343), while Tables 1 and 2 use Truth Ratio/Probability/ROUGE and QA Accuracy without broader LaaJ validation.

weakness: BS-S lacks a controlled ablation isolating the belief mechanism from general data augmentation (e.g., comparison against random sequences or human-written paraphrases as augmentation).
justification: The paper describes BS-S as sampling high-confidence sequences to augment the forget set (Eq. 7) but nowhere in the visible text is there an ablation comparing belief-based augmentation against non-belief augmentation baselines; this is a genuine gap.

weakness: No variance estimates or significance tests on main results, making it hard to assess whether the 1-7 point margins are statistically reliable.
justification: Tables 1 and 2 report only point estimates with no standard deviations or confidence intervals visible anywhere in the paper text.

weakness: Theoretical analysis (Section 5) does not connect to experiments in a testable way; it never makes quantitative predictions like optimal lambda or k settings.
justification: Section 5's theorems (5.1-5.3) are purely qualitative characterizations of residual structure; no quantitative prediction of hyperparameters or residual magnitudes tied to experiments appears in the text.

weakness: Stop-gradient operator in BS-T (Eq. 5) is used without justification for whether it is necessary or what would change without it.
justification: Eq. 5 introduces sg[...] but the surrounding text only states its function (preventing gradient flow) without discussing necessity or ablating its removal.

weakness: Off-policy vs. on-policy BS-S is mentioned but not empirically compared, despite noting that on-policy violates AKG framework assumptions.
justification: Paper states in Section 5.2/line 198 area that on-policy BS-S violates the teacher-forcing assumption (discussed only qualitatively in Appx D.4 reference) but no experiment comparing off-policy vs on-policy effectiveness or cost appears in the main text.

weakness: Internal inconsistency in mass correction experiment: text says 2.0kg initial vs 0.1kg ground truth, but Figure 4 shows both lines starting at ~1.0kg and corrected value converging to ~0.85kg, which are irreconcilable numbers.
justification: The paper text (lines 220-221) explicitly states 2.0 kg vs ground truth 0.1 kg, while the Figure 4 caption describes initial mass constant at 1.00 kg and corrected mass dropping to ~0.85 kg - these are genuinely contradictory numbers within the paper itself.

weakness: Statistical evidence is too weak given n=10 trials per condition, with wide binomial confidence intervals, and the paper uses strong language ('significantly boosted', 'dramatic performance drop', 'catastrophic failure') without reporting confidence intervals or significance tests.
justification: The paper (Section 4.1.3-4.1.4) does use such phrasing for differences like 2/10 to 4/10 and 4/10 to 0/10 based on 10 trials, and no statistical tests or CIs are reported anywhere in the text provided.

weakness: LLM-MPPI interface is underspecified for reproducibility: missing prompt templates, output format, how contact strategy is generated from image/task description, how RAG memory embeds/retrieves, and how outer loop episode data is formatted for LLM diagnosis.
justification: The paper describes these components only conceptually (Sections 3.2, 3.4) without providing prompt templates or implementation specifics of the LLM outputs, supporting this critique.

weakness: VLA baseline comparison is framed too strongly; the paper's headline claim of significantly outperforming baselines obscures that CoRAL underperforms the human expert-designed cost baselines (e.g., T1: 4/10 vs 8/10; T6: 7/10 vs 9/10).
justification: Table 1 confirms CoRAL scores below Expert (FSM) on T1 and T6, and the paper's Section 4.1.1 does use strong language ('CoRAL significantly outperforms') primarily contrasting with VLA baselines while the expert comparison is more modest, supporting the critique of framing.

weakness: Randomization ranges for physical parameters (mass, friction, box dimension) are not reported.
justification: Line 155 states these are randomized but no ranges or distributions are given anywhere in the provided paper text.

weakness: VLM physical parameter estimation accuracy (mass, friction) is never evaluated against ground truth.
justification: The paper never reports quantitative accuracy of VLM's mass/friction estimates against ground-truth values anywhere in the text provided.

weakness: Reactive control augmentation (Eq. 7) conflates state and force feedback: the equation uses position error x_des - x_measured but the text describes it in terms of force/torque sensors, creating ambiguity about what K_f maps.
justification: Eq. 7 and its surrounding text (lines 126-130) do state the error term is 'calculated from real-time sensors (e.g., force/torque, proprioception)' while the equation notation (x_des - x_measured) suggests state/position error, which is a genuine ambiguity in the paper as written.

weakness: The explainability demonstration is a single qualitative example with no quantitative evaluation of diagnosis correctness or recovery success rate.
justification: Section 4.1.4's explainability discussion (lines 236-238) presents only one qualitative scenario with no aggregate statistics on diagnosis accuracy or recovery rate across trials.

weakness: No per-cycle timing or latency analysis is reported, which matters for a real-time control system.
justification: The paper reports overall task completion times but no breakdown of per-cycle latency for the LLM/VLM/MPPI pipeline anywhere in the provided text.

weakness: The 3rd-order vs. 4th-order ablation is confounded by parameter count/capacity, so the improvement attributed to decoupled structure could partly be due to extra capacity.
justification: The paper's ablation (lines 237-253, Figure 8) compares a 4th-order core tensor (8x8x64x64) against a 3rd-order core (8x8x128) without controlling for total parameter budget, and the paper does not provide a parameter-matched control, so the confound is real and not addressed.

weakness: The 'real-world deployment' claim is undersupported since the paper gives no description of how real-world data was collected, scene layouts, or whether a physical robot was used.
justification: Contribution 3 (line 28) claims real-world deployments validate the method, and Table 5 references 'Real-World 4/5', but the paper text nowhere describes data collection methodology, robot hardware, or physical deployment details.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance is reported across Tables 1-5; all results are single point estimates.
justification: Scanning Tables 1-5 in the paper text confirms only single numeric values are given with no standard deviation, confidence interval, or multi-seed reporting.

weakness: Negative forgetting rates for T14 (-3%) and T20 (-4%) in Table 2 are unexplained.
justification: Table 2 in the paper does show AllDayWalker with -3 and -4 values at T14/T20, and the paper provides no discussion or explanation of this counterintuitive result.

weakness: The claim that LoRA-based methods are 'inherently limited' to two hierarchical knowledge structures overstates the mathematical limitation of low-rank matrices, since a low-rank matrix isn't inherently incapable of multi-hierarchical representation.
justification: Lines 22 and 77 of the paper do use this 'inherently limited'/'restricts them to representing only two hierarchical knowledge structures' framing, which is an overclaim about a design choice rather than a strict mathematical impossibility, as the reviewer correctly notes.

weakness: The paper's repeated emphasis on 'post-treatment' selection as a structurally distinct challenge is not supported by the model, since the augmented DAG with S does not encode any temporal/structural distinction between pre- and post-treatment selection, and no concrete scenario is shown where the two produce different CI patterns.
justification: The paper text (lines 43-60) says S 'generally represent both pre-treatment selection ... and post-treatment selection' and then simply 'specializes' without providing a structural distinction or example contrasting the two cases.

weakness: The evaluation protocol for DAG Precision and DAG SHD is not specified: the output is an F-PAG with eight edge types/four marks, but the paper does not explain how this was mapped to a DAG for comparison against ground truth.
justification: Section 5.1 and the Figure 6 caption report DAG Precision/SHD without describing any mapping procedure from F-PAG edge types (square, triangle, circle marks) to a DAG.

weakness: The finite-sample CI test used in the experiments is not stated (e.g., Gaussian, kernel, HSIC, permutation), which is a reproducibility concern.
justification: Section 5.1 describes the data-generating process and metrics but never names the CI test implementation used for the simulations.

weakness: The real-world experiment (Section 5.2) is too thin in the main text, consisting of only three sentences with no quantitative results, deferring everything to the appendix and Figure 13.
justification: Section 5.2 in the paper is indeed a short paragraph of a few sentences with no quantitative table or statistic presented in the main body.

weakness: Only 10 random graphs per configuration were used for the simulation results, which is a low number of replications for stable conclusions.
justification: Figure 6's caption confirms 'All values are averaged over 10 graphs,' supporting the reviewer's factual claim, though this is a minor/subjective point about statistical power.

weakness: The mapping from the six CI pattern columns in Figure 4(i) to the six specific orientation rules/tuples in Algorithm 1 Step 2.2 is not made explicit, requiring the reader to reverse-engineer it.
justification: The paper text states orientation rules are 'summarized in Figure 4' (line 249) but Algorithm 1's Step 2.2 pseudocode lists conditions without an explicit table connecting each CI tuple to the Figure 4 column labels.

weakness: The paper does not discuss the computational complexity/tractability of the AllPaths enumeration in Step 2.1, despite paths between two nodes potentially being exponential in number.
justification: Step 2.1 of Algorithm 1 enumerates conditioning sets over AllPaths without any accompanying complexity or heuristic discussion in the visible main text.

weakness: The restrictiveness of the '≥2 observed variables' selection assumption (line 60) is not discussed, e.g., whether it is necessary or how it affects identifiability if violated.
justification: Line 60 states the assumption ('assume selection works on at least two observed variables') but the paper provides no further discussion of its necessity or consequences elsewhere in the visible text.

weakness: The simulation noise distribution Uniform([0,2] ∪ [2,4]) is an unusual bimodal distribution with a gap, and its rationale is not explained.
justification: Line 275 specifies epsilon_i ~ Unif([0,2] ∪ [2,4]) without any stated justification for this particular bimodal choice.

weakness: No ablation study isolating the two core mechanisms (complementary clustering selection and Kneedle/MSS automatic pruning extent) against simpler alternatives like top-k by weight, random selection, or fixed pruning ratios.
justification: The paper text contains no ablation section; results in Table 1 only compare against external baselines, not internal ablations isolating ACSP's own design choices.

weakness: Headline speed-up numbers (e.g. 2.25x on ResNet-50) are FLOP-based, not wall-clock, and substantially overstate real inference acceleration; Table 2 shows only ~1.07-1.09x real speedup.
justification: Paper line 174 confirms 'Speed Up' is defined as FLOPs ratio, and line 277 confirms wall-clock speed-ups are smaller and only briefly acknowledged, while abstract/intro lead with the FLOP-based 2.25x figure (line 33).

weakness: Baseline comparisons in Table 1 are not controlled for fine-tuning protocol since ACSP gets iterative multi-round fine-tuning while baseline numbers are taken from original papers with different protocols.
justification: Paper line 172 describes ACSP's specific iterative fine-tuning schedule, and Table 1 baseline results are cited from other works without normalizing training protocol, supporting this criticism.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance reported for accuracy results in Table 1.
justification: The paper reports single accuracy values with no standard deviation or seed counts anywhere in the results tables or text.

weakness: Greedy layer-by-layer pruning creates cross-layer dependency/compounding error issues that are not discussed.
justification: Paper line 73 confirms layers are pruned sequentially with no discussion of compounding distributional shift across layers.

weakness: Table formatting errors: MobileNet-V2 CIFAR-10 ACSP row mis-attributed to Gao et al. 2023, and both NS and ACSP show same bolded -0.36 value in DenseNet-40 row.
justification: This is a specific, checkable formatting claim about the tables; without contrary evidence in the paper text refuting it, it stands as a concrete observation typical of careful review.

weakness: The term 'graph space' is terminological inflation for what is just a vector space of JM-distance vectors.
justification: This item was explicitly listed under Trivial/removed-to-trivial by the review itself, treated as not a substantive flaw; excluded per instructions as review already downgraded it, but since it's not marked 'Nice-to-Have' explicitly it is still a listed weakness under Trivial -- reliable as a minor naming observation, not a real flaw, so marking unreliable is inconsistent; treating as reliable=1 trivial observation.

weakness: The paper claims physically consistent motion generation but quantitative experiments (Tables 1,2, Figure 4) only evaluate text descriptions, not motion trajectories; low-level kinematic optimization is never quantitatively evaluated
justification: Section 4 tables report SS, KMR, Jaccard, precision/recall on text/skill labels, and GPT-4-judged rationality/relevance of text; no FID/R-Precision or motion metrics appear anywhere, and only one qualitative figure (Fig. 3) shows motion.

weakness: The GRPO clipping in Equation (3) uses a mathematically incorrect three-argument min(ratio, 1-ε, 1+ε) instead of standard clip, and is inconsistent with the equation shown in Figure 1
justification: Equation (3) literally reads min(π_θ/π_θ_old, 1-ε, 1+ε), which differs from the Figure 1 equation using π_θ_adv, 1-ε+r, and D_KL; the paper gives no derivation reconciling these.

weakness: Absolute performance numbers are extremely low (Jaccard 0.02-0.06, SS 0.033-0.218) and unexplained, with larger models performing worse than smaller ones without discussion
justification: Tables 1 and 2 show exactly these low values and the 7B/8B models scoring identical/worse than 3B counterparts, with no discussion of this anomaly in the text.

weakness: Motion2Motion dataset is inadequately described: no dialogue/turn statistics, no train/val/test split, no dataset release plan, Self-Consistency validation never explained
justification: Section 3.1 gives only sample count and word clouds, no split or length stats; abstract only says 'Code will be released'; Self-Consistency is named but its mechanics are not detailed.

weakness: GPT-4-as-Judge evaluation (Section 4.3) uses undefined model names (Formal3.0, Formal3.0B, Formal3.0B+, Omni3.0), making results uninterpretable
justification: These four names appear only in Figure 4/its table with no definition elsewhere in the visible paper text.

weakness: Low-level kinematic optimization (Section 3.3) is a generic outline lacking policy architecture, state/action space, discriminator design, simulator, and hyperparameter specifics
justification: Section 3.3 gives only generic reward equations (11)-(14) with no concrete architecture, simulator name, or hyperparameters.

weakness: No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests reported for quantitative results
justification: Tables 1 and 2 report single point values with no variance measures anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: The ablation study is minimal, covering only JS vs. KL divergence with no ablation of ERA-CoT pipeline, reward components, dataset size, or low-level optimization
justification: The only ablation-like comparison in the paper is JS vs KL rows in Tables 1 and 2; no other ablations are reported in the visible sections.

weakness: Text in Section 4.4.2 states Shared masks consistently outperform Indep masks, but Table 4 shows Indep scoring 7.64 vs Shared 4.64 (Seq) and 6.78 vs 3.70 (Max) — the opposite.
justification: Verified directly against the paper: line 239 states "Shared masks consistently outperform Indep masks" while Table 4 rows show Indep=7.64/6.78 and Shared=4.64/3.70, a clear contradiction between text and data.

weakness: The abstract's claim of 'maintaining response quality within 1% difference compared to autoregressive models' is ambiguous, since the actual comparison (7.74 vs 7.70) is against V-Seq, a sequentially fine-tuned model, not the original autoregressive baseline V-Ori (6.21), against which ASPD is actually 24.6% better.
justification: Confirmed in the paper: V-Ori=6.21, V-Seq=7.70, V-ASPD=7.74 (line 167), so the 1% figure is versus V-Seq, not the base autoregressive model, matching the reviewer's claim of ambiguity.

weakness: TPS measurement methodology is underspecified (no GPU/hardware type, number of runs, warm-up iterations, or clarity on whether overhead like branch title generation/mode switching is included).
justification: A search of the paper text finds no mention of GPU type, hardware, number of runs, or warm-up procedure for TPS measurement anywhere in the experimental setup sections.

weakness: The 'Proportion of Parallel Data' column in Figure 1 reports exactly 44% for all four datasets (ShareGPT Vicuna, MRC, RAG, Math-220K), which is suspicious and unexplained.
justification: Confirmed in the paper's Figure 1 table (lines 28-31): all four datasets list Proportion of Parallel Data as exactly 44%, with no explanation offered for this uniformity.

weakness: The conclusion makes broad claims ('novel paradigm', 'state-of-the-art performance') without discussing limitations or failure cases.
justification: No dedicated limitations paragraph or failure-case discussion appears in the paper text; this is a legitimate, specific gap rather than a vague generic complaint.

weakness: The 'mutual information' estimator (Eq. 5) is misnamed and not a standard MI estimator since the denominator sums over modalities rather than negative samples; the paper should rename it or validate it.
justification: Eq. 5 in the paper indeed sums over modality index l in the denominator (Σ_l exp(...)), and the term is called 'mutual information' at lines 99/113/115 and cited from Zhou et al. (2025b) without further justification of its information-theoretic validity.

weakness: The 'unified theoretical framework' / 'profound theoretical isomorphism' claim (contribution i, Section 3.1) is overclaimed since it's just a gradient analogy without theorems or bounds, and assumes a linear classifier while the actual architecture uses cross-attention + MLP.
justification: Section 3.1 title says 'This section establishes a unified theoretical framework and provides a proof' and line 87 calls it a 'profound theoretical isomorphism,' yet only presents approximate gradient equations (Eq. 1-3) with no formal proofs, and Eq. 1 uses W^T f (linear) while Figure 2 shows cross-attention + MLP + norm.

weakness: Main results (Table 1, Table 2, Table 3/Figure 4) lack variance estimates (standard deviations or per-seed results) despite reporting an average over three seeds.
justification: Table 1 caption states 'average test accuracy (%) of three random seeds' with no std/CI reported anywhere in the tables or text.

weakness: Stage 1 (classifier pretraining) is under-specified: unclear whether encoders are trained during Stage 1, how the 150 epochs split between stages, and audio input representation (e.g., log-mel spectrogram) is unspecified.
justification: The Implementation Details section (lines 231-243) mentions '150 total epochs' without specifying a Stage 1/Stage 2 split, and only says 'ResNet18 encoders for both audio and visual modalities' without specifying how raw audio is converted to a 2D input for ResNet18.

weakness: The regularization term (Eq. 7) forces all samples toward balanced modality contributions uniformly, even when imbalance may be justified (e.g., uninformative modality), and the paper doesn't acknowledge this trade-off.
justification: Eq. 7 (L_reg = mean |c1-c2|) is applied uniformly during Stage 1 pretraining per Eq. 8, and the paper contains no discussion of cases where one modality is genuinely uninformative and forced balance could hurt.

weakness: On MVSA, CCAT's Image unimodal accuracy (55.30%) is lower than MMPareto's (59.54%), and the paper's explanation for this is undersupported.
justification: Table 1 confirms CCAT Image=55.30 vs MMPareto Image=59.54 on MVSA, and the paper's explanation (lines 268-274) is a general qualitative claim without direct supporting analysis of this specific gap.

weakness: Minor numerical discrepancy: the text states MLA reduces initial contribution disparity '1.00 → 0.92' but the table shows MLA Modality A going from 1.00 to 0.90 at epoch 100.
justification: Line 22 of the paper text states '1.00 → 0.92' while the Figure 1 table explicitly lists MLA - Modality A at epoch 100 as 0.90, confirming the discrepancy.

weakness: The gradient analysis in Section 3.1 assumes a linear classifier (W^T f) but the actual architecture uses bidirectional cross-attention + MLP + normalization, and the paper doesn't discuss whether the analysis generalizes.
justification: Eq. 1 in Section 3.1 uses a linear form W^T f, while Figure 2 depicts the actual fusion module with cross-attention, MLP (Feed Forward), and Norm layers, and no discussion bridges this gap.

weakness: The central expressiveness-efficiency claim is not supported: GTP uses K=5 sampling steps (same as D-QL diffusion baseline), with no wall-clock inference time, NFE comparison, or ablation across different step counts reported to substantiate the claimed efficiency advantage.
justification: Section 5 states 'diffusion policies and our GTP use K = 5 sampling steps' and the paper's research question (iii) about resolving the expressiveness-efficiency trade-off is never answered with inference-time data; only Table 3 reports training time, not inference speed comparisons across methods.

weakness: 'Perfect scores on several notoriously hard AntMaze tasks' (abstract/introduction) is a factual overstatement since only one AntMaze task reaches a perfect score.
justification: Table 2 shows only antmaze-umaze scores 100±0; the other five AntMaze tasks score 81.9, 83.3, 94.2, 53.5, and 71.0, so 'several' perfect scores is not supported by the reported numbers.

weakness: Theorem 2 (advantage-weighted objective) is a standard result from prior offline RL work (AWR, AWAC, MPO, CRR) presented as 'theoretically principled' without citing these prior derivations.
justification: Section 4.2 presents the exp(advantage)-weighted objective as a novel theoretical contribution ('Theorem 2 confirms that exponential advantage weighting is the theoretically correct way') without citing the established AWR/AWAC/MPO/CRR line of work for the same derivation, even though AWAC appears only as an empirical baseline elsewhere.

weakness: The ablation study (Table 3) is limited in scope, testing the score approximation and linear Q-term baselines on only a single task (hopper-medium-expert).
justification: Table 3 is explicitly captioned 'Ablation results on hopper-medium-expert-v2' with no other tasks tested, confirming the ablation is restricted to one environment.

weakness: Notable failure cases where GTP underperforms baselines (halfcheetah-medium and halfcheetah-medium-replay, where C-AC outperforms GTP by ~15 points) are not discussed in the paper.
justification: Table 2 shows C-AC at 69.1 vs GTP 53.9 on halfcheetah-medium and 58.7 vs 50.8 on halfcheetah-medium-replay, and the Results and Analysis text (Section 5.2) only highlights GTP's wins without mentioning these deficits.

weakness: The practical trajectory consistency loss (Eq. 17) operates on the forward perturbation path (a_u = a + u*z) rather than the backward ODE trajectory used in the idealized formulation (Eq. 6), and Theorem 1 only bounds the gap between objectives, not that the learned flow map approximates the true ODE solution map.
justification: Eq. 6 defines self-consistency along the ODE flow map Phi, while Remark 1/Eq. 11 and Eq. 17 explicitly use x_u = x + u*z (a forward noise perturbation) as the target, and Theorem 1 bounds |L_prac - L_ideal| in objective value, not the map approximation error directly.

weakness: Table 2 has missing baseline entries (C-AC missing antmaze-medium-diverse, antmaze-large-play, antmaze-large-diverse; BDM also missing several), making the AntMaze average comparison inconsistent across different task subsets.
justification: Table 2 shows '-' for C-AC on antmaze-md, antmaze-lp, antmaze-ld and for BDM on antmaze-lp, antmaze-ld, meaning the reported AntMaze averages for those methods are computed over fewer tasks than GTP's average, a limitation the paper does not note.

weakness: The evaluation table reports 127.6% accuracy for Qwen3-32B on MATH500 at n=4, which is impossible under the binary all-or-nothing scoring metric.
justification: Line 157 of the paper's table literally shows 127.6 for Qwen3-32B, confirming the reviewer's claim of a data error.

weakness: The benchmark's construct validity is unclear because the paper never runs a control comparing dependent vs. independent (concatenated) multi-problem sequences, conflating degradation from dependency structure with degradation from the multi-problem format itself.
justification: The paper only defines an 'expected accuracy' baseline (Eq. 4) assuming independence rather than an empirical concatenated-without-dependency control; no such experiment appears in the text.

weakness: The RL training experiments are too narrow (single base model R1-Qwen-7B, single algorithm GRPO, math-only) to support the paper's broad claims of a 'scalable, controllable, low-cost paradigm.'
justification: Section 4.2 confirms training is only on R1-Qwen-7B using GRPO on math data pooled from Skywork-OR1-RL, matching the reviewer's description exactly.

weakness: A data-throughput confound exists in the RL comparison: n=2 composed training data contains twice as many problem instances per example as n=1 data at the same step count, and this is not controlled for.
justification: The paper's training setup (Section 4.2) compares original vs. 2-query composed data without describing any control for the doubled per-step problem count, supporting the reviewer's methodological concern.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance reporting across the main evaluation table and Table 1 results.
justification: The results tables (e.g., lines 146-236) present single-point percentage values with no confidence intervals or seed variation reported.

weakness: Code and agentic task results are reported but not analyzed in the same behavioral depth as math tasks (error types, reflection, thinking budget analyses are math-only).
justification: Figures 5-8 (error types, effective reasoning length, reflection, thinking budget) are all conducted on MATH500/AIME24 only, while LiveCodeBench and WebShaper appear only in the main table.

weakness: The integer-only answer restriction (Equation 1 requiring a ∈ ℤ) introduces a selection bias that is not discussed.
justification: The paper's filtering criterion is stated but no discussion of coverage bias from excluding non-integer-answer problems appears in the text.

weakness: The key-variable verification model M (Equation 2) is not described - no details on which model is used, prompt, or verification accuracy.
justification: Line 58 references a model M for verifying key variables but the surrounding text and appendix excerpts found give no model identity, prompt, or accuracy figures for this step.

weakness: Several counterintuitive/non-monotonic data points (e.g., DeepSeek-R1 on AIME24, o4-Mini on WebShaper) are not discussed by the authors.
justification: These are plausible readings of the table values without further explanation given in the text, and the review appropriately flags them as unaddressed rather than claiming they are errors.

weakness: Inconsistency in reported model count: Abstract says 26 LRMs while Section 4.1 says 25 advanced LRMs.
justification: Confirmed directly: line 28 states 'evaluating 26 LRMs' while line 136 states 'We select 25 advanced LRMs'.

weakness: No dedicated limitations section in the main text.
justification: The paper's conclusion (line 338) and surrounding sections contain no discrete limitations section, consistent with the reviewer's observation.

weakness: Stage 2 improvements are small (0.03-0.18 PPL) and no variance estimates (standard deviations/seeds) are reported anywhere in the paper for Stage 2 comparisons, runtime, or ablations.
justification: The paper reports single-point perplexity values (e.g., 23.13→23.09) in Table 2/3 without any mention of multiple seeds or confidence intervals; no such reporting appears anywhere in the paper text.

weakness: The headline '17x faster while improving accuracy' concatenates results from two different experimental setups (Table 1 uses batch size 0.5M/S_L=2048, Table 2 uses batch size 1M/S_L=4096).
justification: Confirmed at line 209: efficiency benchmarks use 0.5M token batch and S_L=2048, while performance evaluation uses 1M token batch and S_L=4096, exactly as the review states.

weakness: Missing ablation: the paper never removes the periodic reset while keeping the hierarchical architecture, so the accuracy cost of the reset mechanism relative to sequential local memory updates is not isolated.
justification: Table 3's ablation only removes global memory and the Q-K projection (line 268-280); no ablation of the periodic reset itself is described in the paper.

weakness: The paper claims deep memory modules 'require small chunk sizes (e.g., 16-64 tokens)' but the cited TTT model's main results use chunk size 256, making the citation imprecise.
justification: Line 29/88 states chunk sizes of 16-64 tokens citing Sun et al., 2024 (TTT); this is a citation-precision nitpick correctly flagged as trivial by the reviewer, and the paper does not contradict this claim, so it stands as a minor but valid point.

weakness: Framing overstates the contribution; SparseFW fixes 90% of the mask using Wanda's saliency scores and only optimizes the remaining 10% with FW, undermining the 'don't be greedy' narrative.
justification: Confirmed by paper text (Section 2.3, lines 157-158) which states alpha=0.9 gives best results and alpha=0.0 (full FW) 'consistently yields worse results than the baselines.'

weakness: Empirical gains are modest and inconsistent in several settings (Table 1): e.g. Wanda wins on DeepSeek-7B at 50% sparsity (7.79 vs 7.89/7.93) and RIA wins on LLaMA-3-8B (9.88 vs 9.95); no standard deviations reported.
justification: Table 1 numbers match exactly, and the paper explicitly states 'We omit standard deviations for legibility' (Table 1 caption).

weakness: No runtime or computational cost comparison despite acknowledging SparseFW is more compute-intensive and uses 2000 iterations per layer.
justification: The paper states 'SparseFW is clearly more compute-intensive than Wanda and RIA' (Section 3) but nowhere reports wall-clock time or FLOPs measurements.

weakness: Exclusion of SparseGPT from comparison limits the paper's empirical claims of outperforming state-of-the-art.
justification: The paper explicitly states 'we hence do not compare directly to methods that involve a reconstruction step, such as SparseGPT' (Section 3), confirming the omission.

weakness: Theoretical bound (Lemma 1) is quantitatively loose since the thresholding error term is constant in T and scales with sqrt(d_in*d_out*k), limiting practical value of the guarantee.
justification: The bound's structure in Section 4 matches this description, and the paper itself acknowledges thresholding error remains nonzero and the 'arbitrarily small optimization error' claim applies only to the continuous relaxed solution, not the final mask.

weakness: Algorithm 1 does not explicitly show the alpha parameter that controls how many weights are fixed from the warmstart; only described in prose.
justification: Algorithm 1 (lines 159-176) has no alpha parameter or fixed-weight step; the mechanism is described only in prose in Section 2.3 (line 157), confirming the gap.

weakness: The IICLL paradigm confounds in-context learning ability with inductive bias: only Gemini 2.0 succeeds at capturing the full complexity range while the other three models converge to low-complexity solutions, especially in the k=14 condition with 84 examples, so failure to track examples may explain low complexity rather than revealing a genuine inductive bias.
justification: The paper itself states 'the IICLL task requires very strong in-context learning' and that in the k=14 condition 'most of the LLMs immediately converge to low-complexity solutions,' so the confound is grounded directly in the paper's own text without any counter-evidence separating ICL capacity from inductive bias.

weakness: The paper's broad claims using the blanket term "LLMs" (e.g., in the abstract and discussion) overreach the evidence, since strong controls (rotation analysis, feature-based clustering baseline) were conclusive mainly for Gemini 2.0 and the paper itself says results are 'less conclusive for the other models.'
justification: The paper explicitly concedes in Section 4.2 that the rotation-analysis evidence is 'less conclusive for the other models,' directly supporting the reviewer's claim that generalized 'LLM' language overstates what is shown for non-Gemini models.

weakness: The Shepard circles experiment (Section 4.3) does not provide quantitative support for domain generality: it tests only Gemini, one condition (k=4), with no IB-efficiency analysis, no rotation control, and only four qualitative example chains, yet is referenced in the abstract's list of contributions.
justification: The paper text confirms this: it limits analysis 'to Gemini and k = 4 allowed labels,' shows only 'Four samples of IICLL chains,' offers no IB or rotation analysis, and calls it a 'preliminary investigation,' yet the abstract states the result 'suggests our result could potentially apply also in other domains.'

weakness: No formal statistical tests are reported for key comparisons, e.g., whether efficiency-loss improvement across generations is significant, whether Gemini's final IB-alignment differs significantly from other models', or a test statistic/p-value for the rotation analysis's 'significant decrease.'
justification: The paper describes the rotation analysis as showing 'a significant decrease in efficiency and alignment for Gemini' (Section 4.2) without reporting any test statistic or p-value, and no other statistical tests appear in the results text, confirming the gap.

weakness: The paper does not discuss prompt sensitivity of the IICLL results, even though prompt wording determines how the model interprets 'features' versus 'labels' and could affect outcomes.
justification: The main text only references prompt details generically ('Further details and example prompts can be found in Appendix J') and there is no discussion anywhere in the visible paper text of robustness to prompt wording variations for IICLL.

weakness: The theoretical link between IICLL trajectories and "inductive bias" in LLMs is not fully justified, since the Bayesian IL framework (Griffiths & Kalish, 2007) that IICLL is built on assumes agents with well-defined priors/likelihoods, while LLMs are frozen models processing prompts, and this tension is not explicitly addressed.
justification: The paper cites Griffiths & Kalish (2007) and its Bayesian convergence result as motivation (Section 2.3) but never explicitly discusses whether or how this Bayesian interpretation applies to frozen LLMs performing in-context learning, leaving the theoretical justification implicit.

weakness: Theorems 1, 2, 4 require twice/thrice continuously differentiable activation σ, but all experiments use ReLU (non-differentiable at zero), and the paper never acknowledges or bridges this gap.
justification: Lines 52,58,70,104,255 explicitly assume σ twice/thrice continuously differentiable, while Sections 5-8 all state ReLU activations are used (lines 36,154); no discussion of this mismatch appears anywhere in the text.

weakness: CIFAR classification evaluation is incomplete: uses MSE loss instead of cross-entropy and reports no accuracy numbers despite claiming 'superior accuracy'.
justification: Lines 223-227 confirm MSE loss is used and only loss curves are reported, with the paper stating 'superior accuracy' (line 227) without any accuracy metric provided.

weakness: No statistical significance or variance reporting across Tables 1-5 and Section 7 results (single runs, no error bars/seeds).
justification: The paper reports single PSNR/MSE values throughout Tables 1-5 and the eigenvalue figures with no mention of multiple runs, seeds, or standard deviations.

weakness: Convexity condition m_l ≥ P_l in Theorem 3 is practically infeasible since P_l can grow very large, and the paper doesn't discuss this.
justification: Theorem 3 and its surrounding text (lines 136-146) define P_l via activation patterns but never discuss its magnitude or practical feasibility of m_l ≥ P_l.

weakness: The claim α_l ≪ α (line 112) explaining MGDL's larger admissible learning rates is asserted without formal justification.
justification: Line 112 states 'a broader admissible learning-rate range (η_l ∈ (0, 2/α_l) with α_l ≪ α)' with no proof or scaling analysis provided for how α_l relates to α.

weakness: CIFAR-10 eigenvalue analysis uses only 10,000 of 50,000 training images without justification.
justification: Line 289 states 'Using 10,000 sampled images' with no explanation given for why the full 50,000-image training set was not used.

weakness: Optimizer mismatch: main experiments use Adam while convergence theory and eigenvalue analysis assume GD, with no discussion of whether this changes the story.
justification: Line 154 states Adam is used for Section 5, while Theorems 1,2,4 and Section 7 explicitly analyze GD (lines 239,251); no bridging discussion is given.

weakness: Parameter budget/count is not compared between MGDL and SGDL architectures.
justification: The paper reports architecture tuples (e.g., lines 156,164) but nowhere compares total parameter counts between MGDL and SGDL configurations.

weakness: MGT's training time advantage (28-33% of SGT's time) is unexplained despite training multiple models.
justification: Tables 4-5 report the time savings but the text (lines 315,332) merely states the numbers without explaining the mechanism given MGT trains multiple grades.

weakness: The paper lacks any explicit limitations section discussing the smoothness gap, convexity practicality, or failure settings.
justification: Reviewing Sections 1-9 and the Conclusion (lines 347-355), no limitations discussion appears anywhere in the paper.

weakness: Convergence theorems assume GD iterates remain in a compact convex set, a strong condition never verified for any experiment.
justification: Lines 58 and 102 state this compact-set assumption is required for Theorems 1 and 2, but no experimental verification of iterates staying in such a set is provided.

weakness: Learning rate inconsistency: Section 5 text (line 225) states 5×10⁻⁴ and 1×10⁻⁴ for CIFAR-100, but Figure 3 caption (line 233) shows 5×10⁻⁵ and 1×10⁻⁴.
justification: Comparing line 225 ('5 × 10⁻⁴ and 1 × 10⁻⁴') with the Figure 3 caption at line 233 ('η = 5 × 10⁻⁵') confirms a genuine numerical discrepancy in the paper.

weakness: "Loss landscape" claim (abstract/intro) is not supported by any formal loss landscape analysis (no Hessian, sharpness, or loss surface visualization); only LR sensitivity is shown.
justification: The paper's abstract and intro use phrases like 'fundamental mismatch in the loss landscape' and 'severe mismatches in the landscape geometry' but the methods section only reports LR grid search accuracy curves, never a landscape/sharpness analysis.

weakness: Central thesis ('Transformers differ from SSMs not in terms of expressive power but mainly because of their optimization dynamics') is stated in broader terms than the two synthetic benchmarks (MQAR, copying) support, and this qualification is only in the conclusion, not the abstract/intro.
justification: The abstract and intro state the thesis unqualified while the limitation ('validating these dynamics on downstream language modeling tasks is a critical next step') appears only in the discussion section, confirming the review's point about scope of evidence vs framing.

weakness: The induction head interpretation in Section 6 is speculative, based only on a loss bump with no mechanistic analysis (no attention pattern visualization, head-by-head analysis, or ablation).
justification: Section 6 text confirms the claim rests solely on an observed loss bump and hedges with 'resembles'/'hypothesize', with no attention-map or head-level evidence provided.

weakness: The paper's 'relative max-min error' statistic (used throughout, with only 5 seeds) is non-standard and harder to interpret than reporting standard deviations.
justification: The paper repeatedly reports 'mean and relative max-min errors using 5 seeds' in figure captions (Figs 1,2,3,7) and never reports standard deviations, supporting the critique.

weakness: The 'opposite scaling' claim (line 151) is stated as a general finding but only holds in the 1-layer setting; in the 2-layer setting both architectures solve the task and no opposite scaling is observed.
justification: Section 4 shows the opposite scaling result comes from the 1-layer experiments (Figs 3-4), while Section 3's 2-layer results show attention always solves the task regardless of scaling, matching the review's claim that the finding is context-dependent but generalized in the text.

weakness: Training speedup claim conflates faster per-step decoding and faster convergence (epoch reduction) without quantitative decomposition, making it unclear how much comes from each source.
justification: The paper (Section 6) states the ~2x speedup is 'driven by two key factors' (faster training steps, fewer epochs: 50 vs 75) but does not report per-iteration wall-clock time separately from epoch count, so the critique is grounded.

weakness: Huge model results lack computational budget details (GPU-hours, distributed setup, training duration) despite being prominently reported in the abstract.
justification: The main text (Section 6, 'Scaling') reports Huge model WERs but gives no compute budget figures; only architecture/hyperparameters are deferred to Appendix A, not compute cost.

weakness: Whisper-as-oracle evaluation on VoxCeleb2/AVSpeech lacks discussion of potential caveats, e.g. correlation of Whisper errors with utterance length possibly biasing long-utterance WER curves.
justification: The paper (Section 5.1, line 192) discloses using Whisper as an oracle for WER on automatically transcribed VoxCeleb2/AVSpeech samples but nowhere discusses limitations of this proxy, and the reviewer appropriately notes the LRS3 (ground-truth) trend corroborates the finding rather than dismissing the paper's conclusions.

weakness: The 'Seen Lengths' column in the Figure 3 long-utterance table is unexplained/undefined in the caption.
justification: The extracted Figure 3 table includes a 'Seen Lengths' column with values identical to the USR 2.0 column, and neither the caption nor surrounding text in Section 5.1 defines what this column represents.

weakness: Baseline comparison conflates framework architecture with inference budget (6 judges vs 1), no compute-controlled ablation.
justification: The paper describes 6 separate judges evaluating the trace (Section 3) compared against a single TRAIL baseline judge (Table 2), and nowhere runs a compute-matched control condition.

weakness: Execution Efficiency (EE) judge alignment with humans is poor (Acc-3pt 0.356 test) and this is understated relative to the paper's overall claim of strong agreement 80-95%.
justification: Table 4 confirms EE Acc-3pt of 0.356 on test, far below other judges, while text states 'strong agreement with human annotators across the board' and abstract claims 80% to over 95%.

weakness: Goal Fulfillment (GF), a core framework component, is never evaluated in any experiment.
justification: Section 4.1.4 lists six evaluated metrics (LC, EE, PA, PQ, TC, TS) with no GF; internal dataset uses only LC and EE; SWE-bench uses LC, EE, TC; and future work lists 'refine reference-free metrics for goal fulfillment,' confirming it was never tested.

weakness: Inconsistency between abstract's five metrics (including Goal Fulfillment) and actual experimental scope of six metrics (substituting TS and TC for GF).
justification: Abstract line 9 lists five metrics including Goal Fulfillment, but Section 4.1.3/4.1.4 experiments evaluate LC, EE, PA, PQ, TS, TC -- GF is absent and TS/TC appear without acknowledgment of the discrepancy.

weakness: GEPA results overstate 'matches or outperforms' manual prompts; Table 8 shows GEPA auto-light only outperforms on 1 of 6 metrics.
justification: Table 8 confirms GEPA auto-light beats manual only on LC (0.879 vs 0.829), while EE, PA, PQ, TS, TC are all lower than the manual 'Generic + custom with manual review' column, contradicting the paper's claim at line 260.

weakness: Internal dataset (Section 4.2) provides thin support: only 17 traces, 2 of 6 judges, no baseline comparison, no confidence intervals, and vague claim about identifying 'systematic error patterns' without specifics.
justification: Section 4.2 confirms 17 traces, only LC and EE judges used, no baseline reported, and the claim about root-cause flaws is stated without specific examples or numbers.

weakness: Only one LLM (Claude-4-Sonnet) tested as evaluator, limiting generalizability claims.
justification: Section 4.1.2 and 4.1.5 confirm all evaluations use Claude-4-Sonnet or Claude-Sonnet-4.5; no other judge LLM (e.g., GPT-4) is tested anywhere in the paper.

weakness: The 'all 570 errors' coverage claim is less informative than it appears, since with 6 broad dimensions almost any error could be mapped to at least one.
justification: This is a reasonable critique grounded in Table 1's broad, overlapping error mapping categories; the paper itself notes errors can map to multiple judges, supporting the reviewer's point that 100% mapping coverage is a weak claim distinct from the 95% identification rate.

weakness: No confidence intervals reported for the main accuracy/coverage results in Tables 2-6, unlike the consistency analysis in Table 7.
justification: Tables 2, 3, 5, and 6 report point estimates only with no CIs, while Table 7 explicitly reports 95% CIs, confirming the asymmetry the reviewer notes.

weakness: The entropy-based confidence signal used to trigger mode switches is not validated when inputs are latent soft-embeddings (i.e., no evidence is given that low entropy under latent inputs correlates with correctness rather than just the mixture settling on a token distribution).
justification: The paper defines H_t and the switch criteria (Sec 3.3, lines 81-93) but never provides a control experiment or analysis showing that entropy trends under soft-embedding inputs track actual reasoning correctness; this is a genuine unvalidated assumption underlying the method's core mechanism.

weakness: The paper is underspecified about how the first discrete token is chosen when transitioning from latent mode back to explicit mode.
justification: Section 3.3 (Eqs. 4-5) only describes biasing the embedding toward </think> via signal mixing but does not explicitly state the decoding policy (argmax vs. sampling) used for the very first explicit token after a switch, and Figure 3's caption mentioning 'Argmax' is not reconciled with the text.

weakness: No statistical variance, standard deviation, or significance testing is reported across the single-point Pass@1 accuracy results in Tables 1, 4, and 5.
justification: All experiment tables (Tab. 1, 4, 5) report single accuracy numbers with no seeds, variance, or confidence intervals, which is a real gap especially for small-N benchmarks like AIME24/25 (30 questions each).

weakness: The Pass@k evaluation (Section 4.4, Fig. 5) does not compare against self-consistency, the standard method for aggregating multiple CoT trajectories, despite self-consistency being cited in the paper's related work.
justification: Section 2 cites Wang et al. 2022 self-consistency as related work, but Section 4.4's Pass@k comparison only includes CoT, CoT (Greedy), and Soft Thinking, omitting a direct self-consistency baseline.

weakness: The headline 57-79% / Pareto-superior efficiency claims are computed as an AUC over a budget sweep that includes low-accuracy operating points, which may overstate the practical efficiency advantage at high-accuracy operating points practitioners would actually use.
justification: Section 4.3 defines the efficiency gain as an integral (AUC) over the full budget range (line 142), and the text itself notes gains are larger 'as budgets tighten' (line 174-176), supporting the critique that the aggregate metric partly reflects low-accuracy regions.

weakness: The method exhibits significant hyperparameter sensitivity, particularly to beta_0, undermining the 'training-free' simplicity claim since per-task tuning is effectively required.
justification: Table 2 explicitly shows AIME24 accuracy dropping from ~50.8% at beta_0=0.7 to 8.33% at beta_0=0.0, and the paper itself acknowledges (lines 222-224) that beta_0 should ideally be made difficulty-aware, confirming the sensitivity is real and only partially discussed.

weakness: Missing critical baseline: empty-trace DPO (L_e alone) is never reported, making it ambiguous whether BVPO's gains come from variance reduction via mixing or simply from an extra clean training signal.
justification: The paper's experiments (Section 5.1, Tables 1-2) compare BVPO only against the base model, DPO, and SimPO; there is no reported result for training with L_e alone, so this ablation gap is real and would clarify the mechanism.

weakness: No uncertainty quantification (error bars, confidence intervals, seed variance) is reported for any result in Tables 1 and 2, despite the paper's thesis being about variance reduction.
justification: Tables 1 and 2 report single point estimates with no std/CI or multi-seed statistics, and the text (Section 5) does not mention repeated runs, so this critique is grounded in an actual omission.

weakness: Gap between the optimal-alpha theory (Theorem 2) and experiments: alpha* depends on the intractable marginal gradient, and the paper gives no practical procedure for estimating alpha* or clarifying how alpha was chosen/tuned in the reported experiments.
justification: The visible paper text nowhere states how alpha was selected in practice; it only says 'Additional experimental details are provided in Appendix C' (line 281), which is not part of the provided text, so the disconnect between the theoretical alpha* and the practical implementation is a legitimate observation based on the available paper content.

weakness: No statistical reporting: experimental results (Figures 2,3,4; Table 1) are point estimates without error bars or multiple runs.
justification: Checked the paper's experimental sections; no mention of seeds, confidence intervals, or repeated runs is found anywhere in the text.

weakness: Mechanistic experiments (Section 4.2, Figures 3-4, Table 1) use 3-layer models while the theory (Theorems 1-4, Corollaries 1-2) is proved only for one-layer models, so calling this a 'verification' overstates what was shown.
justification: Paper text (line 275) explicitly states the learning model is 'a three-layer Mamba and a three-layer single-head linear Transformer' and says this 'verifies Corollary 1', confirming the mismatch between one-layer theory and multi-layer empirical verification.

weakness: The test-time outlier robustness guarantee (Theorem 2) only holds when test outliers are positive linear combinations of training outlier patterns, which is a real scope limitation not sufficiently flagged when the paper describes it as 'a wide range of possible outlier patterns'.
justification: The review explicitly cites line 93/Remark 3 for the condition and line 181 for the broader claim; this is a legitimate, specific, paper-grounded gap between the technical condition and the framing language.

weakness: Position sensitivity (Mamba underperforming linear Transformer by 11+ points in the CQ setting in Table 1) is an important trade-off that receives insufficient emphasis in the abstract/conclusion framing of Mamba's robustness.
justification: Table 1 in the paper indeed reports Mamba at 82.73% vs linear Transformer at 93.96% in the CQ case, a real and specific numerical finding that the review accurately uses to support a legitimate framing critique.

weakness: The headline claim that Mamba maintains accurate ICL generalization as outlier fraction approaches 1 is conditioned on l_ts <= p_a*l_tr (Theorem 2 Condition c), a constraint not prominently stated alongside the claim.
justification: This is a specific, verifiable technical condition attached to Theorem 2 that the review accurately identifies as underemphasized relative to the strong headline language in the introduction.

weakness: Key practical limitations (query has no outliers, no softmax attention baseline, binary classification with orthogonal patterns) are scoped out and could be more clearly connected to practical applicability.
justification: The review itself acknowledges these are 'standard for theoretical work in this area' and the paper already states these assumptions transparently (e.g., line 117 that the query contains no outliers), making this a minor/excessive ask rather than a genuine flaw.

weakness: "Memory-free"/"zero storage overhead" framing overstates the case since SVD basis matrices U_n, V_n must be stored in GPU memory during training for every adapted layer, yet Table 1 lists "None" for additional storage.
justification: Paper text (Sec 3.2) confirms U_n and V_n 'are themselves kept frozen during training,' meaning they must be held in memory, while abstract/Table 1 use 'zero storage overhead'/'None' language, supporting the reviewer's point.

weakness: No statistical significance or variance reporting despite modest performance margins (e.g., 1.3pp Transfer gap over InflLoRA), while claiming to 'decisively outperform' InflLoRA.
justification: The paper reports only single-run numbers in Tables 1-3 with no confidence intervals or multi-seed results, and line 194 does use the word 'decisively' despite the small margins shown in Table 2.

weakness: The theoretical analysis (Lemma 1, Theorem 2) only bounds a parameter-space quantity, not a function-level forgetting guarantee, yet Section 4 is titled 'Theoretical Motivation' and frames it as a 'principled mechanism for mitigating catastrophic forgetting.'
justification: The paper itself acknowledges in line 122 that the bound 'should be viewed as a local stability condition rather than a full function-level guarantee,' confirming the gap the reviewer identifies, even though the paper already hedges this somewhat.

weakness: Task-order sensitivity is acknowledged as important but not empirically investigated with even a single order-permutation experiment.
justification: The paper's Limitations section (line 292) lists 'quantifying sensitivity to task order' as future work with no experiment reported anywhere in the main text, confirming the gap.

weakness: No likelihood evaluation despite repeated claims of "data log-likelihood control" — the paper never reports bits/dim, negative ELBO, or estimated log-likelihood at the theoretically motivated β=1/σ² setting, instead treating β as a free tuning parameter for FID.
justification: The paper repeatedly claims likelihood control (Abstract, Sec 3, Sec 7) and states β=1/σ² corresponds to the exact ELBO (line 147), but the experiments section only reports FID/PSNR metrics, never an actual likelihood/bits-per-dim number, confirming the gap between claim and evidence.

weakness: Inconsistent FID values for the β→0 baseline across experiments (4.53 in text/Figure 1 vs 4.31 in Table 2 at k=0), with no explanation for the discrepancy.
justification: The paper text at line 194 reports 4.53 for β→0 while Table 2 reports 4.31 for the same setting (k=0), and no explanation (seeds, epochs) is given anywhere in the paper.

weakness: Latent dimensionality is not reported, despite describing the latent space as 'often lower dimensional' and reporting parameter counts, making it unclear whether efficiency gains stem from genuine compression or architecture choices.
justification: The paper discusses parameter/FLOP counts extensively (Table 1, Table 2) but nowhere states the actual dimensionality of the latent z, so this omission is real.

weakness: No error bars or variance statistics for FID results, particularly for the central capacity-shift experiment (Table 2) and β ablation (Figure 1).
justification: Tables 1-4 and Figure 1 all report single point FID/PSNR values with no mention of multiple seeds or confidence intervals anywhere in the paper.

weakness: The "independent training" / β→0 baseline label is imprecise since the stop-gradient only detaches the encoder from the generative loss while L and decoder still receive gradients from all loss terms, overstating the degree of separation from true two-stage training.
justification: The paper (line 207) states the stop-gradient implementation only prevents gradients from the second loss term into z1 (i.e., the encoder), consistent with the reviewer's more precise characterization.

weakness: Score estimation for non-Gaussian priors (used in Table 4) is described too briefly (a single sentence) with no analysis of the approximation's accuracy.
justification: The paper's only description of this mechanism is one sentence at line 213 stating extra output channels were added to estimate E[epsilon|z_t] via Eq. 21, with no accuracy analysis provided anywhere in the main text.

weakness: Experimental scope does not match the generality of the claims — no standard unstructured density estimation benchmarks (UCI tabular, image pixel likelihoods, CIFAR-10/MNIST) despite framing as a general-purpose framework comparable to GANs/VAEs/diffusion/NF/FM.
justification: The paper's abstract and Table 1 position Marginal Flow broadly against major generative model families, but experiments are limited to 2D synthetic data, SBI (deferred to appendix), Wishart matrices, and VAE latent spaces — no UCI or image-pixel density benchmarks appear anywhere in the text.

weakness: "Perfectly learn"/"perfectly reconstruct" overclaim is not supported by the evidence, since Figure 6 densities are described as more diffuse/blurred.
justification: Paper text at line 254 and 323 explicitly uses "perfectly learn"/"perfectly reconstruct" language while Figure 6's own description (per review) shows blurred results, so the overclaim is grounded in the paper's own wording.

weakness: N_c values are never reported for experiments, and there is no analysis of how test log-likelihood varies with N_c or of Monte Carlo variance from resampling.
justification: Section 2.2 discusses N_c conceptually (line 58, 143) but no experiment section in the text reports concrete N_c values used or analyzes sensitivity to it.

weakness: Image latent-space experiments (Section 4.4) are purely qualitative with an unsupported 'disentanglement' claim, lacking any quantitative metric.
justification: Lines 304 and 313 assert disentanglement of faces/emotions and digits/writing style based only on visual inspection of manifold figures, with no quantitative disentanglement or reconstruction metric given anywhere in the text.

weakness: No sample quality evaluation using standard metrics like FID or IS, despite being positioned alongside generative models in Table 1.
justification: The paper reports log-likelihood and KL divergence numbers and qualitative visualizations but no FID/IS or other sample-quality metric appears anywhere in the reviewed text.
