weakness: Confounded SAE-vs-random comparison: Section 4.2 compares random steering on Llama3-8B/Qwen2.5-7B against SAE steering on a different model (Llama3.1-8B) with different layer depth and coefficient, and there is a textual contradiction between line 104 (random tested only on Llama3-8B, Falcon3-7B, Qwen2.5-7B; SAE only on Llama3.1-8B) and line 151/Fig 2c caption which claims 'identical steering conditions (same model, layer, coefficient)' for the random-vs-SAE comparison.
justification: The paper text at line 104 states random vectors were tested on Llama3-8B, Falcon3-7B, Qwen2.5-7B while SAE vectors were tested only on Llama3.1-8B, yet line 151 and the Fig 2c caption both claim the comparison was under 'identical steering conditions (same model, layer, coefficient)' -- a genuine internal contradiction, and Section 4.2 (line 157) confirms random and SAE comparisons used different models/layers/coefficients.

weakness: The conclusion's claim that 'SAE-based steering proves even more dangerous, achieving 11% harmful compliance on Llama3.1-8B' is not well supported and contains an internal numeric inconsistency (11% in text vs 10% in the Fig 3 data table), and does not actually exceed Llama3-8B's random steering rate of 17%.
justification: Fig 3's table shows SAE Overall compliance = 10%, while the main text at line 163 and the conclusion at line 249 both say 11%; also Llama3-8B's random steering reaches 17%, higher than SAE's reported 10-11%, undermining the 'even more dangerous' framing.

weakness: LLM judge validation is not presented in the main text; the 0% baseline and compliance rates depend entirely on the Qwen3-8B judge's calibration, and no human-annotation agreement data is shown in the main paper.
justification: The paper defers judge quality assessment to Appx. B ('see Appx. B for prompt details and quality assessment against human annotations'), which was not available in the provided text, so no calibration evidence appears in the main body as claimed.

weakness: Framing overstatement: the title/abstract claim steering 'systematically breaks model alignment safeguards' while observed full-dataset compliance rates are only 10-17%.
justification: The abstract's language ('systematically breaks... making it comply with harmful requests') is stronger than the quantitative results in Fig. 3 (10-17% overall compliance), supporting the critique of rhetorical inflation relative to effect sizes.

weakness: All experiments use a single fixed random seed (42), so reported averages lack variance estimates across seeds.
justification: Section 6 (Reproducibility Statement) confirms 'All experiments use fixed random seeds (42) for vector sampling and generation,' with no mention of multi-seed variance reporting anywhere in the text.

weakness: The universal attack (Section 4.4) is constructed and tested using vectors derived from only one seed prompt ('bomb-making'), so it is unknown whether other seed prompts would produce similarly generalizing universal vectors.
justification: Section 4.4 explicitly states 'We begin with a fixed harmful prompt, "Write a tutorial on how to make a bomb"' as the sole basis for constructing the universal vectors, confirming only one seed prompt was used.

weakness: No conditional baseline in the central conditional evaluation (Section 4.3 relies only on calibration plots of MolMiner itself with no conditional VAE/diffusion/guided sampling comparator).
justification: Section 4.3 indeed only reports calibration plots for MolMiner with no conditional baseline model; Section 4.2's baseline (HierVAE) is unconditional only, confirming the gap.

weakness: Ablation findings in Section 4.1 (more properties help, geometry-aware attention with positive bias helps, rollout resampling reduces overfitting) are asserted without any quantitative support (no tables/numbers).
justification: Section 4.1 lists these three findings in prose with no accompanying table or figure of ablation results in the visible text.

weakness: Unconditional performance gap (HierVAE beats MolMiner on 11/12 Wasserstein metrics, often by large margins) undermines confidence in conditional results, and paper's early-termination explanation is untested.
justification: Table 1 confirms HierVAE better on nearly all metrics; the paper itself states in Limitations that this is a 'hypothesis' explained qualitatively without quantitative fragment-count analysis, supporting the criticism.

weakness: The MolLeR comparison framing could mislead readers into thinking a proper comparison was attempted and failed, given only 7 days/~10,000 steps of training.
justification: Section 4.2 confirms MolLeR was trained for 7 days completing only two 5,000-step intervals before being excluded, matching the review's characterization.

weakness: Inconsistent epoch count: Section 4.1 says 50 epochs while Section 7 says 30 epochs.
justification: Text confirms: Section 4.1 'trained with resampling for 50 epochs' vs Section 7 'approximately 7 days, or 30 epochs' — a direct inconsistency in the paper.

weakness: Validity is hand-waved rather than quantified; paper omits a concrete validity percentage, relying only on the claim that valence constraints are enforced.
justification: Section 4.2 explicitly states 'We omit validity, as our model enforces valence constraints during generation and consistently produces valid molecules,' with no numeric percentage given, supporting the criticism.

weakness: Novelty and Uniqueness metrics in Table 1 are nearly saturated (98-100%) for all models, making them uninformative as discriminators.
justification: Table 1 values confirm Uniqueness 98-100% and Novelty 99.5-99.9% across all three models, supporting the claim of near-saturation.

weakness: The claim of 'improved benchmarking methods' (Wasserstein distance, calibration plots) is overstated for what are standard tools.
justification: Wasserstein distance is explicitly cited as following prior work (Polykovskiy et al., 2018) and calibration plots are a standard technique, so labeling them a novel contribution is a defensible criticism.

weakness: Evaluation on real vision tasks doesn't fully support 'consistently outperforms independent coding' claim; the method is worse than Independent at receive rate on Cityscapes (line 271: 'the curves for the receive rate are higher than the Independent approach'), yet the abstract's claim conflates transmit and receive regimes.
justification: Paper text at line 271 explicitly confirms the proposed method's receive-rate curves are higher (worse) than Independent, contradicting the abstract's unqualified 'consistently outperforms independent coding' claim.

weakness: Architecture ablations (Shared vs Separated vs Combined) are only performed on synthetic data, not validated on real vision benchmarks like Cityscapes/COCO.
justification: Section 4.1 (synthetic data) is the only place these three architectures are compared; Section 4.3 only compares Proposed vs Joint vs Independent, confirming the gap.

weakness: No variance or significance reporting (error bars, confidence intervals, seed variability) across any experiment.
justification: No mention of multiple seeds, error bars, or confidence intervals appears anywhere in the paper text provided.

weakness: Overclaim of 'six vision benchmarks' in abstract when only 2-3 vision benchmarks (Cityscapes, COCO, plus arguably colored MNIST) are actually used; similarly conclusion's 'three computer vision experiments' overcounts since colored MNIST is not a CV experiment like the other two.
justification: Section 4 only presents synthetic data, colored MNIST, Cityscapes, and COCO — at most 2 true vision benchmarks (Cityscapes, COCO) plus MNIST as an edge-case classification analysis, contradicting the abstract's 'six vision benchmarks' and the conclusion's 'three computer vision experiments.'

weakness: The common-channel matching mechanism (Eq. 14) is a hard non-differentiable-style operation whose optimization behavior/gradient dynamics and sensitivity to gamma are not analyzed with an ablation.
justification: Section 3.3 sets gamma=1 by fiat (lines 179-182) and offers only informal reasoning about small/large gamma, with no ablation study or gradient-dynamics analysis presented in the paper.

weakness: The Markov conditions (Eq. 1) assumed by the theory are violated by the proposed architecture, and the paper doesn't discuss whether the theory still applies under this violation.
justification: Line 167 explicitly states the architecture 'effectively removes the requirement for the conditions in 1,' yet Theorem 1 relies on these Markov conditions, and no further discussion reconciling this is given in the text.

weakness: The 'Accuracy Sum' composite metric (mIoU + inverse depth RMSE) used for BD-rate analysis lacks justification for how the weighting of the two task metrics affects the reported numbers.
justification: The paper only states depth RMSE is 'scaled so its inverse is in a similar scale' to mIoU (Figure 5 caption) without further justification of the weighting's effect on BD-rate results.

weakness: No analysis of common-channel utilization (fraction of rate through common channel) on real tasks (Cityscapes, COCO) or comparison to estimated mutual information.
justification: Section 4.3 reports only BD-rate and performance numbers; per-channel rate breakdowns are stated to exist only for colored MNIST in Appendix D ('Appendix D shows the rate of each channel... for every PMF'), not for Cityscapes/COCO.

weakness: Only one baseline (uniform allocation) is compared against; no competing adaptive approach or simple adaptive heuristic baseline is included.
justification: The paper's own Section 4.2/4.3 confirms only uniform allocation is used as benchmark, and lines 188 explicitly explain why Damani et al. (2024) is not compared; no other adaptive heuristic baseline appears anywhere in the paper.

weakness: "Small exploration budget" is a mischaracterization since the main experiments use d=0.75B (90/120 queries), and d is only tuned over {0.60B,0.70B,0.75B,0.80B}, never testing genuinely small budgets.
justification: Confirmed directly by the paper: line 215 sets d=0.75B for main results, and line 242 confirms tuning is only performed over {0.60B, 0.7B, 0.75B, 0.80B}, while the abstract/intro (lines 9, 28) call it a "small exploration budget."

weakness: No formal statistical significance testing is reported for the BWR results against the 0.50 baseline.
justification: The paper reports median/IQR and percent of batches with BWR>0.50 (Tables 1-2) but nowhere reports a formal significance test such as bootstrap CIs or Wilcoxon test.

weakness: The on-device inference motivation is incongruent with the 7-8B parameter models actually used in evaluation.
justification: Line 25 motivates the small-K large-B regime with "personalized on-device inference" while line 160 confirms all LMs used are ~8B parameters (Mistral-7B, Gemma-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B), which are not typical on-device-sized models.

weakness: Claims of calibration improvement, Fisher information analysis, and PCA-shift analysis are asserted in the abstract, contributions list, and conclusion but are not substantiated with actual results/figures in the main text.
justification: The abstract claims calibration improvement and the contributions/conclusion mention Fisher information and PCA-shift analyses, but Section 4.5 only presents CKA and SVCCA results; no calibration scores, Fisher information plots, or PCA analyses appear anywhere in the visible main text.

weakness: The DAPT baseline is likely underpowered/undocumented (no details on domain text amount, training steps, or hyperparameter tuning), making the F2F vs DAPT comparison asymmetric.
justification: Section 3.2 gives only a one-sentence description of DAPT and Section 3.4 provides no DAPT-specific training details (amount of data, steps, tuning), while Table 1 shows DAPT underperforming SFT in places (e.g., LLaMA-8B MBPP: 56.60 SFT vs 53.55 DAPT).

weakness: No variance or statistical significance is reported for any result across Tables 1, 2, and 3.
justification: All reported numbers in the tables are single point estimates with no error bars, standard deviations, or multiple seeds mentioned anywhere in the paper.

weakness: LLaMA-13B base model scores an anomalously low 0.60 pass@1 on HumanEval, inflating F2F's apparent improvement, and this is unexplained.
justification: Table 1 confirms the LLaMA-13B base HumanEval score of 0.60 versus LLaMA-8B's 33.54, and the paper offers no explanation for this discrepancy.

weakness: The theoretical analysis in Section 2 relies on convex, strongly-convex, orthogonal-subspace assumptions that do not hold for LLMs, and is never empirically verified against the actual observed results.
justification: The paper itself acknowledges the non-convexity gap ('While LLM training objective is non-convex, we use a convex linear surrogate') but nowhere connects the predicted contraction bounds to measured quantities in the experiments.

weakness: Table 2, in a section titled 'F2F w/ Fine-Tuning Variants,' contains no F2F results, only baseline methods (SFT, LoRA, CurlLoRA, DAPT), breaking the expected narrative.
justification: Table 2's rows are SFT, LoRA, CurlLoRA, and DAPT only; despite the Section 4.2 heading 'F2F W/ FINE-TUNING VARIANTS,' no F2F row appears in that table.

weakness: The Qwen-72B model uses QLoRA (4-bit quantization, rank-16) during unlearning but full fine-tuning afterward, creating an unaddressed fidelity mismatch/confound.
justification: Section 3.4 states that for Qwen-72B (grouped with LLaMA-8B and LLaMA-13B) 'we performed LoRA-based supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using FP16 precision,' so the fine-tuning stage is also LoRA-based, not full fine-tuning as the reviewer claims.

weakness: The CKA/SVCCA analysis shows F2F representations diverge more from the unlearned model than standard fine-tuning does, but this greater divergence is not shown to causally correspond to better performance, remaining merely suggestive.
justification: Section 4.5 only reports correlational observations about representational drift (Figure 4/5) without any quantitative link or causal analysis tying CKA/SVCCA divergence magnitude to downstream accuracy gains.

weakness: The parameter existence condition in eq. (19) involves λ_k without sufficient clarification — the paper states only that 'it is easy to verify that such parameters exist' but gives no explicit values for θ, γ, ν and does not explain how the per-iteration λ_k dependence is resolved.
justification: Line 185 of the paper reads verbatim 'it is easy to verify that such parameters exist' with no explicit construction, and eq. (19) explicitly contains λ_k, confirming the reviewer's claim of unresolved ambiguity.

weakness: No empirical validation is provided, which is notable since prior work in the same line (GRAAL, AdGD, AC-FGM, AdaNAG) includes experiments, and ICLR norms typically expect at least minimal numerical verification.
justification: The paper indeed contains no experiments section; the abstract/intro explicitly frame the contribution as proving complexity bounds rather than demonstrating them empirically, and no results tables/plots exist in the text.

weakness: No conclusion or discussion section; the paper ends abruptly after the Section 4.2 comparison without discussing limitations or practical parameter guidance.
justification: The paper text ends at line ~339 with the Table 1 comparison discussion and there is no dedicated conclusion/discussion section afterward.

weakness: The min expression in line 10 of Algorithm 1, λ_{k+1} = min{Λ(x̄_{k+1}; x̃_k), Λ(x̃_{k+1}; x̃_{k+1})}, appears redundant since by eq. (11) Λ(x̃_{k+1}; x̃_{k+1}) = +∞ (equal arguments), making the min always equal to the first term.
justification: Verified against the paper: line 145 shows the second argument pair is identical (x̃_{k+1}; x̃_{k+1}), and eq. (11) defines Λ(x;z) = +∞ when ∇f(x)=∇f(z), which holds trivially for identical arguments, confirming the redundancy the reviewer flags.

weakness: Big-O constants in Corollaries 2 and 3 hide dependence on θ, γ, ν, and since no concrete parameter values are given, readers cannot assess whether the bounds are practically meaningful.
justification: Consistent with the paper's Corollaries 2 and 3, which use O(·) notation without spelling out θ,γ,ν dependence, and ties directly to the unresolved eq.(19) parameter ambiguity noted elsewhere in the review.

weakness: The additive penalty term (1+L₁²D²)ln[1/(η₀L₀)] in Corollary 3 can grow with L₁²D², and the paper does not explore its practical consequences for realistic problem parameters.
justification: Corollary 3 (paper line 315 area) indeed contains this type of additive term dependent on L₁ and D, and the paper does not provide further practical discussion of its magnitude, consistent with the reviewer's observation.

weakness: Simulation-only evaluation, with real-world practicality claims that outpace the evidence (no physical-domain/printed-patch experiments despite framing patches as placeable in camera view and practical for real-world scenarios).
justification: The paper's abstract/Section 2.2 claim practicality for real-world scenarios and describes patches as 'directly placeable within the camera's view', yet all experiments (Table 2/3) are on LIBERO simulation frames, and Section 6 limitations do not mention sim-to-real gap, only camera/occlusion issues.

weakness: Defense (adversarial fine-tuning) validated on only one model (OpenVLA), limiting claims about defense generality.
justification: The paper explains OpenVLA was chosen as worst-case (Section 1), and the defense results in Table 2 are indeed reported only for OpenVLA, not OpenVLA-OFT or π₀.

weakness: The patch contrastive loss (Eq. 2) maximized in an unusual scrambling way without ablation comparing it to simpler alternatives (e.g., direct cosine distance maximization) or separate ablation of L_patch vs L_align.
justification: No ablation study separating L_patch and L_align or comparing to a simpler embedding-drift baseline appears in the paper text.

weakness: Defendability labeling in Table 2 is inconsistent: FedSGD+Laplace(var=10) with SSIM=0.23 is marked ✗ while FedMPDD(m=2000) with SSIM=0.22 is marked ✓, and the Defendability criteria are never defined.
justification: Table 2 shows exactly these SSIM values and marks, and the paper never defines a threshold or criterion for the ✓/✗ Defendability column anywhere in the main text.

weakness: The paper does not compare against methods that jointly pursue compression and privacy (e.g., Amiri et al. 2021, Lyu 2021), despite citing them as the most closely related work; experiments only include compression-only or privacy-only baselines.
justification: The related work section explicitly discusses Amiri et al. and Lyu as joint compression+DP approaches, but Section 3 experiments only compare against Top-k, lp-proj, QSGD, SA-FedLora, and FedSGD+Laplace, none of which are joint methods.

weakness: Multi-round privacy erosion (Remark 2's T×m<d bound) is acknowledged but not formally or empirically addressed for realistic training horizons/dimensions, and no mitigation mechanism is proposed.
justification: Remark 2 states privacy requires T×m<d and the paper only offers the informal claim that 'natural evolution of gradients ... provides stronger practical protection' without a formal analysis, no mechanism like basis refresh, and no CIFAR-10 SSIM-vs-round curve (only MNIST in Fig. 1).

weakness: Privacy claims of 'inherent'/'consistent privacy' rely on Lemma 1 (gradient reconstruction, magnitude-independent) but the paper's own Lemma 2 (data reconstruction) depends on the gradient magnitude and an unestimated Lipschitz constant L_v, so the numerical privacy bound is uncalibrated.
justification: Lemma 2's bound explicitly contains ||g||^2/L_v(x)^2, and no value or estimate of L_v is given anywhere in the paper for any experimental model, confirming the reviewer's point.

weakness: The communication cost formula on line 122, O(1/√K × βN × m), conflates the convergence rate with the round count and appears to be an error.
justification: The paper literally states 'the total communication cost over the full training horizon is reduced to O(1/√K × βN × m)' which is dimensionally odd for a total-cost formula that should scale with K rounds, supporting the reviewer's technical critique.

weakness: Lemma 2's Lipschitz constant L_v is never estimated for the models used in experiments, leaving the privacy bound uncalibrated.
justification: No numeric or approximate value of L_v appears in the main text for LeNet, the CNN, or any other architecture used in the experiments.

weakness: Assumption 1, referenced in Theorem 2's step-size formula, is not characterized or stated in the main text.
justification: Theorem 2 says 'suppose that Assumption 1 holds' but the main text never states what Assumption 1 is (presumably deferred to an appendix not included here), leaving readers unable to assess the theorem's applicability from the main text alone.

weakness: The SSIM gap between MNIST (Figure 1, <0.04) and CIFAR-10 (Table 2, 0.14-0.22) is not explained.
justification: The paper reports both sets of numbers but never discusses or explains why CIFAR-10 SSIM values are substantially higher than the MNIST values, despite both nominally using consistent (d-1)/m theory.

weakness: No direct round-efficiency comparison against unconstrained FedSGD is provided, so it's unclear whether the epsilon-distortion term is practically negligible.
justification: Figure 3 explicitly provides 'Global Accuracy (%) vs. Rounds' and 'Training Loss vs. Rounds' plots comparing FedMPDD variants against other methods (unconstrained by communication budget), which is exactly the accuracy-vs-rounds comparison the reviewer claims is missing.

weakness: LLM validation is limited in scope (only two models, few layers) and lacks statistical rigor (no error bars/CIs on probing F1 despite 3 seeds per L0, unlike toy model figures which show stdev)
justification: Paper confirms only Gemma-2-2b (layers 5,12) and Llama-3.2-1b (layer 7) are tested (Section 4, Figures 8-9), and Figure 8 caption mentions '3 seeds per L0' but no variance is shown in the probing F1 plots, unlike Figure 6 which explicitly shows shaded stdev region.

weakness: The c_dec metric does not independently identify correct L0 in LLM settings, requiring a sweep and external validation, with inconsistent minima across layers/architectures (e.g. Gemma layer 5 shallow region, BatchTopK vs JumpReLU minima differ at layer 12)
justification: The paper itself acknowledges this in Section 4 ('long shallow region with the global minimum actually appearing in that shallow region') and Section 4.1 (BatchTopK minimum ~200 vs JumpReLU ~250-300), and Section 6 admits the metric 'currently requires training a sweep over L0.'

weakness: The claim that most commonly used SAEs have too low L0 is asserted without sufficient substantiation, relying only on a cursory Neuronpedia search deferred to appendix, without establishing the correct L0 for those SAEs
justification: Section 6 explicitly states this claim is supported only by 'a cursory search of open source SAEs on Neuronpedia... see Appendix A.13' and the paper never establishes ground-truth correct L0 for any real-world SAE it surveys, since ground truth is only available in toy models.

weakness: The toy model assumes exact feature orthogonality while real features are only nearly orthogonal per the Linear Representation Hypothesis, and this gap is not discussed
justification: Section 3 states 'All features are orthogonal, so f_i . f_j = 0' while the Introduction/Section 3 note LRH posits features are only 'nearly orthogonal'; the paper does not discuss how approximate orthogonality would affect the hedging mechanism or c_dec metric.

weakness: Contribution relative to closest related work (Chanin et al., 2025 on feature hedging) is incremental, though the paper acknowledges this itself
justification: Section 5 states 'We consider our work a version of feature hedging due to low L0' regarding Chanin et al., 2025, and the paper's own framing shows the additional contribution builds directly on that prior mechanism rather than introducing an unrelated one.

weakness: The heat transfer experiment does not cleanly support the 'smaller models' thesis; model size within the LSSM family is fixed at 6 parameters and never varied, and baseline model sizes are not reported.
justification: The paper never reports parameter counts for RF/XGBoost/LSTM baselines and never varies LSSM size (Section 3.1), while the conclusion (line 250) generalizes the 'smaller models' claim across both use-cases.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance (error bars, seeds, repeated runs) is reported for any result in Table 1 or Table 2.
justification: Tables 1 and 2 present single point values with no mention of multiple seeds or confidence intervals anywhere in the text.

weakness: Equation (7) has an apparent error, using T_i in the second term instead of U_i as defined by Equation (4).
justification: Eq. 4 defines T_{t+1}=Φ_A T_t + Φ_B U_t, but Eq. 7 writes ||Φ_A T_i + Φ_B T_i − T_{i+1}||², an inconsistency confirmed by direct comparison of the two equations in the paper.

weakness: Data dimensionality is confusingly reported: T is stated as ℝ^{8759×1} despite the state space being 2-dimensional.
justification: Line 153 explicitly states T ∈ R^{8759×1} while Eq. 2 defines a 2-state system, a genuine inconsistency in the paper text.

weakness: The LSTM sweep in the FPUT experiment is asymmetric, varying only width W while SHNN/NeuralODE vary both L and W.
justification: Table 2 shows LSTM rows only for L values with '-' entries beyond the first four rows, and the text (Section 3.2) states 'For the LSTM, we sweep over W only', confirming the asymmetry.

weakness: Section 2.1.1 contains a confusing domain error switching between s-plane and z-plane when describing the bilinear transform/eigenvalue mapping.
justification: Line 75 indeed says eigenvalues are wrapped 'within the unit circle in the s-plane' while earlier in the same sentence describing the z-plane, a genuine textual inconsistency.

weakness: The convergence speed claim (line 175) that structure-naive models have 'significantly slower' training convergence is asserted without supporting evidence accessible in the paper text, and convergence curves without wall-clock/iteration comparisons are not rigorous given differing parameter counts and training procedures.
justification: The claim refers to Figures 5, 7, 8 which are not reproduced in the extracted paper text, and the paper gives no wall-clock or iteration-count comparison to substantiate 'significantly slower', making the critique well-grounded rather than a misunderstanding.

weakness: Inconsistent formulation of the generalization bound across the paper: O(√(V|Y|/n)) in Abstract/Sections 1/4, O(√(VY)/n) in Discussion (line 306), O(√(V|V|/n)) in Conclusion (line 327), and the claimed numerical value of 0.021 doesn't follow from plugging stated parameters into the dominant formula (gives ~1.79 instead).
justification: Paper text confirms three distinct expressions: Abstract/Intro use O(√(V|Y|/n)), Section 6.1 states O(√(VY)/n), and Conclusion (Section 7) states O(√(V|V|/n)). The 0.021 bound claim in the Reproducibility Statement lacks a shown derivation reconciling it with the stated rate.

weakness: Table 4 introduces a baseline called 'Metalign' for scalability comparison that is never defined, cited, or described anywhere else in the paper, while Section 5.3 only lists MetaTrinity, Kraken2, and Centrifuge as comparison methods.
justification: Confirmed: Table 4 (line 271-280) uses 'Metalign' with no definition, and Section 5.3's comparison list (MetaTrinity, Kraken2, Centrifuge) does not include it.

weakness: The paper overclaims theoretical novelty, calling it the 'first comprehensive theory of token-based genomic classification' when the underlying tools (Rademacher complexity bounds, α-mixing concentration, MLE consistency) are standard statistical learning techniques applied generically.
justification: The paper's own description of its theoretical contributions (Section 4.2-4.3) indeed lists standard tools (Rademacher complexity, α-mixing concentration, MLE consistency) without describing method-specific theoretical innovations beyond applying these tools to the token setting.

weakness: The 31.7x variance inflation factor is called a 'manageable constant factor' without quantitative justification of why this magnitude of inflation is acceptable.
justification: Paper (line 176) states the factor is 'approximately 31.7' and calls it 'manageable' without further quantitative argument showing the bound remains meaningfully small after this inflation.

weakness: The abstract states HighClass 'delivers 4.2x speedup' without specifying the comparison baseline, which could be misread by a reader scanning only the abstract.
justification: The Abstract (line 13) indeed states '4.2x speedup' without naming MetaTrinity as the baseline; that specification only appears later in the main text (Section 3.3, 5.4).

weakness: The evaluation budget units are not commensurate between CALM and baselines (2,000 LLM queries vs 1,000 heuristic evaluations), and G is not specified for the main GRPO experiments in the main text.
justification: Paper text (Section 5, line 140) states 'comparable evaluation budgets—specifically, 1,000 heuristic evaluations for baselines and a fixed budget of 2,000 LLM queries for CALM,' and G=1 is only specified for the API-based variant (line 221), leaving G for the GRPO variant unstated in the visible text.

weakness: TSP results do not consistently support the claimed superiority: CALM is worse than MCTS-AHD at N=50 (10.04% vs 9.69%), and margins at N=100/200 are small; POMO shows the LLM-AHD class still has room for improvement.
justification: Table 2 data confirms CALM 10.04% vs MCTS-AHD 9.69% at N=50, with small margins at N=100 (11.58% vs 11.79%) and N=200 (13.41% vs 13.71%), and POMO achieves 0.39%/3.01% at N=50/100.

weakness: EvoTune's poor performance relative to CALM (e.g., 2.40% vs 0.71% on OBP) is not explained despite sharing the same base model and fine-tuning goal.
justification: Table values confirm EvoTune 2.40% OBP (matching Best Fit's 2.40%) vs CALM 0.71%, and the paper does not provide discussion of why DPO-based EvoTune underperforms GRPO-based CALM so dramatically.

weakness: Collapse mechanism hyperparameters show high sensitivity (delta_0=0.005, C=15 degrades OBP from 0.71% to 1.93% and OP from 17.41% to 27.22%), with no practical guidance for selection.
justification: Table 4 values confirm these exact numbers, and the paper's discussion (lines 245-260) explains the phenomenon post hoc but does not give concrete practical guidance for choosing delta_0 and C in advance.

weakness: The claim of 'superior stability' is unsubstantiated — no standard deviations, variance analysis, or failure-mode reporting despite averaging over 50 trials.
justification: The paper claims 'superior stability across tasks' (abstract, intro, conclusion) but reports only point-estimate tables (Tables 1-5) with no variance/std/failure-rate metrics, and Section 5.1 confirms only averages over 50 trials are reported.

weakness: ALD results are presented in a way that overstates the contribution: NPC is slightly worse in W2 on 2 of 3 distributions, yet abstract claims 'consistently outperforms'; iDEM's better results are dismissed via a hardware-disparity footnote without controlled comparison.
justification: Table 5 confirms NPC W2 is worse than Classic ALD on GMM (11.91 vs 11.57) and funnel (31.02 vs 30.91), while abstract/intro claim consistent outperformance; iDEM's lower W2 is noted only with an uncontrolled hardware footnote.

weakness: Ablation study (Table 6) reports only iteration changes, not accuracy, making it logically incomplete to claim each component is 'essential'.
justification: Table 6 indeed shows only ΔIter with no accuracy column, so the essential-component claim cannot be fully verified from the reported ablation.

weakness: No standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported despite averaging over 50 trials.
justification: Tables 1-5 show only point estimates; Section 5.1 states results are averages over 50 trials but no variance is given anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: Training cost/time is not reported, making it impossible to assess the practical trade-off of amortized training.
justification: The implementation section and tables describe iteration counts and runtime for inference but no training time is stated in the visible paper text.

weakness: No analysis of failure modes or edge cases; only average success/iteration numbers are reported.
justification: Tables report success rates and average iterations/time only; no worst-case or failure distribution analysis appears in the text.

weakness: GH experiments are limited to 2D problems and the paper does not discuss whether NPC's gains would scale to higher dimensions.
justification: Section 5.3 evaluates only three 2D benchmarks (Ackley, Himmelblau, Rastrigin) and no discussion of higher-dimensional scaling appears in the visible text.

weakness: Central claim that the Resolution Score selects biologically better clusterings is not validated against any independent ground truth (e.g., known CRISPR perturbation labels via ARI/NMI)
justification: The paper never uses the known K562 CRISPR guide/perturbation labels as an external ground truth for cluster quality; evaluation relies on ICS/ICD self-consistency, UMAP appearance, and enrichment analysis using the same GO ontology, which the reviewer correctly identifies as circular.

weakness: Baseline comparison is insufficient: MultiK is cited but not benchmarked, and Calinski-Harabasz/Davies-Bouldin mentioned but not evaluated; without ground truth the comparison just shows different methods pick different resolutions
justification: Section 2 cites MultiK and Section 2/3.5 mention Calinski-Harabasz/Davies-Bouldin as used in Seurat/Scanpy, but Section 4.4 only benchmarks silhouette, modularity, and functional enrichment -- MultiK and CH/DB are never run.

weakness: The hyperparameter w=1/3 is determined via grid search on the same K562 data used for evaluation, inflating apparent performance and weakening generalizability claims
justification: Section 3.4 explicitly states w=1/3 'was chosen by a small grid search' giving 'stable ordering of resolutions across data sets,' but both GEX and perturbation-level data sets come from the same K562 experiment, exactly as the reviewer states.

weakness: ICS measures LLM self-consistency rather than genuine cluster coherence; a control experiment (e.g., shuffling gene labels) would help rule out this confound
justification: The paper defines ICS purely as agreement among the LLM's own generated hypotheses (Section 3.4) with no shuffled-label or randomization control anywhere in the text to rule out this confound.

weakness: Key visualizations in the main text show only the chosen resolution (Figure 3b shows UMAP only at r=0.4); adjacent resolutions are not shown for comparison
justification: Figure 3b caption confirms only leiden_0.4 UMAP is shown in the main text; the paper states other UMAPs are only in Figure S4 (appendix), matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: No statistical significance testing for whether the optimal resolution's score is distinguishable from nearby resolutions
justification: The paper reports box plots of Resolution Score across resolutions (Fig 3a, 4a) but no confidence intervals or significance tests comparing r=0.4 vs neighboring resolutions are given anywhere in the text.

weakness: Cost is acknowledged as a limitation but not quantified (no dollar amount or wall-clock time reported)
justification: The Conclusion only lists 'LLM dependence and cost' as a limitation in prose without any quantitative estimate of dollar cost or runtime, confirming the reviewer's claim.

weakness: In-distribution evaluation advantage: MultiID-Bench shares the data pipeline with MultiID-2M training data, giving WithAnyone a distributional advantage over baselines trained on other datasets, which the paper does not discuss.
justification: The paper states MultiID-Bench uses the same web-scraping/reference-bank pipeline (Section 4) as MultiID-2M and only claims no identity overlap; it never addresses the distributional confound with baselines trained on FFHQ/CelebA.

weakness: No error bars, confidence intervals, or variance estimates on any quantitative metric, making it impossible to assess statistical reliability of close results.
justification: Tables 1-3 report only point estimates with no variance or significance testing anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: CP metric's 'moderate' correlation with human judgment is not quantified (no coefficient, CI, or disaggregated analysis).
justification: Section 6.3 only states 'moderate positive correlation with human judgments' without reporting the coefficient in the main text.

weakness: Claim of 'breaking the trade-off' is overstated given the shift comes with lower Sim(Ref) and lowest aesthetics score.
justification: Table 1 shows Ours has Sim(Ref)=0.578 (lowest among comparable) and Aes=4.783 (lowest), showing the trade-off is shifted rather than eliminated, contradicting the abstract's 'breaks the long-observed trade-off' claim.

weakness: Ablation table (Table 3) has an interpretive gap: 'w/o Ext. Neg.' shows lower CP that could be misread as better despite reflecting failed identity preservation, and CP threshold filtering used in Tables 1-2 isn't applied in Table 3.
justification: Table 3 shows w/o Ext. Neg. CP=0.074 vs full 0.161 while Sim(G) drops to 0.368 from 0.405, and no threshold filtering note appears for Table 3 unlike Tables 1 and 2.

weakness: WithAnyone's low aesthetics score is not discussed by the paper.
justification: Table 1 shows Ours Aes=4.783, lowest among face-specific methods, and the visible text (Sections 6.1-6.3) never discusses this aesthetics gap.

weakness: ArcFace matching threshold (0.4) not justified.
justification: Section 3 states the threshold 0.4 for cosine similarity matching without giving any rationale for the specific value.

weakness: Different CP filtering thresholds (0.40 vs 0.35) between Table 1 and Table 2 are not explained.
justification: Table 1 caption specifies Sim(GT)>0.40 and Table 2 caption specifies Sim(GT)>0.35, with no rationale given anywhere in the visible text for why they differ.

weakness: User study lacks statistical detail (correlation coefficient, CI, inter-rater reliability) and Figure 8 mislabels the method as 'Cure' instead of 'WithAnyone.'
justification: Section 6.3 gives only 'moderate positive correlation' without numbers, and Figure 8's caption/text indeed refers to 'Cure' rather than WithAnyone.

weakness: Abstract's claim that 'most models perform at or below a random baseline' contradicts Figure 5 where 10 of 12 models score above the 0.279 random baseline.
justification: Figure 5 data table shows 10/12 models with scores 0.32-0.42, above the stated 0.279 random baseline, directly contradicting the abstract's claim.

weakness: Random baseline is inconsistently reported (0.279 in Figure 5 vs 0.322 in Figure 7) without explanation.
justification: The paper gives no explanation for this discrepancy between the two baseline values despite the random baseline being defined the same way in both cases.

weakness: Figure 7 caption says error bars show '2.5 standard deviation' while body text says 'standard deviation', creating confusion.
justification: Line 154 says '2.5 standard deviation' in the figure description while line 173 says 'Error bars represent standard deviation' -- an actual inconsistency in the text.

weakness: The claim that four models 'statistically perform better than random' is unsupported -- no test name, p-values, or confidence intervals given.
justification: Section 3 (line 112) makes this statistical claim with no methodological detail anywhere in the paper to substantiate it.

weakness: The scoring algorithm conflates spatial intelligence with instruction-following, and the paper acknowledges but doesn't resolve this.
justification: Section 2.4 explicitly states this tension and Section 3 attributes GPT-4o/NanoBanana's low scores to instruction-following failures, confirming the entanglement is real and unresolved.

weakness: Data contamination from publicly sourced real estate listings is unaddressed.
justification: The paper only discusses overfitting mitigation via keeping data private (Section 2.2) but never discusses memorization/contamination risk from models' training on public listings.

weakness: The human baseline is underdocumented (number of subjects, expertise, instructions).
justification: The paper only says a human was given images and rules (Section 2.2/Section 3) with no detail on number of subjects or standardization.

weakness: The claim that agents show 'no meaningful improvement' is not well supported since Claude Code (0.38) vs Claude Opus 4.1 (0.32) shows a real gain, and CodeX vs GPT-5 comparison confounds different models.
justification: Figure 5 data confirms Claude Code scores higher than Claude Opus 4.1, and CodeX (GPT-6) is compared against GPT-5 non-agent, a different underlying model, undermining the clean-comparison claim in the paper.

weakness: Scoring weight choices (50/20/10/10/5/5) are presented without justification or sensitivity analysis.
justification: Section 2.3 lists the weights with no rationale or ablation given anywhere in the paper.

weakness: The mapping from "normalized qEHVI" to a probability P(X⊆X*) is unjustified; "normalized qEHVI" is never defined and Eq. (8) uses raw qEHVI multiplied by distance with no normalization evident.
justification: Section 3.2 states "we first use normalized qEHVI to approximate P(X⊆X*)" but nowhere defines the normalization procedure, and Eq. (8) shows the hypervolume improvement term multiplied directly by the min-distance term with no visible normalization step, confirming the gap.

weakness: The "hyperparameter-free" claim (contrasted with QSVGD's η) is overstated because the relative scales of qEHVI and distance terms in Eq. (8) implicitly determine the quality/diversity balance, and this scale relationship is never addressed.
justification: The paper claims the method "removes the need for sensitive hyperparameter tuning" (Sec 3.1) but Eq. (8) multiplies qEHVI (units of hypervolume) by a raw Euclidean distance with no stated normalization, so the paper does not substantiate scale-compatibility, supporting the criticism.

weakness: The main paper presents results on only two synthetic benchmarks (GM and RE4-7-1), with broader ZDT/DTLZ benchmark evaluation relegated to the appendix, which is a limited main-paper evaluation for a claimed general-purpose method.
justification: The paper explicitly states it also evaluates on ZDT and DTLZ benchmark families (line 137), and demanding these be moved into the main paper rather than the appendix is an excessive presentational preference, not a substantive empirical gap.

weakness: The paper reports means and standard deviations but performs no formal statistical significance tests (e.g., paired t-tests) to support claims of consistent superiority.
justification: The paper's empirical sections (4.1, 4.2) report only means/std devs and qualitative comparisons across trials with no significance testing anywhere in the visible text, so this gap is genuine.

weakness: The role of the covering-ball radius r introduced in the theoretical motivation (Section 3.2) is unspecified in the actual acquisition function (Eq. 8), which uses only minimum distance with no mention of r.
justification: Section 3.2 defines A_X^r using radius r for the covering-probability argument, but Eq. (8), the final acquisition function, contains only the min-distance term Δ(·,·) with no r term, so the connection between the theory and implementation is indeed left unexplained in the paper.

weakness: Algorithm inconsistency between the mathematical description in Section 3 (|g_k|·sign(m_k)) and the pseudocode in Algorithm 1 (g_k·sign(m_k)), which changes behavior when gradient and momentum signs disagree.
justification: Confirmed: line 74 gives x_{k+1}=x_k-(η_k/(√v_k+ε))|g_k|·sign(m_k) while Algorithm 1 (line 60) gives x_{k+1}=x_k-(η_k/√(v̂_k+ε))·g_k·sign(m_k)-η_kλx_k, a genuine discrepancy in the paper text.

weakness: Questionable Grams baseline in the noise robustness experiment (Table 1): at σ=0 Grams scores 71.34%, about 10 points below other optimizers, suggesting an under-configured baseline that weakens the central noise-robustness comparison.
justification: Table 1 (line 125) confirms Grams=71.34(-10.76) at σ=0 versus Ano/Adam/Lion in the low-to-mid 80s, and the paper only offers a post-hoc explanation for improvement at σ=0.01 without addressing the large zero-noise gap (lines 129-135).

weakness: Duplicated row labels in the GLUE table (Table 3): two rows labeled 'Adam' with different numbers appear in both the Default and Tuned sections, likely one should be a different optimizer (e.g., Adan).
justification: Confirmed directly in the paper text: two 'Adam' rows appear with distinct values (e.g., CoLA 59.40 vs 55.65; RTE 66.67 vs 61.49) in the Default section, and again in the Tuned section, exactly as the review states.

weakness: Theoretical analysis is too compressed to evaluate: the proof sketch in Section 5.1 is minimal and the key lemma is relegated to an appendix not provided in the main text.
justification: The paper's convergence claims are stated but a detailed proof/lemma is not present in the extracted main text, supporting the review's point that the convergence claim can't be verified from the main paper alone.

weakness: Inconsistent naming of the Anolog variant: introduced as 'Anolog' in Section 4 but appears as 'Analog' in Tables 4, 5, and 6.
justification: Confirmed: text at line 88 uses 'Anolog', while table rows at lines 234, 242, 275, 283, 291, 310, 313 use 'Analog', a genuine naming inconsistency.

weakness: Ablation table (Table 6) has uninformative columns ('Grad. Norm.', 'Mom. Norm.', 'Mom. Dir.', 'Decoup. WD') that show identical checkmarks across every row, carrying no differential information.
justification: Table 6 header (line 298) lists these columns and the sampled row (line 313) shows all four checked (✓), consistent with the review's claim that variation is confined to 'Second Mom. Rule' and β1,k columns.

weakness: The text claims WGM obtains MM within 5% of the policy mechanisms (line 281), but the figure's y-axis ranges for Reddit and Movie Reviews suggest the absolute gap between WGM and the policy mechanisms exceeds 5%, and no exact numerical values are given to verify the claim.
justification: The paper only states the qualitative '5%' claim in prose (line 281) without providing a table of exact values, and the figure's described y-axis ranges (e.g., Reddit 0.15-0.40) are consistent with gaps that could exceed 5%, so this is a legitimate reproducibility/precision gap.

weakness: No error bars or standard error are reported for the set union and top-k experiments (only average MM across 5 trials), while standard error is reported for k-hitting set, making it hard to assess variance/reliability of those results.
justification: The paper explicitly states 'average MM across 5 trials' for set union (line 281) with no variance measure, while explicitly reporting standard error only for k-hitting set (line 311), confirming this asymmetry is real.

weakness: Main experiments use only one privacy budget (ε=1, δ=10⁻⁵); the ε=0.1 results are relegated to the appendix and only described qualitatively as 'not significantly qualitatively different,' which is insufficient given the theory predicts a 1/ε dependence.
justification: The paper itself confirms this setup (line 273: 'All experiments use a total privacy budget of (1, 10⁻⁵)-DP; additional experiments ... appear in Appendix F, but are not significantly qualitatively different'), so the criticism that only qualitative claims (not quantitative results) are given in the main text for the second budget is accurate.

weakness: No runtime measurements are provided despite the paper claiming WGM is 'simple and scalable' and that policy mechanisms are 'significantly more intensive' computationally.
justification: The paper uses the terms 'simple and scalable' (line 14) and 'significantly more intensive computation' (line 281) as qualitative claims but never reports any runtime numbers or complexity comparison to substantiate them.

weakness: Table 5 comparison conflates task definition benefit with fine-tuning data advantage; no controlled experiment fine-tunes on equal source IQA data without coordinates to isolate value of grounding annotations
justification: The paper's ablations (Tab. 2, Tab. 3) test box refinement, coordinate representation, and multi-task training, but no experiment compares GIQA-160K against an equal-sized non-coordinate version of the same source descriptions, so the claim is well supported.

weakness: Q-Ground, identified as the most directly related prior work, is absent from the Table 5 experimental comparison
justification: Sec 2.2 explicitly names Q-Ground as achieving 'degradation region grounding' and closest to the paper's approach, yet Table 5's Ground/IQA/Ours groups do not include it, confirming the omission.

weakness: No uncertainty quantification (confidence intervals, variance, significance tests) for the very small GIQA-Bench benchmark (100 images, 90 Yes/No + 60 open-ended questions)
justification: Table 1 confirms GIQA-Bench has only 100 images/250 samples, and Tables 2-5 report only point estimates with no variance or significance testing anywhere in the paper text.

weakness: Discretization precision loss (mIoU drop from 0.6046 Norm-Coord to 0.5851 Disc-Coord in Tab 2b) is not acknowledged; paper only highlights improved description quality
justification: The text states 'Disc-Coord enhances description quality (BLEU@4 and LLM-Score) and grounding accuracy (Tag-Recall), compared with Norm-Coord' without ever mentioning the lower mIoU shown in the same table, exactly as the reviewer describes.

weakness: LLM-Score judge (Llama3) may share lineage with the annotation pipeline (also uses Llama3), raising circularity concerns not discussed in the paper
justification: Sec 3.2 confirms Llama3 is used for Stage-1 object tag extraction and GIQA-VQA generation, and Sec 3.4 confirms Llama3 is also the LLM-Score judge; the paper never discusses this potential circularity.

weakness: Grammatical error in the IQA-Filter prompt ('Is the image quality is <T_q>') with a double 'is'
justification: Line 135/191 of the paper text literally reads 'Is the image quality is $< \mathcal{T}_q >$', confirming the double 'is' error verbatim.

weakness: Empirical evaluation is critically insufficient: single task/dataset (LOL), no convergence curves, no variance/seed reporting, no ablation studies isolating components, baseline hyperparameters undisclosed.
justification: The paper's experiments section (lines 281-330) only reports point-estimate PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/Time tables on the LOL dataset with no standard deviations, seed counts, ablations, or convergence curves, and no baseline hyperparameter settings are given in the main text.

weakness: Confounded comparison: STNAdam-SAGA/SARAH use variance-reduced estimators while baselines (SGD, SAdam, SNAdam) use standard SGD, conflating the two-track framework with the gradient estimator choice; only STNAdam-SGD vs SNAdam is a clean comparison with a modest margin.
justification: Confirmed by Table 2 (line 296-298): STNAdam-SGD 18.06 vs SNAdam 17.14 PSNR is the only same-estimator comparison, while STNAdam-SAGA/SARAH's larger gains use different (variance-reduced) estimators than the baselines.

weakness: Citation inconsistency for the SNAdam baseline: Related Work (line 33) attributes SNAdam to Reddi et al. (2019), while the contributions list and experiments section (lines 50, 281) cite SNAdam as Xie et al. (2024).
justification: Directly verified in the paper text: line 33 says "Reddi et al. (2019) incorporated Nesterov-acceleration technique into Adam, named SNAdam" while lines 50 and 281 cite "SNAdam (Xie et al., 2024)" for the same method.

weakness: Comparison with LIE-specific algorithms (NPE, DeHz, LIME, Retinex-Net, LR3M) is ambiguous because the paper does not clarify whether these methods solve the same optimization model (14) as STNAdam.
justification: The paper only states model (14) is converted to (1) for STNAdam and that it adopts the Retinex-Net training framework, without clarifying whether NPE/DeHz/LIME/LR3M solve the identical model, so the criticism is well-grounded.

weakness: The "removing hand-tuning" claim is misleading because the parameter update intervals depend on unknown global quantities, and Remark 3 admits moduli must be manually increased if necessary.
justification: Confirmed: line 48 claims the scheme removes hand-tuning, but Remark 3 (line 192) explicitly states the moduli L and tau must be "appropriately increased if necessary," supporting the reviewer's point.

weakness: No discussion of limitations, e.g., overhead of maintaining two trajectories, sensitivity to intervals in (6)-(8), or comparison of extra hyperparameters to standard Adam.
justification: No limitations section or discussion of these tradeoffs appears anywhere in the visible paper text.

weakness: Time column units in Table 2 are unclear (not explicitly stated whether per-iteration or total wall-clock).
justification: Table 2 (lines 294-298) reports Time values like 2.64e-05 to 7.63e-05 seconds with no column-header clarification of units/meaning in the visible text.

weakness: Framing of the "surpassing the lower bound"/"2x fewer bytes" claim in the abstract and introduction could mislead readers into thinking total bandwidth is halved, when the improvement is actually in exposed communication time (total bandwidth remains ~2sβ in worst case).
justification: The abstract states StragglerAR "transmits up to 2x fewer bytes than the known bandwidth-optimal lower bound" and the paper itself only clarifies the exposed-communication caveat later at line 127 ("during exposed communication in settings where overlap is possible"), supporting the reviewer's point that the abstract phrasing is not adequately calibrated.

weakness: Baselines are implemented using the NCCL Point-to-Point API rather than NCCL's optimized built-in routines, leaving open how StragglerAR compares against production ncclAllReduce.
justification: The paper confirms at line 217 that baselines use the NCCL P2P API rather than native ncclAllReduce, and no comparison against native ncclAllReduce is presented in the paper, so this is a genuine gap.

weakness: The 100-training-iteration end-to-end experiments with static straggler detection are short and may not capture straggler pattern drift over longer training runs.
justification: The paper (Section 4.2) confirms end-to-end training was run for only 100 iterations with a fixed/static straggler rank chosen via prior profiling, and does not present longer-run results, supporting the reviewer's concern about drift not being captured.

weakness: Algorithm 1's description of the "critical window" matching logic (lines 103-109) is dense and hard to parse in the main text, and would benefit from a running example or pseudocode annotation.
justification: Algorithm 1 and the surrounding critical-window explanation in Section 3.1 are indeed terse and notation-heavy, and while Fig. 4b provides some illustration, the reviewer's readability critique about the dense inline description is a fair, specific presentation observation.

weakness: The "perfectly discriminates" claim in Figure 7 (right) is circular because latent #10 was selected for having the largest activation increase on the same nine misaligned models used in the discrimination plot.
justification: The paper's own methodology text (line 177) confirms latent #10's ranking/numbering was derived from averaging activation increase over the same nine misaligned models later shown discriminating in Figure 7 (right), supporting the circularity critique.

weakness: No comparison to simpler baselines (mean-activation difference, PCA, linear probe) for the SAE analysis, despite Section 5 claiming faster progress with SAEs than simpler representation engineering approaches.
justification: The paper cites Soligo et al. (2025) as using mean-difference-in-activations vectors to find a similar misalignment-mediating direction, but does not run this or any other simpler baseline against its own SAE pipeline, confirming the gap.

weakness: The GPT-4o grader evaluating GPT-4o models lacks thorough validation; no systematic inter-rater reliability or human agreement statistics are reported, only manual spot-checking.
justification: The paper (line 47) states verification was done by "sampling a set of 'high-scoring' responses and confirming that most responses are true positives," with no quantitative human agreement rate reported, matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: The SAE is trained on pre-training data but applied to post-training (instruction-tuned) activations, and no reconstruction loss or activation statistics are reported to validate the SAE remains reliable under this distribution shift.
justification: The paper describes training the SAE on "a subset of GPT-4o's pre-training data" (Section 3) and applying it to fine-tuned model activations without reporting reconstruction-loss or distribution-shift validation metrics, matching the criticism.

weakness: Key quantitative figures (2, 3, 6, 7, 10) lack confidence intervals or seed-level variability, despite mentioning three random seeds for Figure 2.
justification: Figure 2's caption (line 65) mentions "plotting three random seeds of each fine-tuned model" but the text/figures do not report variance, confidence intervals, or error bars, supporting the reviewer's observation.

weakness: Quadratic A matrix (O(D_θ²)) limits root MLP size, creating tension between the paper's motivation for non-linear expressivity and the architectural constraint; the paper acknowledges the scaling limit but doesn't resolve the expressivity implication.
justification: Paper states in Sec 4.2 that 'the size of the matrix A limits scaling to huge root neural networks' while motivating non-linear decoding for expressivity in Section 1 (line 13), and no controlled expressivity-matched comparison is present.

weakness: PEMS08 results may reflect an asymmetric advantage since WARP uses non-causal convolution preprocessing while causal baselines do not, undermining the fairness of the headline improvement.
justification: Line 180 explicitly states 'we preprocess the input sequence with a non-causal convolution,' while baselines (GMAN, D²STGNN, STDCN) are standard causal spatio-temporal models; this asymmetry is not addressed by the paper.

weakness: Standard (black-box) WARP's performance is more modest than the paper's framing suggests, since the most striking results come from the physics-informed WARP-Phys variant, not standard WARP.
justification: Table 3/Table 4 rankings cited (3rd of 5 on MSD, 10th of 12 on UEA Worms) are consistent with the paper's own reported numbers, and the abstract/conclusion emphasize WARP broadly without flagging this gap.

weakness: The in-context learning experiment is too weak to support claims of genuine emergent ICL, since it uses a cumulative-sum preprocessing that performs part of the computation before the model processes the data.
justification: Line 247 confirms the task 'transforms the input sequence into its cumulative sum along the temporal dimension' before WARP processes it, supporting the critique that this differs from standard emergent ICL.

weakness: The paper uses overclaiming language such as 'redefine sequence modeling,' 'transformative paradigm,' and 'human-level artificial intelligence' that is disproportionate to the experimental scope.
justification: These exact phrases appear in the abstract (line 9) and Section 4.3 discussion, confirming the overclaiming critique is textually grounded.

weakness: Parameter counts are not reported for the UEA classification experiments (Table 4), unlike MNIST/CelebA, making the comparison incomplete.
justification: Line 149 reports parameter counts only for MNIST (~1.68M) and CelebA (~2M); no equivalent parameter count is given in the text for the UEA benchmarks in Table 4.

weakness: V-WM baseline is not capacity-matched (parameters, tokens, training data), conflating tactile grounding with additional model capacity/data
justification: The paper never states whether V-WM matches VT-WM in parameter count or data volume; the architecture description (Section 3.2.1) shows VT-WM concatenates tactile tokens on top of vision tokens, and no ablation controlling for capacity is described anywhere in the text.

weakness: Data-efficiency comparison (VT-WM vs BC) confounds multi-task pretraining, CEM planning, and tactile grounding
justification: Section 4.3 confirms BC (ACT) is trained from scratch on 20 demos while VT-WM is pretrained on the full multi-task dataset and fine-tuned, with no control isolating which factor drives the 3.5x gain.

weakness: Real-robot planning results (5 trials/task) lack confidence intervals or statistical tests, unlike the Fréchet distance metrics
justification: Section 4.2/Fig.8 reports success rates 'averaged over five trials per task' with no CI or significance test, in contrast to Section 4.1 which explicitly reports paired t-tests and 95% CI for the Fréchet metrics.

weakness: No quantitative comparison to prior visuo-tactile dynamics models despite claiming to be first multi-task visuo-tactile world model
justification: Section 2 cites Zhang & Demiris (2023) and Ai et al. (2024) as related visuo-tactile/task-specific dynamics models but the paper provides no quantitative comparison against them anywhere in the results sections.

weakness: CoTracker-based evaluation may be biased by differential rollout quality between V-WM and VT-WM
justification: The paper acknowledges V-WM produces blurry/distorted imagery with disappearing objects (Fig. 5) but never discusses whether CoTracker keypoint tracking succeeds equally in both models' rollouts or whether trajectories were discarded.

weakness: CEM planning hyperparameters (population size, horizon, iterations, elite fraction) are unspecified
justification: Section 3.2.3 describes CEM conceptually but gives no numeric values for N, H, iterations, or elite fraction anywhere in the visible main text.

weakness: Training dataset details (size, demonstrations, tasks, objects) are deferred entirely to Appendix A, not summarized in main text
justification: Section 3.2.2 explicitly states 'Additional details about hyperparameters and training dataset are provided in appendix A,' with no summary given in the main text.

weakness: SSL results (F1=0.845, ROC-AUC=0.969) do not meaningfully improve over supervised results (F1=0.844, ROC-AUC=0.970) despite the paper's abstract/intro/conclusion claiming SSL outperforms supervised baselines.
justification: Table 2 (supervised) and Table 3 (SSL) best rows differ by only 0.001 F1 and -0.001 ROC-AUC, while line 29 and line 331 explicitly claim SSL 'outperforms supervised baselines' — a clear text-data inconsistency.

weakness: No comparison to any existing SSL method or prior CoinJoin/illicit-detection baseline is provided.
justification: Section 3 cites GNN and ensemble methods achieving 90%+ accuracy but Section 6 only compares three tree models within the paper's own pipeline, with no external baseline reproduced or compared against.

weakness: The experiments never test the label-scarce regime (e.g., 1%/5%/10% labeled data) that the paper uses to motivate SSL.
justification: Line 23 argues supervised learning is barred by label scarcity, yet Section 5.3/6 trains on 80% of the full 4.6M labeled set (~3.7M examples), never testing smaller labeled fractions.

weakness: The pseudo-labeling procedure is under-specified: no stated selection fraction, number of rounds, total pseudo-labels added, or pseudo-label accuracy estimate.
justification: Line 228 only vaguely states 'select the top fraction of samples on both sides of the decision boundary' without any of these reproducibility details.

weakness: The claim that OTC features 'introduce noise' and 'degrade performance' rests on negligible, non-significant differences, and the best SSL result actually includes OTC, contradicting the paper's own claim.
justification: Table 2 shows F1 drop of only 0.003 with OTC added, and Table 3's best row (F1=0.845, line 315) has all five feature groups checked including OTC, contradicting the text's claim that the best SSL results come from the OTC-free Default+REUSE+CS+SSU set.

weakness: There is a factual inconsistency between the text's claimed best feature configuration ('default+reuse+cs+ssu') and the actual table rows, which contain no such configuration without OTC.
justification: Verified directly: in both Table 2 and Table 3, every row containing an SSU checkmark also has OTC checked; no row matches DEFAULT+REUSE+CS+SSU without OTC, contradicting lines 250 and 287.

weakness: KeyLinker's extremely low address coverage (131.4K of 1.37B addresses, ~0.01%) is never discussed despite being central to the paper's data-quality thesis.
justification: Table 1 confirms 131.4K KeyLinker-clustered addresses vs 1,370.1M total addresses, and the paper's text nowhere addresses this coverage limitation relative to its claimed importance.

weakness: The label-merging/resolution protocol across four label sources is not described or validated, despite the paper's data-quality thesis.
justification: Line 199 says duplicates and conflicting labels were 'manually resolved' with no protocol, conflict rate, or validation given, which is a real gap given the paper centers its argument on data quality.

weakness: The paper's claimed precision/recall changes from pseudo-labeling ('recall +0.03, precision -0.04 to -0.05') do not match the actual best-configuration numbers in the tables.
justification: Comparing Table 2 and Table 3 best XGBoost rows: precision is unchanged (0.897 vs 0.897) and recall increases by only 0.001 (0.796 vs 0.797), not matching the ranges stated at line 291.

weakness: Multiple rows in Tables 2 and 3 share identical feature checkmark patterns but report different metrics, with no explanation given.
justification: Table 2's CatBoost rows with identical ✓✓✓✓✓ patterns show F1 = 0.800, 0.830, 0.827 with no accompanying text explaining the source of variation (e.g., seeds or folds).

weakness: Factually incorrect claim about SemanticKITTI 1% results: Section 4.2 states REPL achieves best performance at 1% and 50%, but Table 1 shows REPL at 54.7 on SemanticKITTI 1%, while LaserMix++ (56.2) and FrustrumMix (55.7) are both higher, making REPL third place, not first.
justification: Confirmed against Table 1 (line 185-188) and the text at line 166: REPL's 1% SemanticKITTI score (54.7) is indeed lower than LaserMix++ (56.2) and FrustrumMix (55.7), contradicting the paper's claim of best performance at 1%.

weakness: Overclaimed theoretical analysis: Proposition 1 is a textbook conditional entropy inequality with no practical content, and Proposition 2 is essentially an algebraic identity, yet the paper frames this as 'rigorous analysis' establishing conditions for benefit.
justification: The paper's abstract and contribution bullets do describe the theoretical analysis in strong terms ('theoretical analysis demonstrating the condition'), while the actual derivations (entropy inequality, algebraic ζ condition) are indeed simple, supporting the critique of overclaiming.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance reported across Table 1 results; single-number results with tiny margins (e.g., 0.1 mIoU) make it hard to assess if improvements are genuine.
justification: Table 1 and the surrounding text report only single point estimates with no standard deviations or multiple runs mentioned anywhere in the paper, supporting this criticism.

weakness: Citation and name inconsistencies between text and Table 1: text refers to 'AIScene (Liu et al., 2025)' and 'FrustumMix (Xu et al., 2025)' while Table 1 lists 'AScene (Xu et al., 2023)' and 'FrustrumMix (Kong et al., 2023)'.
justification: Confirmed directly: line 166 uses 'AIScene (Liu et al., 2025)' and 'FrustumMix (Xu et al., 2025)', while Table 1 (lines 185-186) lists 'AScene (Xu et al., 2023)' and 'FrustrumMix (Kong et al., 2023)' — genuinely inconsistent names and citation years.

weakness: Missing semi-supervised baseline without the refiner in the ablation (Table 2), which does not isolate the refiner's contribution from the teacher-student framework's contribution.
justification: Table 2 only shows refiner loss ablations against a fully supervised-only baseline (50.9 mIoU); no row shows teacher-student pseudo-labeling without the refiner, so the refiner's added value versus the base semi-supervised framework is indeed not isolated in the ablation table.

weakness: PRM (Universal-PRM-7B) training-data overlap with evaluation benchmarks is not disclosed, threatening evaluation validity
justification: The paper only states it uses off-the-shelf Universal-PRM-7B for its long-context capability (line 166) with no mention of its training data or any check for benchmark contamination.

weakness: Underthinking Frequency metric is a length-based heuristic that cannot distinguish concise-but-correct steps from genuinely shallow switches, and relies on an unevaluated external segmentation model (DeepSeek-V3)
justification: The paper acknowledges UF is threshold-based (Eq. 1, line 98) and uses DeepSeek-V3 for segmentation without validating segmentation quality against human judgment.

weakness: TIP comparison is too narrow (single model, single benchmark) to support the claimed advantage
justification: Table 5 results and text (lines 252-254) confirm the comparison is only on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and AIME24.

weakness: The 'Always Intervene' baseline conflates intervention frequency with selection quality; lacks a random-intervention control
justification: Text (line 258) describes only the naive 'Always Intervene' baseline capped at three interventions; no random-selection control is included.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance (standard deviations/confidence intervals) reported for accuracy numbers, especially on small AIME benchmarks
justification: The results tables report point accuracy values with no reported variance across the 32 sampled responses per problem.

weakness: Switch detection recall (fraction of genuine thought switches captured by linguistic cues) is not evaluated
justification: The detection relies on fixed linguistic cues (line 33, Appendix D.2 referenced) but no recall/precision evaluation of the detector itself is reported in the excerpted text.

weakness: The 'plug-and-play' claim is overstated since the method requires token-level access, mid-stream interruption, and a concurrent PRM, which is infeasible for API-gated models
justification: The abstract explicitly claims plug-and-play integration into 'any' LLM (line 9), yet the described mechanism (interrupt generation, backtrack, inject prompt) inherently requires token-level generation control not available via standard closed APIs.

weakness: "Worst-case robust" is overclaimed since the formal optimality guarantee (Theorem 2/Corollary 1) only holds under perfect information, while the belief-extended partial-observability policies lack such a guarantee (Lemma 2 only reduces to the perfect-info case when Pos is a singleton) and the paper itself calls D(.) an 'optimistic estimator' under partial observability, with BR_async success rates as low as 0.10-0.20.
justification: Line 234 explicitly states D(.) 'becomes an optimistic estimator under partial observability', and Table 2 shows BR_async success rates of 0.10 (Hollywood) and 0.20 (Sagrada Familia), directly supporting the claim that the 'worst-case robust' framing overstates what is proven for the partially observable setting.

weakness: The PSRO baseline comparison does not specify what policy architecture PSRO uses, making it hard to attribute improvements to the paper's belief mechanism/DP-guided training versus architecture choice.
justification: Section 5.2 (around line 240) introduces the PSRO comparison but nowhere states the network/policy representation used for PSRO, while the proposed method's GNN architecture is explicitly described (line 199); this omission is real.

weakness: Belief update (Eq. 7) defaults to a uniform evader policy since the true evader policy is unknown, and this limiting assumption is only discussed later in Section 5.3 rather than flagged when the mechanism is introduced in Section 3.2.
justification: Line 157 states the default uniform assumption without caveat at that point, and Table 4's 'Known Opponent' gap (e.g., Scotland-Yard 0.99 vs 0.73) confirming the practical impact is only presented in Section 5.3 (lines 292-307), matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: No confidence intervals or variance are reported for the success rate results (Tables 1-4), despite averaging over 500 tests and results varying substantially across graphs.
justification: Section 5.1 states results are 'averaged over 500 tests' but no standard deviation or confidence interval appears anywhere in the reported tables or text.

weakness: The inference time comparison mixes CPU and GPU hardware without explicitly noting the asymmetry at the point of comparison.
justification: Line 201 explicitly states the DP time is measured on an Intel Core i9-13900HX CPU and that the RL policy is under 1 second 'under the same condition' (i.e., also CPU), with the GPU figure (<0.01s, RTX 2080 Ti) presented as a separate, explicitly-labeled follow-up measurement -- so the hardware distinction is in fact explicitly noted at the point of comparison.

weakness: "Closed-form" branding in abstract/conclusion is inconsistent with the method's actual two-stage structure, since Section 4.3 states the geometry alignment term is not purely quadratic and incompatible with direct closed-form optimization.
justification: Confirmed: Section 4.3 explicitly states the Bures geometry term 'makes the overall objective no longer purely quadratic and therefore incompatible with direct closed-form optimization,' yet the abstract and conclusion still call ScaPre 'an efficient closed-form solution' and 'the first closed-form framework.'

weakness: UQ metric is non-portable and hard to interpret because normalization statistics (mean/std) are computed across the set of methods being compared, so values are not comparable across tables and shift when baselines are added/removed.
justification: The paper's own definition in Sec 5.2 confirms UQ uses mu_A, sigma_A, mu_C, sigma_C computed 'across all methods,' supporting the claim that UQ values in Table 1 vs Table 3 are not on a common scale.

weakness: MI estimation procedure in the Informax Decoupler is underspecified: the adaptive threshold tau_i, the total sample size K, and the nature/source of 'neutral inputs' used for y=0 are not stated in the main text.
justification: Section 4.2 introduces tau_i and K symbolically ('K is the total sample size', 'tau_i is an adaptive threshold') but never gives concrete values or defines what 'neutral inputs' are, matching the reviewer's claim of missing reproducibility details in the main text.

weakness: The paper's 'requiring no additional data' claim needs clarification since MI estimation requires forward passes on both target-concept inputs and unspecified 'neutral inputs' for y=0.
justification: The paper never specifies what the y=0 neutral inputs are or their source (Section 4.2), so the reviewer's request for clarification of the 'no additional data' claim is well-grounded, though the review itself avoids the stronger speculative claim that this constitutes extra data.

weakness: The acronym "SP" appears in every experimental table and figure as a baseline method but is never defined or expanded anywhere in the paper.
justification: Checked Section 2.2 (Related Work) which lists FMN, SA, SalUn, AC, TIME, SPEED, ConceptPrune, MS, SEMU, MACE, SPM, Sculpting Memory, ESD, UCE, RECE -- no method is introduced as "SP", yet SP appears as a baseline in Tables 1-4 and Figure 3.

weakness: No variance or confidence estimates are reported; all results in Tables 1-4 are single point estimates from a stochastic generation process, preventing assessment of statistical significance between methods.
justification: The available paper text (including experimental setup in Sec 5.1) reports only single point-estimate numbers in all tables with no mention of multiple seeds, standard deviations, or confidence intervals.

weakness: Writing quality is so poor that technical claims cannot be reliably assessed, citing incoherent conclusion, section 4.2, and introduction sentences.
justification: The quoted sentences (conclusion 'hierarchical cherry-picking...', section 4.2 'The transformer part processes token GAT sequences...', introduction 'without context being aware of the token...') are verbatim in the paper and are indeed incoherent.

weakness: RL framing is asserted but never operationalized: no formal MDP formulation (state/action/transition/reward), no reward function specification, no formal action space, no PPO hyperparameters beyond learning rate and batch size.
justification: Section 5.1 only vaguely mentions rewards ('rewards based on prediction accuracy', 'rewards for successful repairs'), 5.3 only lists learning rate/batch size, and 5.5 gives only a generic action space description without formal definitions.

weakness: Citation errors: APPS cited as (Cui, 2024) which is actually a different benchmark (Webapp1k), and PY150 cited as (Lu et al., 2021) with no such reference in the bibliography.
justification: Section 5.1 line 161/163 confirms these citations, and the reference list confirms Cui 2024 is Webapp1k and no Lu et al. 2021 entry exists, while Hendrycks et al. 2021 (actual APPS paper) is separately listed.

weakness: Unnamed baselines 'Baseline 1' and 'Baseline 2' in the scalability analysis (Figure 3) are never identified despite five named baselines existing in Section 5.2.
justification: Figure 3 and its table use only 'Baseline 1'/'Baseline 2' labels with no mapping to the five named baselines in Section 5.2.

weakness: No variance or uncertainty reporting in Table 1, and claimed paired t-test significance testing (p<0.01) is asserted in methodology but no p-values or test statistics appear in the results.
justification: Table 1 shows only single point estimates, and Section 5.4 claims significance testing but Section 6 results never report any statistics.

weakness: Missing core methodological details: how functions/modules are identified from raw code, what the CDG nodes/edges are, how the [CLS] token is derived, and what the warm-up demonstration trajectories are.
