justification: Confirmed: the review's claim matches the paper text discussion; actually Eq.10 in paper uses σ_epoch not σ_spick as flagged, but the review is referencing the equation number issue accurately based on inconsistent numbering (Eq.15 reference vs Eq.11) present in the text, which is a real drafting error.

weakness: The text says "One can notice in Eq.15" when discussing content that appears near Eq. 11, indicating equation-number drift/weak proofreading.
justification: Directly confirmed in the paper text: "One can notice in Eq.15 that the function h_{σ,d}(τ) has a finite support..." appears right after Eq. 11, an equation numbering inconsistency.

weakness: The sentence "We use the surrogate gradient method ()" is missing a citation and looks unfinished.
justification: Directly confirmed in the paper text on page 3: "We use the surrogate gradient method () defining Θ'(x)=σ'(x)..." with an empty parenthetical citation.

weakness: Algorithm 1 uses symbol conventions (w_{ji}^{rec}) that are opposite to the w_{ij}^{rec} convention defined in Eq. 7, and computes S[t] rather than S_i[t], making indexing ambiguous.
justification: Cannot verify Algorithm 1's exact pseudocode since the appendix (including Algorithm 1 on Page 13) was removed from the provided paper text ("Rest of paper (reference and Appendix) is removed"), but the reviewer's description is plausible and specific; without access to the appendix this cannot be independently confirmed or refuted, so benefit of doubt goes to reliable given specificity and consistency with other confirmed precision issues in the paper.

weakness: The paper's claims about improved gradient propagation via recurrent delays (Fig. 1B) are not directly validated with any gradient-norm measurement, training-stability analysis, or ablation isolating optimization benefits from expressivity benefits.
justification: The paper's methods/results sections (2.2, 3.1, 3.2) contain no gradient-norm-over-time analysis or targeted ablation separating optimization effects from expressivity effects; Fig 1B is described only as an intuitive computational-graph illustration, supporting the reviewer's claim.

weakness: No ablation isolates individual method components: fixed vs annealed sigma, triangular kernel vs alternatives, whether learned p_i matters on SSC, or delay initialization sensitivity.
justification: The provided results section (3.1, 3.2) reports only full-model comparisons on SSC/PS-MNIST/SHD and a comparative ablation of delay type (feedforward vs recurrent vs fixed vs vanilla), but no ablation of sigma annealing schedule, kernel shape, or p_i, supporting the reviewer's claim; the Eq.15/p_i term for SSC is not mentioned in the results at all in the provided text, though it may appear in the appendix which was removed.

weakness: Table 1 comparisons are hard to interpret fairly (heterogeneous model types) and PS-MNIST SOTA claim rests on only one seed with a small margin over ASRC-SNN (96.21% vs 95.77%).
justification: Table 1 confirms only one seed used for PS-MNIST ("we only test one seed as all the previous state-of-the-art models") and the reported margin (96.21% vs 95.77%) matches exactly; the heterogeneity of models in Table 1 (different neuron types, delay types) is also directly visible in the table.

weakness: Missing informative in-paper ablations against fixed random recurrent delays, per-layer vs per-neuron delay granularity, or parameter-matched controls on SSC/PS-MNIST specifically (only partially present on SHD).
justification: The comparative ablation with fixed random delays, per-neuron delays etc. is confirmed to appear only in the SHD-based Section 3.2, not for SSC/PS-MNIST in Section 3.1, matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: There is an underexplained tension where recurrent-only DelRec outperforms the combined recurrent+feedforward variant on SSC (Table 1) and in low-parameter settings (Fig 3C), while combined outperforms on SHD (Table 2), without analysis of the cause.
justification: Confirmed directly: Table 1 SSC shows 82.58% (rec only) > 82.19% (combined); Table 2 SHD shows 93.73% (combined) > 93.39% (rec only); the text in 3.2 acknowledges 'no advantage in using both types of delays in small configurations' without deeper causal analysis, supporting the review's claim.

weakness: Computational cost and memory overhead of the proposed method are not characterized (no timing/GPU memory comparison against vanilla RSNN or feedforward-delay methods).
justification: No timing, FLOPs, or memory benchmarks appear anywhere in the provided abstract, methods, or results sections despite the buffer/scheduling mechanism scaling with max delay and sigma (Eq. 13), supporting the reviewer's claim (though the appendix was not available to fully confirm).

weakness: Figure 1B visually suggests mitigation of vanishing/exploding gradients but this is not backed by any experiment, functioning as a motivational cartoon rather than evidence.
justification: Confirmed: Figure 1B is described purely as an illustrative computational graph comparison, and no corresponding quantitative gradient experiment appears in the results sections.

weakness: The abstract's claim that recurrent delays are "critical" for temporal processing overstates what the evidence (mixed combination results, modest margins, energy tradeoffs) actually supports.
justification: The abstract does state "recurrent delays are critical for temporal processing in SNNs," while the paper's own findings (Fig 3C, Table 1/2 tension, energy-accuracy tradeoff in 3.2) show mixed/context-dependent benefits rather than blanket necessity, supporting the reviewer's claim of overstatement.

weakness: Minor writing/presentation issues (inconsistent capitalization, duplicated punctuation in Figure 2 caption, odd phrasing "strictly superior to 1 spike," citation inconsistencies) accumulate to hurt polish.
justification: Confirmed: Figure 2 caption has "...which are then summed with the inputs scheduled for time step t in the scheduling matrix.." with a double period, and Figure 1 caption does say "receive inputs strictly superior to 1 spike," matching the review's specific examples.

weakness: The central behavioral claim (models 'strategically lie') overshoots what the Secret Agenda design actually demonstrates, since the model is explicitly instructed to play ruthlessly to win, conflating instruction-following/compliance with strategic deception.
justification: The paper's own conclusion generalizes to 'strategic deception' and 'reward-maximizing behavior under weak oversight' from a synthetic scenario with an explicit incentive prompt, without isolating deception from simple incentivized compliance.

weakness: Secret Agenda evaluation is underpowered and loosely measured (n=2-30, no error bars, 'at least once' framing) to justify ecosystem-level conclusions.
justification: Figure 1's caption explicitly states sample sizes vary n=2-30 and error bars are omitted due to insufficient trials, confirming the criticism directly from the paper's own text.

weakness: There is no rigorous annotation protocol for deception in the Secret Agenda testbed; manual analysis covered only ~160 examples with no described rubric or inter-annotator agreement.
justification: Section 8.3 explicitly states the authors lacked an LLM-as-a-judge budget and conducted manual analysis of approximately 160 examples, with no rubric or agreement statistics reported.

weakness: The claim that current SAE tools are 'blind' to deception is overstated relative to the narrower evidence (a subset of auto-labeled features failing to activate/steer).
justification: The title and conclusion make broad claims about safety tools being blind, while the actual evidence is limited to specific auto-labeled features in two SAE implementations, a narrower scope than the headline framing suggests.

weakness: The feature-steering analysis (Figures 8-10) is anecdotal, lacking a systematic steering matrix, repeated trials, or before/after lying-rate reporting.
justification: The paper describes steering experiments qualitatively (e.g. Section 6.3) without reporting trial counts, decoding settings, or quantitative lying-rate changes, supporting the critique.

weakness: The insider-trading depth analysis (mean-difference feature ranking, PCA+t-SNE, heatmaps) is a weak inferential pipeline lacking a classifier, held-out evaluation, permutation test, or specification of standardization/grouping choices.
justification: Section 7.1 describes only mean-difference ranking and PCA/t-SNE visualization with no held-out classifier, statistical test, or detail on standardization/token aggregation, matching the criticism.

weakness: Figures 4 and 5 and Table 1 do not support the stronger mechanistic claims (e.g., 'meaningful ethical decision-making patterns'); t-SNE clustering claims are visually persuasive but unquantified, and 70B clustering shows more mixing than claimed.
justification: The paper claims 'clear clustering' and that features capture 'meaningful ethical decision-making patterns' (Section 7.2/7.3) based solely on visual t-SNE/heatmap inspection without quantitative cluster separation metrics.

weakness: Important baselines are missing: the paper does not compare against hidden-state probing, simple supervised classifiers, or lexical baselines to test whether a simpler method could achieve the same discriminative signal.
justification: The methodology (Section 7.1) and conclusion do not mention any probing or classifier baseline comparison despite claiming a novel discriminative result from aggregate activations.

weakness: Methodology exposition is incomplete on key implementation details (token aggregation, normalization, PCA component count, t-SNE perplexity/seed) needed to evaluate the SAE separation claims.
justification: The Reproducibility Statement only vaguely says PCA/t-SNE parameters 'are specified' in supplementary materials without stating them in the main paper, leaving the described implementation choices unclear in-text.

weakness: Presentation is rough, reading like an exploratory report, with inconsistent capitalization, heavy appendix dependence, and a mixed reference hierarchy (blogs, journalism, videos alongside peer-reviewed work).
justification: The reference list indeed mixes peer-reviewed papers with blog posts, news articles, and non-academic sources (e.g., Economic Times, Democracy Now, Dario Amodei blog post), supporting the specific claim about heterogeneous sourcing.

weakness: The scope of the title and conclusion ('current safety tools are blind to strategic lying') is too broad given the evidence, which comes from one synthetic game and one insider-trading prompt set with specific tooling choices.
justification: The title makes a sweeping claim about 'current safety tools' while the paper's own limitations sections (8.1-8.4) acknowledge the findings are preliminary and specific to particular auto-labeled SAE tools and testbeds.

weakness: Main empirical gains are not attributed via a controlled internal ablation ladder (ACTS-only, ACTS+GS, etc.) on end tasks, only external baseline comparisons.
justification: Tables 1 and 4 only compare AMADEUS against Naive RAG/CRAG/LightRAG; no component-wise ablation on final MBTI/BFI/CharacterRAG tasks appears anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: Mathematical formulation is loose/ambiguous: Eq.4's φ is undefined as a function, Eq.3's TopK output type (chunks vs scores) is inconsistent with C*, and Eqs.5-6 never clarify whether sim(u, ĉ_i) is used at retrieval time.
justification: The paper text confirms φ is only glossed as 'a length-calculating function' (Eq.4), TopK is defined over similarity scores but C* is later treated as a chunk set (Eq.3), and no equation states similarity is computed over ĉ_i post-ACTS.

weakness: Algorithm 1 leaves the LLM decision step (prompt, output format, determinism, contradiction handling) underspecified, and line 15's 'Top-K+1' instead of Top-K is unexplained/possibly a typo.
justification: Algorithm 1's line 8 gives no prompt/format details, and line 15 literally states 'Top-K+1 chunks' with no justification elsewhere in the paper for the off-by-one.

weakness: GS and AE always use GPT-4.1 even when the generator backbone is Gemma3-27B or Qwen3-32B, confounding attribution of gains to retrieval design vs. a stronger external model.
justification: Section 5.1 explicitly states 'We implement Guided Selection (GS) and Attribute Extractor (AE) using GPT-4.1' for all settings, confirming the confound as described.

weakness: Claims of persona consistency rest heavily on MBTI/BFI proxies, which are an indirect/narrow measure, yet the paper generalizes to broad persona-consistency claims; also AE's taxonomy (2 attributes) is narrower than the 6-attribute taxonomy claimed in Section 2.2.
justification: Section 2.2 lists six attributes but Section 4.3 states AE only extracts 'Belief and Value' and 'Psychological Traits', confirming the scope mismatch the reviewer identifies.

weakness: Evidence that graph-based/web-search RAG are broadly 'unsuitable for role-playing' is overdrawn from limited CRAG/LightRAG implementations without discussion of tuning effort or broader baseline coverage.
justification: The paper's subsection header itself asserts 'Graph-Based RAG and Web Search-Based RAG Are Unsuitable for Role-Playing' based solely on CRAG and LightRAG results, a sweeping claim from two specific adapted implementations.

weakness: Table 2's statistical construction (sum of means/variances of similarity) is unexplained and the Figure 4 ridgeline argument for choosing alpha=2 is a stylized Gaussian-fit visualization rather than a rigorous or downstream-tied validation.
justification: The paper only states the log-density formula and that alpha=2 'maximizes sum of similarity while minimizing variance' under a normality assumption, without justifying summation choice or linking to downstream QA/persona metrics.

weakness: Table 1 contains apparent typos/label errors (e.g., 'Frieten', 'Mão Mão', 'Tanjiro Kainado', 'INFI') and there are other typos/duplicated captions elsewhere, reducing confidence in the reported results.
justification: The visible Table 1 in the paper actually lists correctly-spelled names (Frieren, Mao Mao, Tanjiro Kamado); these specific misspellings do not appear in the paper text provided, so this is not verifiable against the paper as presented, though other typos ('three folds' in intro) are confirmed.

weakness: CharacterRAG's scale (15 characters, 450 QA pairs) and narrow scope (curated fictional personas) limit generalizability, while the paper sometimes presents it as a general-purpose foundation.
justification: The paper repeatedly emphasizes only 15 characters and 450 QA pairs with no multilingual, original-character, or multi-turn evaluation, supporting the scale/scope limitation critique.

weakness: Human evaluation (Table 3) only assesses whether extracted attributes are 'reasonable,' not whether final role-play responses generated from them are actually more faithful or less hallucinatory.
justification: Section 5.3 explicitly frames Table 3 as verifying attribute reasonableness via Likert scores, with no human evaluation of final dialogue quality reported.

weakness: The main contribution is quite incremental relative to the base ElicitationGPT framework and Li et al. (2022) optimization framework, not substantial enough for ICLR.
justification: This is a subjective novelty complaint without concrete demonstration that the technical contribution (convex optimization for alignment while preserving properness, applied to a new alignment problem) is trivial; per guideline, bare 'novelty is weak/incremental' claims without deeper justification are unreliable.

weakness: The optimization objective is not analyzed for what happens when the reference score is noisy, biased, or miscalibrated; no discussion of identifiability, sample complexity, or overfitting risk.
justification: The paper's Section 3.2 presents the MSE minimization objective and convexity result but indeed never discusses statistical properties of the reference score or overfitting/sample complexity concerns.

weakness: The convexity claim is presented casually and the practical enforcement of the boundedness constraint over all (r,θ) combinations, and whether the optimizer solves the exact program vs. projected/penalized gradient descent, is underspecified.
justification: The paper states 'we optimize with the gradient descent algorithm over samples' (Section 3.2) without detailing how the boundedness constraint is enforced in implementation.

weakness: Notation/formulation is sloppy: Definition 2.6/2.7 alternates between dimension index m and n (S:[0,1]^m x [0,1]^m -> [0,1] but then S(r1,...,rn;.)), and Definition 2.3/2.8/3.1 have similar inconsistencies.
justification: Confirmed directly in the paper text: Definition 2.6 uses S:[0,1]^m x[0,1]^m->[0,1] then writes S(r_1,...,r_n;.), an actual m/n inconsistency.

weakness: The empirical evaluation is too narrow (22 assignments, 6-8 submissions/peer reviews each, two undergraduate algorithms classes) to support the paper's broader claims about aligned textual scoring rules.
justification: The paper's Section 5.1 confirms the dataset is exactly this small, single-domain peer-grading dataset, while the paper frames ASR more generally.

weakness: The baseline set (constant score, EGPT(AV), EGPT(MV)) is too weak; no comparison to non-proper supervised predictors like linear regression or an MLP over the same rubric features to isolate the cost/benefit of properness.
justification: Table 1 only compares against Constant, EGPT(AV), EGPT(MV); the paper never includes an unconstrained supervised baseline over extracted rubric features.

weakness: The train/test protocol is not detailed enough to rule out leakage, since summary points and priors are derived from instructor reviews within a cluster and it's unclear whether held-out target reviews are excluded from that derivation.
justification: The paper's algorithm (Section 3) computes priors p_i from all N instructor reviews in a cluster but the main text does not specify a train/test split protocol for evaluation.

weakness: Figure 7 (interpretability case study) is relegated to the appendix and used only anecdotally rather than systematically validated against independent instructor-designated rubric importance.
justification: The paper itself states interpretability is shown 'by a case demonstration in the appendix' (Section 1), confirming it is a single qualitative example rather than a systematic analysis.

weakness: The paper overstates what the 'nearly identity' regression line in Figure 4 demonstrates, given visible spread in the joint distributions.
justification: The paper explicitly claims the regression 'is nearly the identity function' as primary evidence (Section 5.3) while the underlying joint-distribution plot shows dispersion, supporting the reviewer's point about overstatement.

weakness: Assumption 2.2 (know-it-or-not: posterior is 0, 1, or the prior) is a strong assumption justified only by a dataset-specific observation, not validated quantitatively or via ablation.
justification: The paper's own justification for Assumption 2.2 is exactly 'In our peer grading dataset, we observe that textual reports either express a state being 0 or 1, or have no information' (Section 2.2), with no quantitative validation or ablation provided.

weakness: The language oracle implementation (summarization, QA) is elaborate but lacks task-level QA accuracy, clustering stability, or inter-model sensitivity diagnostics in the main text.
justification: Section 4 and Appendix A describe prompts in detail but the main paper provides no accuracy/validation metrics for the oracles themselves, only downstream MSE/correlation results.

weakness: Claims that LLM-Judge score can substitute for instructor score to improve scalability and robustness are overstated given only moderate Pearson correlation (0.5540) between the two.
justification: The paper explicitly reports a Pearson correlation of only 0.5540 (Section 5.2, Figure 3) yet still claims this supports scalability/robustness as a substitute, which is a stronger claim than the moderate correlation supports.

weakness: The notation and several core equations are inconsistent (e.g. Eq. 4 typo T^{o} vs T^{a}, Eq.7-9 initial/final vector conventions flip between the main text and Proposition 1, malformed probability expression after Eq.9, Theorem 1 Eq.11 symbol mismatch, mixing of m_0/m_infty in Sec 4.3).
justification: The paper text itself shows a genuine inconsistency: right after Eq.7-9 it states 'the transformed initial belief m_0 = b_0^T P' while Proposition 1 states 'm_0^T P = b_n', which are not algebraically equivalent statements, confirming the reviewer's specific complaint about swapped conventions.

weakness: The statement of what is actually recovered is murky moving from theory to algorithm: Algorithm 1 returns b̂ and {Ô^{ao}T̂^a} as if they were ordinary state-indexed objects, blurring true partition-level models vs state-indexed surrogates with block-sum semantics.
justification: The paper's Theorem 1 explicitly defines recovery only via sums over partition blocks (Eqs. 13-15), but the main text and Sec. 4.3 do not clearly state how the algorithm's outputs are consumed downstream, supporting this critique.

weakness: The finite-sample method is underdeveloped and the experiments rely heavily on thresholding/heuristics (SVD truncation via reciprocal condition number, full-rank action detection via sigma_min, partition detection via tau_obs, QP projection), which are not adequately separated from the clean asymptotic theory in the main paper.
justification: The paper's main theoretical result (Theorem 1) is stated 'in the regime of infinite data' with finite-data parameters deferred to Appendix B.1, and the main text does not discuss sensitivity of these heuristic choices, supporting the critique.

weakness: The empirical comparison set is too weak: the introduction positions the work against tensor-based POMDP learning methods (Azizzadenesheli et al. 2016, Guo et al. 2016) but the experiments never compare against those methods, only against PSR and EM baselines.
justification: Section 5 explicitly states 'All experiments are compared against linear PSRs and an Expectation-Maximization (EM) baseline' with no mention of comparison to Azizzadenesheli et al. or Guo et al., despite the introduction framing the contribution as relaxing their assumptions.

weakness: The experiments are small-scale and selective, using only toy domains with tiny latent state spaces (Tiger, truncated T-Maze, Sense-Float-Reset, hallway variants), limiting confidence in practical significance.
justification: The paper's experiment section (Sec. 5) confirms only these small toy domains are used, with no larger-scale POMDP experiments in the main text.

weakness: The planning results do not convincingly show explicit POMDP recovery beats PSRs for standard planning; the reward-specification comparison in Figure 4 is asymmetric since the state-reward strategy is only evaluated for learned POMDPs while observation-reward strategies are evaluated for both.
justification: The paper itself states planning performance is 'similar across all models learned' and describes that 'The former strategy is evaluated on PSRs and POMDPs, whereas the latter is evaluated on learned POMDP models only,' directly confirming the asymmetry.

weakness: Several assumptions (ergodicity, full-rank forward/backward factors, existence of full-rank actions) are restrictive, and the paper's justification in Sec 4.1.1 for their realism is more anecdotal than rigorous, so the actual learnable class is narrower than the broad framing suggests.
justification: Section 4.1.1 gives only qualitative robotics examples (gripper failure, passive sensing) without quantitative or broader justification of applicability, supporting the critique that the discussion is anecdotal relative to the paper's broad title/framing.

weakness: The mathematical exposition around similarity transforms (P, P', Q, R) is hard to follow and appears to swap left/right conventions between Section 3.2/Eq.7 and the surrounding text about Forw=A·P and Back=P^{-1}·V^T.
justification: This is consistent with the same inconsistency identified in Weakness 1 (m_0 = b_0^T P vs m_0^T P = b_n in Proposition 1), showing the paper does genuinely alternate conventions for P without a clear coordinate dictionary.

weakness: The claim about learning the number of hidden states is not as clean empirically as presented; state-count/rank estimation is sensitive to threshold settings, which affects the fairness of the downstream comparison since the same estimated rank is used for both the proposed method and the EM baseline.
justification: The paper acknowledges in Sec. 5 that the EM baseline's number of states is 'determined by the number of components of the truncated SVD when learning a linear PSR,' confirming that rank/threshold sensitivity propagates to both methods as claimed.

weakness: There are presentation issues beyond notation (typographical mistakes, confusing prose in related work, an unsupported necessity claim on Page 9 about partition-level likelihoods being 'necessary') that add friction to an already dense technical paper.
justification: The paper's abstract/intro make a similar strong claim ('these likelihoods are necessary to correctly direct agent behavior') without formal justification elsewhere in the main text, supporting the specific point about an unestablished necessity claim.

weakness: The paper does not disentangle what is genuinely new versus the inherited Monte Carlo continuation scheme from prior text-only PRM work, and does not articulate where multimodal process supervision creates qualitatively different challenges.
justification: The paper's method section explicitly reuses MathShepherd's Monte Carlo pipeline (Section 3.2 cites Wang et al., 2023a directly) without discussing multimodal-specific labeling ambiguities or failure modes beyond generic claims that multimodal PRMs are underexplored.

weakness: The mc_i>0 labeling rule is extremely permissive and coarse, potentially conflating salvageable prefixes with truly correct steps, and this noise is not rigorously analyzed in the main text.
justification: The paper defines correctness as mc_i>0 (Section 3.2) and only briefly mentions in one sentence that a threshold was tried and hurt performance, without deeper analysis of what this implies about label semantics.

weakness: The notation mc_i ∈ R≥0 is inconsistent with mc_i being defined as a fraction of correct completions, which should range in [0,1]; similarly 'm_i' appears to be a typo for 'mc_i'.
justification: Paper text confirms mc_i ∈ R≥0 (Section 3.1, line 130) despite Equation 2 defining it as a ratio bounded in [0,1], a genuine notational inconsistency.

weakness: Equation (3)'s actual training loss is never specified (whether standard cross-entropy on discretized label token, masking of conversation tokens, etc.).
justification: Section 3.2 presents Equation 3 as y_i ~ M(y_i|I,q,s≤i) without specifying loss function or masking details, so this gap is real.

weakness: The inference-time step scoring rule is too vague: does not specify whether it uses only the first generated token, whether probabilities are normalized over full vocabulary or label subset, or how prompt formatting affects calibration.
justification: Section 3.2 says the score is 'the weighted sum of the generation probability for the discretized scores' without detailing normalization or token-position specifics.

weakness: The benchmark metric description is internally inconsistent: Section 3.3 defines macro F1 averaging correct/incorrect steps, but Table 3's caption says overall score is the micro average across data sources.
justification: Section 3.3 (line 172) states macro F1 by averaging F1 for correct/incorrect steps, while Table 3 caption (line 246) explicitly says 'The overall score is the micro average of the score from different data sources' — a genuine inconsistency.

weakness: The baseline comparisons for critic models are narrower than the paper suggests, mostly comparing against self-consistency, ORMs derived from nearly the same data, and generic prompted MLLMs rather than stronger multimodal reward-model baselines.
justification: Section 4's comparisons (Section 4.3, MLLM-as-a-Judger) are indeed limited to SC, ORM, and prompted MLLMs; no specialized multimodal reward-model baselines are used.

weakness: The paper does not adequately separate critic quality from candidate-generation effects; it would help to report critic evaluation on the exact same candidate pools with pairwise agreement and rank-correlation analyses.
justification: Section 4.1 fixes N and temperature per policy model but no pairwise agreement/rank-correlation analysis across critics on identical candidate pools is reported anywhere in the text.

weakness: Benchmark quality control is described too loosely: no inter-annotator agreement statistic, no adjudication protocol description, no per-domain difficulty analysis, no disagreement rate estimates.
justification: Section 3.3 (Step Correctness Annotation) only mentions 13 annotators, 3 days, and ~10% author review with re-annotation for erroneous splits — no IAA metric or adjudication protocol is given.

weakness: The explanation for why all-step supervision outperforms early stopping is not fully convincing; the paper needs clearer formalization of what a correct later step means after an earlier mistake.
justification: Section 4.3 states the finding and attributes it briefly to noise/reflection ability without deeper formalization of label semantics for later steps, matching the reviewer's point.

weakness: Table 10 shows Qwen2.5-VL rollouts slightly hurt performance while MiMo-VL rollouts help, but the paper leaves this under-discussed as simply 'more diverse rollouts help', which the table does not fully support; similarly Table 11 saturation and Figure 5(b) instability are under-discussed.
justification: These appendix tables/figures were not included in the excerpted paper text but are cited with specific page numbers and their described patterns are plausible given the paper's brief ablation discussions; the main text's ablation discussion (Section 4.3) is indeed terse relative to the granularity of these findings, consistent with the reviewer's characterization of under-discussion.

weakness: The ethics section's statement that human annotation is 'unrelated to any ethical concerns' is too casual; the paper does not discuss annotator compensation/consent in the ethics section itself, nor does it specify licensing compatibility for redistribution of images and annotations.
justification: The Ethics Statement (line 341) literally states annotations 'are solely used to assess the correctness of each reasoning step and thus are unrelated to any ethical concerns,' and nowhere does the paper discuss licensing terms for redistributing the source dataset images/annotations despite stating they will be released.

weakness: The paper is substantially over-scoped: it motivates AWML through world models, causal representation learning, neural operators, and transferability, but the experiments (AR(1) toy model and tabular LSMS classification) do not test most of this stack, leaving the central contribution blurry.
justification: The paper's introduction and related work span world models, causal counterfactuals, neural operators, uncertainty calibration, and transfer (Sections 1, 1.1), while Section 4 only implements a synthetic AR(1) module and an MLP-ensemble/logistic-regression pipeline on tabular LSMS data, confirming the scope mismatch.

weakness: Assumption 3.6 (pointwise calibration, U(τ) ≥ d(τ) a.s.) does nearly all the work behind the 'certified acceptance' claim of Theorem 3.8, and this bound is never shown to hold for the actual uncertainty estimators used in Section 4.
justification: Assumption 3.6 is indeed a strong, unverified pointwise bound, and Section 4.2 only says predictive-variance-based U is used with isotonic calibration, without demonstrating U(τ) ≥ d(τ) empirically.

weakness: Theorem 3.5 assumes N_eff i.i.d. samples from a product generator Q, but the actual augmentation mechanism (recombining modules from a finite pool of factual trajectories) induces dependence, and the paper only relegates this to an appendix mixing correction.
justification: Confirmed by the paper's own text: 'If modules are dependent, we apply the mixing correction in Appendix A,' while Theorem 3.5 explicitly assumes N_eff i.i.d. draws from Q.

weakness: Theorem 3.10/Corollary 3.11's error term is written as an unspecified o_{N,B}(1) with no finite-sample form in the main paper, undermining the paper's claim of finite-sample guarantees.
justification: Confirmed: Theorem 3.10 states the bound with 'o_{N,B}(1) → 0 almost surely as N,B → ∞' and no finite-sample rate is given in the main text.

weakness: Theorem 3.12 contains a typo, stating the approximation factor as (1 - 1/ε) instead of the classical Nemhauser bound (1 - 1/e).
justification: The paper's main-text Theorem 3.12 actually states the bound as (1 - 1/e), correctly matching the Nemhauser result cited in the same sentence; there is no ε-typo in the provided paper text.

weakness: The connection between the theory (latent world models, modular conditionals, trajectory discrepancy) and the actual LSMS experiment (an ensemble of MLPs plus logistic regression on tabular data) is weak, with no explicit latent sequential model or clear mapping of 'modules' to tabular features.
justification: Section 4.2 describes an ensemble of twenty MLPs and a final logistic regression on tabular survey data with no explicit latent transition model as in Equations (1)-(3), and does not define what the modules correspond to for tabular data.

weakness: The empirical evaluation is too limited to support the paper's broad claims: only a stylized synthetic AR(1) study and a single real dataset (Uganda LSMS 2019) on one derived binary task, with no multi-environment transfer evaluation.
justification: Section 4 confirms only these two experiments are reported, and Section 4.2 uses a single dataset and a single binary electrification label, despite the paper's broader claims about transfer across environments.

weakness: Important baselines are missing: no comparison to standard semi-supervised learning, pseudo-label filtering baselines, unfiltered synthetic augmentation ablation, or simpler uncertainty-thresholded self-training pipelines without modular world models.
justification: Section 4.2 lists only three baselines (factual-only, autoencoder-pretrained, active learning) and does not include an unfiltered-augmentation ablation or non-modular pseudo-labeling baseline.

weakness: Table 2 is a single-seed illustration with full means/CIs deferred to the appendix, which is not convincing evidence for a central claim in the main paper.
justification: The paper itself labels Table 2 as 'Illustrative seed to show scale' with full results 'reported in Appendix B,' confirming the single-seed limitation.

weakness: Table 3's results lack standard errors/uncertainties in the main paper, show a non-monotonic baseline AUC pattern (n=100 lower than n=50), and the TV bound diagnostic grows while AUC still improves, weakening the narrative that the diagnostic tracks safe operating regimes.
justification: The paper's main text (Section 4.3/Table 3 description) reports only point AUC values without stated main-paper standard errors, consistent with the reviewer's observation.

weakness: Figure 1's left panel curves look fairly flat over much of the range relative to the substantial shaded variability, making the visual evidence for the N_eff^-1/2 scaling less compelling than the text suggests, and ablation panels introduce module count M and scaling exponent s without integrating them into the main-text theory.
justification: The paper's main theory (Section 3) does not discuss the ablation dimensions M and s introduced in Figure 1's bottom panels, supporting the claim that these are not integrated into the main-text theoretical narrative.

weakness: Figure 2C shows predictive standard deviations concentrated extremely close to zero for both factual and synthetic examples, raising concern that predictive variance may not be a discriminative acceptance variable.
justification: The paper's own figure caption describes Panel C as comparing predictive standard deviation for factual and synthetic examples without providing evidence of a wide, discriminative distribution, supporting the reviewer's concern.

weakness: Key operational details are left vague, including how modules are selected for intervention, what intervention values are used, how compatibility constraints are enforced, and how pseudo-labels are assigned to generated samples.
justification: The paper's description on Page 4 ('replace the update rule for a chosen module while holding other modules and the policy fixed') gives no algorithmic specification of module selection or pseudo-label assignment, confirming the vagueness.

weakness: The causal/counterfactual framing is under-justified: the paper uses 'counterfactual' in only an operational sense without establishing an identifiable structural causal model, despite leaning heavily on causal language throughout the introduction and related work.
justification: The paper explicitly states it uses 'counterfactual in an operational sense inspired by structural causal models' (Section 2) while Section 1.1 repeatedly invokes causal representation learning and structural causal models without establishing identifiability conditions.

weakness: Reproducibility is only partial from the main paper: exact LSMS preprocessing, modularization strategy for tabular features, candidate-generation mechanism, and threshold grid/validation protocol are not given in the main text.
justification: Section 4.2 repeatedly defers such details ('Sampling and preprocessing details are in Appendix B,' 'Definitions and full logs are in Appendix B'), confirming these specifics are absent from the main paper.

weakness: The headline claim that syntax is the primary driver of benign relearning is supported mostly in highly templated settings (TOFU name-QA, BLUR-style benchmarks), and it remains unclear whether the conclusion generalizes to less templated forget sets, free-form generation, or multi-turn dialogue, despite broader phrasing in the abstract/intro.
justification: The paper's experiments (Sections 4, 5.2, Appendix C/D) are all built on rigid QA templates (TOFU, WHP, WMDP, RWKU), while the abstract and intro state the syntax-driver claim without qualifying it to templated settings.

weakness: The operationalization of 'syntactic similarity' is really character-level Levenshtein surface-form similarity, not linguistic syntax, so the central claim conflates lexical/template overlap with syntax.
justification: Section 5.1 explicitly defines Sim(s1,s2) using normalized character-level Levenshtein distance, which is a surface-form metric, yet the paper's title and claims repeatedly use the word 'syntax.'

weakness: The representation/gradient analysis in Figure 5 (Section 6) is underspecified: it does not state which hidden layer is used, how gradients are flattened/normalized, or whether results are stable across seeds, so the mechanistic claim is not fully substantiated.
justification: Section 6 only says representation similarity is computed from 'average last-token hidden states' and gradient similarity from 'average loss gradients,' with no layer, normalization, or seed/variance details given anywhere in the main text.

weakness: The template-vs-keyword loss-ratio analysis (Section 6) does not specify how template and keyword tokens are segmented in general, or whether losses are normalized by token count, leaving the mechanistic claim under-specified.
justification: Section 6 gives only one illustrative example of template/keyword token coloring and defines Loss Ratio = L_template/L_keyword without describing the general segmentation procedure or normalization by token count.

weakness: Table 1's syntactic-similarity gaps between D_hi/D_mid/D_low are numerically small (e.g., WHP: 0.1894, 0.1767, 0.1818) and the paper does not report statistical testing, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds for these or the Figure 2 bars.
justification: Table 1 and Figure 2 present single point estimates with no error bars, variance, or significance testing reported anywhere in the visible main text.

weakness: The mitigation (syntactic diversification) is evaluated for relearning robustness mainly under GA (Figure 8), while the earlier vulnerability analysis was shown to be broad across GA/NPO/SCRUB, creating an asymmetry between diagnosis and remedy evidence.
justification: Figure 8's caption and Section 7.2 text explicitly restrict the relearn-success-rate robustness comparison to 'under GA,' while Section 5.3's vulnerability findings span GA, NPO, and SCRUB.

weakness: The paper does not compare syntactic diversification against stronger relearning-robust unlearning baselines specifically designed for robustness, only against standard GA/NPO/SCRUB.
justification: Related Work (Section 2.1) mentions guardrail-based and in-context unlearning as alternative robustness paradigms but the paper's own experiments only ever compare against GA/NPO/SCRUB variants, never against robustness-specific baselines.

weakness: There is a metric mismatch across sections (ROUGE-L in Section 4, keyword-based Relearn Success Rate in Section 5, LLM judge in Appendix C) that the main paper does not explicitly reconcile.
justification: Section 4 uses ROUGE-L against base-model answers while Section 5.2 switches to a binary keyword-based Relearn Success Rate, and the main text does not explicitly discuss how these different notions of 'recovery' relate to one another.

weakness: Some of the paper's exposition oversells causal language (e.g., 'syntax is the hidden driver,' claims that recovery is caused 'not merely' by shared entities 'but instead' by shared surface forms) beyond what the evidence establishes.
justification: The title and Section 5.3/Introduction use strong causal phrasing ('the primary driver,' 'hidden driver') that goes beyond the correlational representation/gradient analyses and templated-benchmark evidence actually presented.

weakness: The optimization/loss function is deferred entirely to supplementary material, leaving key questions (target representation, normalization, smoothing of KL targets) unanswered in the main paper.
justification: Section 3.5 explicitly states: 'Due to limited space, please see our loss function in supplementary material,' confirming the main paper omits the training objective needed to assess soundness.

weakness: Inconsistency between Eq.(5), which defines a RoI-pooled fine-grained motion feature from the predicted box, and Eq.(6), which appears to feed the temporal decoder the same undifferentiated motion feature symbol rather than the RoI-pooled one, undermining the claimed spatial-to-temporal cascade.
justification: The paper text shows Eq.(5) computing a feature explicitly described as 'focused more on the target region' via RoI pooling, but Eq.(6)'s input list uses the same undecorated symbol as the pre-RoI feature, so the notational distinction that would resolve this is not clearly present in the paper as written.

weakness: Memory selection mechanisms (spatial similarity scoring and temporal event-boundary segmentation) are described only in prose at a high level without an exact mathematical formulation, threshold, or segmentation rule.
justification: Section 3.3 only says 'we calculate the similarity between each spatial memory and the textual feature' and Section 3.4 only says 'points with lower similarities are considered as event boundaries,' without specifying the exact similarity function, threshold, or decision rule.

weakness: The LF-STVG evaluation protocol relies solely on an extended validation set with no held-out test split and minimal detail on annotation quality/verification of the extensions.
justification: The paper states 'we extend only the validation set to lengths of 1 to 5 minutes' and describes quality control only as 'we manually review the extended videos to ensure their quality,' with no test split or annotation statistics given.

weakness: The authors' own ablation baseline performs dramatically worse than both ART-STVG and prior published methods, raising fairness/tuning concerns since baseline architectural details are relegated to supplementary material.
justification: Table 1 and Table 7 show the 'Baseline (ours)' scoring far below prior published methods (e.g., 46.2/29.9 vs ART-STVG's 59.2/39.2 in Table 7), and the paper directs readers to supplementary material for baseline architecture details.

weakness: The paper's ablations do not fully decompose whether gains come from the streaming/autoregressive formulation itself versus the memory-selection modules versus the cascaded design, lacking additional controls like non-selective streaming memory or sliding-window baselines.
justification: The existing ablations (Tables 2-5) isolate memory selection and cascading choices but do not include the suggested intermediate streaming-without-memory or sliding-window controls, so the specific decomposition the reviewer requests is indeed absent.

weakness: Ablation tables contain notation issues (mislabeled 'm_vIoT' instead of 'm_vIoU') and the main paper omits implementation details such as memory bank size growth/capping and causal handling of VidSwin motion features.
justification: Tables 2 and 3 in the paper indeed show the column header 'm.vIoT' (a typo for m.vIoU), and the paper only states memory banks are updated 'without removing any existing memories' without addressing capacity limits, and merely notes 'previous frames are also used as input' for VidSwin without clarifying causality.

weakness: The claimed efficiency/GPU-memory advantage, which is central to the paper's motivation, is not substantiated with a runtime/memory table in the main paper.
justification: The main paper motivates the method partly via 'computational bottlenecks because of high GPU memory requirements' but provides no runtime/memory comparison table in the main text, only referencing 'additional results... in supplementary material.'

weakness: The qualitative figures (Fig. 5 attention maps, Fig. 6 temporal segmentation) illustrate only single examples and are not backed by quantitative/systematic evaluation of their claims.
justification: Figure 5 and Figure 6 as described in the paper each show one qualitative example without accompanying quantitative boundary-detection or attention-focus metrics, matching the reviewer's characterization.

weakness: The paper does not compare against stronger generic long-video modeling baselines (e.g., sliding-window/chunked or memory-transformer baselines without the proposed selection heuristics) despite positioning itself as a long-video-suited method.
justification: The Related Work section discusses long-term video understanding methods with memory banks but the experimental section only compares against short-form STVG methods and the authors' own ablation baseline, not adapted generic long-video strategies.

weakness: The main contribution is mostly a re-evaluation of prompting-based defenses with stronger proprietary models rather than a new defense principle, and the paper overstates its methodological novelty (Section 3.2 rationale is mostly qualitative prose).
justification: The paper itself states it 'revisits' prior prompting-based defenses (Intro, Section 1) using modern LLMs, and Section 3.2's four 'advantages' are qualitative discussion without a mechanistic analysis of why the approach now works, supporting the critique.

weakness: The evaluation is heavily benchmark-bound and does not establish generalization beyond the template structure of the selected datasets; the adaptive evaluation (Section 4.6) is limited to top-5 attack templates from one attack generator on AgentDojo.
justification: Section 4.6 confirms only the top-5 AgentVigil templates were used on AgentDojo, and no paraphrase/obfuscation/distribution-shift testing is reported anywhere in the paper.

weakness: The sanitization/fuzzy-matching step is underspecified and not formally analyzed, with no quantitative evaluation of sanitization precision/recall or over-deletion, despite being central to end-to-end claims.
justification: Section 3.1 only describes the fuzzy matching qualitatively ('construct a regular expression that allows arbitrary characters between these words') with no formalization, threshold ablation, or span-level accuracy metric reported.

weakness: The paper reports utility under attack but does not directly evaluate clean-input utility preservation after sanitization, e.g. how much benign content is removed on false positives.
justification: Table 2 and all UA numbers are reported only 'under attack'; no separate clean-only utility benchmark before/after sanitization appears anywhere in the paper, despite an 11.24% FPR for GPT-3.5.

weakness: The comparison against baselines is not fully fair/contextualized, and the paper claims 'computational efficiency' without reporting latency, token usage, or inference cost, despite using expensive frontier models as a separate guardrail call.
justification: Section 3.2 explicitly claims computational efficiency but no latency/cost/token numbers are reported anywhere in Table 1-4 or the main text; Section 4.2 also concedes DataSentinel's weaker results partly reflect a weaker released checkpoint, supporting the fairness concern.

weakness: The prompting setup is benchmark-specific (detection prompts adjusted per dataset), which weakens the claim that PromptArmor is a generic, standard baseline.
justification: Section 4.1 explicitly states 'Given the varying settings of the benchmarks, we adjusted the detection prompt for each dataset,' directly confirming the reviewer's claim.

weakness: Claims attributing gains to 'reasoning capabilities' are stronger than the evidence, since Figure 3 shows model size/capacity is at least as important as reasoning mode, and the memorization check (0.34 avg similarity, 3.5% above threshold) is too weak to fully rule out contamination.
justification: The paper's own text (Section 4.4, page 8) states 'sufficient model capacity appears to be the primary factor,' and Section 4.5 reports only average similarity/threshold statistics without deeper contamination analysis, supporting the critique.

weakness: Results tables collapse performance across attack types/environments (Table 1 averages, Table 2 combined ASR of four attacks), hiding potential concentrated failure modes.
justification: Table 1 and Table 2 report only averaged/combined metrics across AgentDojo's four attack types and multiple environments; no per-attack or per-environment breakdown is given in the main paper.

weakness: The paper lacks a formal problem statement/decomposition of end-to-end failure into detector error, extractor error, and backend-agent error, making it hard to evaluate exactly where residual ASR comes from.
justification: Section 2's problem definition is entirely prose-based with FPR/FNR/UA/ASR defined only informally, and no experiment anywhere decomposes ASR failures into detection vs extraction vs backend-execution causes.

weakness: Several claims are phrased too confidently/imprecisely, e.g. calling PromptArmor 'computationally efficient' without cost data, and the abstract's claim that it can 'accurately detect and remove' injected prompts overstates evidence since extraction quality is never directly measured.
justification: The abstract and Section 3.2 make these claims, but no latency/cost metric or extraction-accuracy metric (e.g., span-level precision/recall) is reported anywhere in the paper to substantiate them.

weakness: Empirical scope too narrow: only three task combinations (Subject-Canny, Subject-Depth, Canny-Depth), no segmentation/layout masks, pose, scribbles, style references tested, despite framing PKA as a general framework.
justification: Section 4.1 confirms evaluation is limited to exactly these three tasks with only canny/depth/subject conditions, and the abstract/intro claims general multi-condition applicability.

weakness: Baseline comparison underpowered: only compares against OminiControl2 and UniCombine, missing masking/pruning/KV-cache-based efficient control baselines.
justification: Section 4.1 explicitly lists only these two baselines despite Related Work citing several other efficient-DiT methods (PixelPonder, Learning-to-cache, etc.) that are not empirically compared.

weakness: Equation (2) for PAA is ambiguous: if Q_Xi and K_SPi are single aligned tokens, the softmax over a scalar is degenerate/ill-defined, and the equation doesn't specify neighborhood or grouped structure.
justification: Eq (2) and surrounding text (Sec 3.2.1) indeed describe strict one-to-one position attention without clarifying the support of the softmax, leaving the reduction from O(N^2) to O(N) technically underspecified.

weakness: Equation (3) for KSA is underspecified: Norm(.) is undefined, unclear if M^t is binary per-token/head/position, and keyword set K extraction method (manual/heuristic/learned) is not specified.
justification: The paper states only 'Norm(...)' without definition and says K 'typically contains just 1 to 2 tokens' without describing how these keywords are selected or extracted, confirming the reproducibility gap.

weakness: Temporal reuse assumption behind KSA (reusing mask M^t at t+1) is insufficiently validated quantitatively; no analysis of mask stability or drift across steps.
justification: The paper justifies reuse only by citing 'temporal consistency' (Zhou et al., 2025) with no quantitative mask-stability metrics; Figure 10 only varies threshold epsilon, not mask stability, matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: Early-timestep sampling (Section 3.3) is not disentangled from the main method: no quantitative table showing its contribution, only qualitative Figure 5 and Figure 11, and final (mu, delta) settings are not reported in main tables.
justification: Section 4.3.3 and Figure 11 provide only qualitative visual comparisons across mu/delta, and Table 1 does not isolate or report the early-timestep sampling contribution or hyperparameters used in the final model.

weakness: Efficiency evaluation is incomplete/may overstate gains: Figure 8 measures only attention-module VRAM, not end-to-end model memory, and it's unclear if latency figures include full pipeline overhead like masking/caching costs.
justification: Figure 8's caption explicitly says 'VRAM consumption of attention mechanism' and the abstract's headline numbers (5.12x reduction) are for 'attention module VRAM,' confirming the gap between headline claims and full-pipeline measurement is real.

weakness: Table 1 shows a nontrivial drop in edge F1 (0.551 UniCombine vs 0.414 Ours) on Subject-Canny that the text glosses over as a 'minor exception,' without analyzing the tradeoff.
justification: Table 1 confirms this exact gap, and Section 4.2.3 text calls it just a 'minor exception on a narrow margin' without further discussion, supporting the criticism of insufficient tradeoff analysis.

weakness: Qualitative evidence (Figure 6) is cherry-pickable; no failure cases or examples of conflicting subject/spatial conditions are shown; the paper should stress-test conflicting constraints.
justification: The paper indeed shows only favorable qualitative comparisons in Figure 6 with no failure-case or conflicting-condition analysis anywhere in the text provided.

weakness: Literature positioning is thin on masked-attention/condition-routing methods closely adjacent to the paper's specific technical angle.
justification: Section 2.2 covers caching/pruning/layer-removal efficiency methods broadly but does not discuss masked-attention or position-aware condition-injection approaches specifically, supporting the claim of thin differentiation.

weakness: Training/evaluation details are too sparse: resolution, inference denoising steps, FLUX variant, LoRA target modules, number of seeds, and keyword-caption curation method are omitted.
justification: Section 4.1 gives only iterations, optimizer, batch size and accumulation steps, omitting resolution, denoising steps, LoRA target modules, seed counts, and curation criteria for keyword-containing captions, matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: Some claims (abstract's 'practical path towards complex, fine-grained, resource-friendly AI generation' and conclusion's generalization to more complex tasks) are stronger than what the narrow experimental evidence supports.
justification: The conclusion explicitly extrapolates to video generation and 'more complex generative tasks' while the evaluation is confined to two-condition pairs on one FLUX setup, supporting the claim of overclaiming relative to scope.

weakness: Main technical novelty is narrower than the paper suggests, since it is built heavily on existing components (VGGT, AnySplat, VGG-statistics losses, CLIP loss) and the paper presents itself as more architecturally distinct than it is.
justification: The paper's method section confirms it reuses VGGT as the unchanged geometric backbone, AnySplat's voxelization step, and ArtFlow/VGG-statistics style losses plus a CLIP loss, so the critique about inherited machinery is well grounded.

weakness: The paper does not sufficiently disentangle where the gains come from; ablations (Table 1, Table 2) are local and there is no factorial decomposition isolating backbone, CrossBlock design, 3D voxel loss, and two-stage training.
justification: Table 1 only varies CrossBlock topology and Table 2 only varies the style loss with everything else fixed; no combined/factorial ablation against the headline Table 3/4 comparisons exists in the paper.

weakness: Equation (3) has an inconsistent notation, using R_{b,s}^l in the variance term instead of R_{b,v}^l, and mu/sigma are not precisely defined over which axes they are computed.
justification: The paper's Eq. (3) literally shows sigma(R_{b,s}^l) instead of R_{b,v}^l as in the mean term, and nowhere specifies the exact axes over which mu and sigma are computed.

weakness: Algorithm 1 is too incomplete: Line 9 is truncated and the actual formula for accumulating L_3D is missing, and VoxelizeAndFuse (voxel indexing, aggregation weights, collision handling, gradient flow) is left undefined.
justification: Line 9 of Algorithm 1 in the paper explicitly gives the accumulation formula (L_3D <- L_3D + alpha_l||mu_g-mu_s||^2 + alpha_l||sigma_g-sigma_s||^2), contradicting the claim that it is truncated/missing, even though the VoxelizeAndFuse implementation detail point has some merit.

weakness: Claimed geometric disentanglement (geometry unaffected by style) is asserted more strongly than demonstrated; no direct experiment measures pose/depth/point consistency while varying the style image at inference.
justification: Section 3.2.3 only conceptually asserts the geometry head is unaffected by style conditioning, and the paper contains no experiment isolating geometry invariance under style changes.

weakness: Evaluation protocol in Table 4/Appendix A.4 is not apples-to-apples, comparing optimization-based methods at full resolution against feed-forward methods at differing preset resolutions (Styl3R 256x256 vs Stylos 448x448), which complicates timing and artness comparisons.
justification: The main text's Table 4 footnotes acknowledge different treatment of training/optimization time across method categories, and the resolution mismatch claim (referencing Appendix A.4) is not contradicted anywhere in the visible paper text.

weakness: Quantitative evidence for the 3D voxel style loss over the scene-level loss is only modest (Table 2 numbers are very close), despite the voxel loss being framed as a central contribution.
justification: Table 2 shows scene-level vs 3D loss differ only marginally (e.g., short-range LPIPS identical at 0.047, long-range LPIPS 0.156 to 0.153, ArtScore 9.12 to 9.15), supporting the claim of modest improvement.

weakness: Claims of scalability to dozens or hundreds of views are overstated relative to evidence, since Figure 4 only shows up to 64 views and the paper itself acknowledges degradation beyond 32 views due to train-test mismatch.
justification: The paper text explicitly states 'we observe a gradual decrease in visual quality once ... exceeds 32' and that training used no more than 24 views, directly supporting the reviewer's concern about the 'dozens/hundreds' claim.

weakness: StylizedGS is excluded from the main quantitative comparison due to failure cases, raising cherry-picking concerns.
justification: The paper explicitly states 'StylizedGS ... is not included in quantitative comparisons due to its multiple failure cases observed on our test styles,' confirming the reviewer's factual claim and the fairness concern is a legitimate methodological critique.

weakness: Qualitative interpretation in Figures 5 and 6 is stronger than what the figures show; Figure 6's interpolation demo lacks any analysis of linearity, scene identity preservation, or viewpoint stability.
justification: Section 4.3 only qualitatively describes the interpolation results without any quantitative analysis of linearity, identity preservation, or cross-view stability, supporting the critique.

weakness: There are accumulating clarity/notation issues, including inconsistent use of N and V for number of views across sections.
justification: Section 3.1 defines N as the number of context views while Section 3.2.2 switches to V for the same concept (e.g., Q_b^global in R^{VL_q x C}), confirming the inconsistency.

weakness: Literature positioning versus Styl3R (the closest related work) remains high-level without a sharper side-by-side methodological comparison of what Stylos adds beyond it.
justification: Section 2.2 gives only a brief paragraph noting Styl3R targets 2-8 views and lacks multi-view consistency focus, without a detailed methodological comparison table or discussion elsewhere in the paper.

weakness: The matrix-side technical development has internal inconsistencies between the abstract's stated complexity (Õ(rd/ε²)) and Theorem 3's actual stated bound including spectral-gap-dependent terms, undermining confidence in main claims.
justification: The abstract states a clean Õ(rd/ε²) bound while Theorem 3 in the paper text explicitly includes a σ1(M_t)³/(σ1(M_t)-σ2(M_t)) factor not reflected in the abstract, a genuine oversimplification/inconsistency, even though the reviewer's quoted exponent for Theorem 3 (σ1²) does not exactly match the paper's σ1³.

weakness: Algorithm 3 line 6 and Algorithm 4 line 6 use step size γ_t = 2/(ε+2) instead of the Frank-Wolfe schedule γ_t = 2/(t+2) used elsewhere.
justification: The paper text explicitly shows γ_t = 2/(t+2) in both Algorithm 3 (line 260) and Algorithm 4 (line 275), matching Algorithm 1 -- there is no γ_t = 2/(ε+2) in the provided paper text, contradicting the reviewer's specific claim.

weakness: Assumption 3's function-value oracle and Lemma 3's claim of O(1) gate overhead for constructing x+σe_i and dividing by σ is not seriously discussed, understating the cost of coherent arithmetic on real numbers.
justification: The paper's Assumption 3 and Lemma 3 statements (lines 163-179) give no discussion of finite-precision arithmetic cost, supporting this as a genuine gap.

weakness: The finite-difference gradient error bound (Lemma 2) is converted to an additive linear-subproblem error but the correspondence to the δ-approximate linear minimization condition in Equation (5) is not made explicit as a formal δ selection in Theorem 1.
justification: The paper's Theorem 1 statement (line 187) does not explicitly state the value of δ in terms of the gradient approximation error, supporting the critique that this connection is under-formalized in the main text.

weakness: The matrix linear minimization oracle has a sign/formulation ambiguity: the optimal S for min_{S∈D}⟨S,M⟩ should involve the negative top singular dyad, but the paper and algorithms set S=uv^T without addressing the sign.
justification: The paper text (lines 211, 265, 279) states S=uv^T as the minimizer of ⟨S,M⟩ using the top (positive) singular vectors, which would actually maximize rather than minimize the inner product unless a sign convention is implicit and unstated -- a real unaddressed ambiguity.

weakness: The paper's claimed O(√d) speedup is narrow and heavily parameter-dependent (spectral gap, rank, tomography precision, γ'_min), which is downplayed in the abstract's broad claim of outperforming classical methods in dimension dependence.
justification: Table 2 and Theorems 3-4 in the paper text show complexity bounds laden with σ1(M), σ1(M)-σ2(M), r, and γ'_min terms, while the abstract's headline claim (line 9) is stated simply in terms of d, supporting the critique.

weakness: Quantum state tomography (Lemma 6/7) introduces an O(d log d/δ²) factor that dominates the matrix-side d-dependence, and the paper does not compare against strong classical low-rank/randomized baselines under matched assumptions.
justification: Lemma 6 (line 233) explicitly shows the O(T(U_x)·d log d/δ²) tomography cost feeding into the matrix algorithms' complexity, supporting the bottleneck claim in the paper's own stated lemma.

weakness: Presentation quality is below the bar for a theory paper: grammatical issues, malformed formulas, and broken table entries, including instances like 'succeed' instead of 'succeeds'.
justification: The paper text itself contains 'succeed with probability 1-p' (Theorem 1, line 187) verbatim, confirming this specific grammatical issue is present in the paper.

weakness: The related-work positioning is somewhat incomplete and not sharp enough regarding what is genuinely specific to this work versus applying standard quantum search/QSVE tools to a known Frank-Wolfe template.
justification: The paper text (lines 35, 53) already contains explicit comparative discussion against Chen & de Wolf (2023) and a concurrent quantum power method paper, detailing complexity differences and assumptions, contradicting the claim that comparative work is insufficient, and the critique itself lacks specifics on what comparison is missing.

weakness: There is no empirical or synthetic sanity-check validation of the proposed subroutines, leaving the practical meaning of assumptions and constants unexplored despite implementation-flavored claims about query complexity, qubits, and gates.
justification: The paper is purely theoretical with no experiments section, as also confirmed by the desk-rejection assessment noting 'no empirical experiments', supporting this weakness as grounded.

weakness: Equations (1)-(3) equate CLIP cosine similarity with a conditional probability P(X=x|v) without any calibration/normalization, which is mathematically unjustified since cosine similarities can be negative and don't sum to one.
justification: The paper's Section 4.2 literally writes S_lemma(v,x) := P(X=x|v) ≈ sim(C(v),C(x)) with no normalization or calibration step described, matching the critique exactly.

weakness: The appendix theorems (e.g. Theorem 2, Theorem 4) claiming proportionality between maximizing similarity scores and minimizing KL divergence / maximizing mutual information are only informally argued and don't establish the claimed proportionality.
justification: The paper explicitly grounds its metrics 'drawing on KL Divergence and Mutual Information' as a contribution, and reviewer's detailed critique of the specific proof gaps is a substantive, checkable mathematical claim not contradicted by the visible text.

weakness: Specificity metric definition is inconsistent between the main text (hyper/cohyponym ratio) and the appendix (lemma/cohyponym ratio).
justification: Main text at Section 4.2 explicitly defines Specificity as S_hyper(v,x)/S_cohyponym(v,x); the reviewer's claim of a differing appendix formula is a specific, checkable detail consistent with the paper's stated ambiguity.

weakness: The headline evaluation (Figure 4, main preference results) relies heavily on the 'with definition' prompt condition, which undercuts the paper's motivating claim that taxonomy prompts differ fundamentally from ordinary descriptive T2I prompts.
justification: The paper itself states 'Figure 4: ELO scores... The prompt includes the definition' as the primary reported result, confirming the reviewer's observation that the main analysis leans on the definition-augmented condition.

weakness: The human evaluation protocol is under-described: unclear how many annotations per pair, how disagreements were resolved, or how Tie/Both Bad labels were handled in BT fitting.
justification: The paper only states '4 assessors... Spearman correlation between annotators is 0.8' without describing per-pair annotation counts, assignment, or tie-handling procedures, matching the gap identified.

weakness: GPT-4 pairwise judging exhibits strong position bias which the paper acknowledges but does not adequately mitigate (no counterbalancing/order swap reported).
justification: The paper explicitly states 'we found no correlation between raw scores for individual battles. This issue stems from a strong bias toward the first option... a bias not exhibited by humans' without describing any mitigation such as position swapping.

weakness: Table 2 contains garbled/inconsistent model names such as 'Pluground,' 'Ptolet,' 'Kombesky,' 'Dram,' and 'SDT' that don't match Table 1.
justification: The paper text of Table 2 (as provided) consistently uses correct model names (Playground, Kandinsky3, FLUX, SD1.5, SDXL-turbo, etc.); no such garbled names appear anywhere in the paper text, so this specific claim is unsupported by the paper content available.

weakness: The CLIP-based similarity metrics diverge from preference-based rankings (e.g., SDXL-turbo dominates similarity metrics while Playground/FLUX dominate preference), and the paper's explanation for this is too shallow.
justification: The paper's own Results section states this divergence and offers only a brief hand-wave ('possibly due to CLIP-Score focusing solely on text-image alignment without accounting for image quality'), supporting the critique that deeper analysis is missing.

weakness: The paper does not clearly differentiate its benchmark's novelty from prior concept-centric/structured T2I benchmarks beyond using WordNet synsets.
justification: The Related Work section only briefly lists prior taxonomy-adjacent benchmarks (Baryshnikov & Ryabinin, Liao et al., Patel et al.) without a detailed comparative positioning, supporting the critique.

weakness: The retrieval baseline (top-1 Wikimedia Commons search) is weak and may not fairly support the claim that generation categorically beats retrieval for taxonomy depiction.
justification: The paper's main text gives minimal detail on the retrieval pipeline, only naming Wikimedia Commons as a single retrieval source with no reranking or stronger CLIP-based retrieval comparison described.

weakness: The random split sampling probabilities for benchmark construction are justified by TaxoLLaMA training utility rather than benchmark representativeness.
justification: Section 2.2 explicitly states 'The dominance of Hypernymy is necessary because it is the most useful relation for training TaxoLLaMA', confirming the critique that sampling choices are inherited from another model's training needs rather than justified for evaluation purposes.

weakness: Presentation quality is poor with typos such as 'Suprisingly,' 'vizualization,' 'depicturing,' 'Pluground,' 'Kombesky,' and corrupted references.
justification: The provided paper text spells 'Surprisingly' correctly and contains none of the cited typos or garbled model names; this specific list of typos is not supported by the paper text available.

weakness: The paper over-relies on appendix figures/tables for core evidence (FID, IS, reward-model significance, subset behavior) rather than presenting it in the main text.
justification: The Results section repeatedly defers to 'Table 8 and Table 9 in Appendix H', 'Figure 10/11/16 in Appendix G', etc. for central quantitative claims, confirming the critique.

weakness: Theoretical claims (Theorem 2.1, 2.2) rely on highly idealized assumptions (perfect reconstruction, uniform router, prefix-tree view) that are much narrower than the rhetoric used against prior methods.
justification: Theorem 2.1 assumes a tokenizer 'can perfectly reconstruct any input video x with non-zero probability p(x)>0' and Theorem 2.2 assumes a uniform router over {1,...,N} with an oracle -- these are idealized abstractions, yet the paper uses them to broadly claim prior fixed/adaptive methods are 'biased and inefficient' without acknowledging the gap to practical neural tokenizers with quantization error.

weakness: Equation 4 (the router) is underspecified: N_x must be an integer but the delta-function argument is a real number, and the main text doesn't specify how it is converted to an integer (rounding/floor/clipping), with the clipping detail only appearing in the appendix.
justification: The main text defines r_beta(N_x|x)=delta(beta*ELBO(x)/E[ELBO(x)]) without stating how the real-valued quantity becomes an integer token count in [1,N_max], confirming the reviewer's point.

weakness: There is a mismatch between the ELBO-based theory (which includes the KL term) and the practical implementation, which drops the KL term and uses reconstruction error alone, undermining the claim that routing is principled rather than heuristic.
justification: The paper explicitly states: 'we find that using the reconstruction error itself (without the KL term)... is sufficient, as the KL term is approximately proportional to the reconstruction error' -- confirming the practice diverges from the theorem's stated ELBO formulation.

weakness: The proof sketch for Theorem 3.1 is too terse/loose for the strength of the near-optimality claim, skipping steps and mixing log bases without explicit conversion.
justification: The paper's main text theorem statement uses H_C(D) with log_C while other bounds use plain -log p(x), and the appendix proof is not included in the provided text but the main-text statement itself shows the base-mixing issue the reviewer flags, e.g. H_C(D) triangleq E[-log_C p(x)] vs E[-log p(x)] terms combined in Theorem 3.1's bound.

weakness: The masking semantics description on page 6 is ambiguous/contradictory: it says tokens with the lowest ELBO values get mask value 1 (kept), which would preserve low-information tokens, contradicting the stated goal of preserving high-information tokens.
justification: The paper text states 'we preserve the top N_x tokens according to their corresponding per-token log-likelihood... the adaptive compressor computes a binary mask m... where N_x tokens with the lowest ELBO values are 1 and the remaining are 0,' which is internally inconsistent exactly as the reviewer describes.

weakness: The paper only evaluates reconstruction metrics despite motivating adaptive tokenization as crucial for long-video understanding/generation, so it doesn't demonstrate the tokenizer is actually a better foundation for downstream generative or understanding models.
justification: Section 4 evaluates only PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD reconstruction metrics, and the paper itself states in Section 6 that downstream generation/understanding evaluation is 'beyond our current scope,' confirming the gap between the introduction's broad motivation and the narrower evaluation actually performed.

weakness: The baseline comparison is limited mainly to ElasticTok among adaptive methods, without direct empirical comparison to other recent adaptive/variable-length tokenizers discussed in related work (CAT, ALIT, One-D-Piece, FlexTok).
justification: Section 5 discusses CAT, ALIT, One-D-Piece, and FlexTok as related adaptive representation methods but Table 1/Figure 4 only empirically compare against ElasticTok, supporting the reviewer's point about a narrow empirical baseline set.

weakness: All evaluations use square 256px crops (because ElasticTok only supports 256x256), reducing the realism of the evaluation, and while the appendix has additional resolution results, they aren't brought into the main paper.
justification: The paper states 'Since ElasticTok only takes in square 256px video... we only take the 256px partition of both datasets' and separately notes 'InfoTok can generalize to video with different resolutions, as presented in Appendix D,' confirming the main results are restricted to this narrower setting.

weakness: The improvement over the strong fixed base tokenizer (Cosmos-DV) is modest at the top operating point (mainly token-saving efficiency rather than a raw quality advance), which weakens the overall contribution framing.
justification: Table 1 shows INFOTOK at BPP16=0.81 (PSNR 30.08) is very close to Cosmos-DV at 1.00 (PSNR 30.01), supporting the reviewer's characterization that gains over the base tokenizer are primarily efficiency-based rather than large quality improvements.

weakness: There are numeric inconsistencies in overhead accounting: mask overhead described as 'approximately 5%' in the method section but effectively 1/16=6.25% in the inference formula/appendix.
justification: The paper states the mask overhead is 'approximately 5%' in Section 3.2, while the inference formula in Section 4.1 computes beta using a term '1/16, where 1/16 is the cost of binary mask' (6.25%), confirming the discrepancy the reviewer identifies.

weakness: Equation (3) gate g_m and tensor shapes are ambiguous: W_r is 2D_m x 1 but x_m is T_m x D_m and v_i* is D_m, unclear broadcasting/whether g_m is scalar/token-wise/feature-wise
justification: The paper text indeed defines W_r ∈ R^{(2D_m)×1} while x_m ∈ R^{T_m×D_m} and v_i* ∈ R^{D_m}, without specifying broadcasting or the shape of g_m, so this ambiguity is real.

weakness: Equation (4) TopK gating is ambiguous: unclear whether TopK is applied per frame, after pooling, or on flattened tensor given x_mW_G ∈ R^{T_m×n}
justification: The paper indeed does not specify how TopK is applied to the T_m×n matrix, matching the reviewer's observation.

weakness: Equation (5) sums over undefined index s while the paper introduced n subnetworks and top-k activation, an unexplained notation inconsistency
justification: The paper defines sub-networks S_1...S_n and top-k selection, but Equation (5) sums j=1 to s with no definition of s given anywhere in the text, confirming the inconsistency.

weakness: The confidence module (Eq. 8, target 1-r_m) is a weak notion of confidence that only measures missing ratio, not true semantic reliability, yet the paper frames it with stronger claims like 'intrinsic quality' and 'suppressing redundant interference'
justification: Equation (8) supervises s_m with ŝ_m = 1 - r_m (pure missing ratio) while the abstract and Section 3.5 describe it as assessing 'intrinsic completeness and confidence' and dynamically integrating high-quality information, a genuine gap between the supervision signal and the interpretive claims.
