justification: The paper's reward is defined with r_t notation on page 4 but Algorithm 1 line 19 uses r^(k) with phase index k, and the paper never clarifies intermediate reward assignment or truncation handling, matching the reviewer's critique.

weakness: Algorithm 1 contains genuine errors: line 13 updates δ* = δ_t when the check in line 12 tests f(δ_{t+1}) < f(δ*), and line 16 manually increments t=t+1 inside a for-loop.
justification: Verified directly in the paper's Algorithm 1 text: line 12 checks f(δ_{t+1}) but line 13 sets δ*=δ_t, and line 16 has a manual t=t+1 inside the for-loop, exactly as described.

weakness: The paper overstates empirical conclusions, claiming GAMA 'maintains superior solution quality across all instance sizes' when Table 1 shows only marginal differences from HGS/LKH3 on CVRP20/50.
justification: Table 1 numbers (HGS avg 6.0812 vs GAMA avg 6.0810 on CVRP20; HGS avg 10.3548 vs GAMA avg 10.3533 on CVRP50) are confirmed in the paper and show only marginal margins, while the text claims broad superiority without variance/significance testing.

weakness: The comparison against classical solvers in Table 1 is uneven (LKH3 has no average cost, HGS only one average, neural methods run 30 times) and lacks equal-time or quality-vs-time analysis.
justification: Table 1 as shown in the paper (lines 227-244) indeed omits LKH3 average cost entries and reports only a single HGS average, confirming the asymmetry the reviewer points out; no equal-time analysis is provided in the main text.

weakness: The ablation evidence in Table 2 is weak/inconsistent with the stability narrative: GAMA's reported std (0.0215) on CVRP100 is much higher than GAMA_NG (0.0042) and GENIS (0.0053), contradicting claims of lower variance, and Figure 2 only covers CVRP50 with modest visual differences.
justification: Confirmed directly from the paper's Table 2 (line 269: GAMA std 0.0215 vs GENIS 0.0053 and GAMA_NG 0.0042), a genuine mismatch with the paper's claim of 'notably lower variance' illustrated only via Figure 2 on CVRP50.

weakness: Important implementation details (e.g., precise definition of graph adjacency matrices G_dis and normalization used in Equation 2) are deferred to supplementary material and remain ambiguous in the main paper.
justification: The paper does not specify in the main text whether G_dis contains raw distances, similarities, or a thresholded graph, and how these interact with the standard GCN normalization in Equation 2, supporting the reviewer's concern about mathematical ambiguity.

weakness: The method is only weakly positioned against the broader learned neighborhood-search literature, offering little clarity on what conceptual bottleneck is being resolved beyond an architectural combination.
justification: The related work and comparison to GENIS largely frame the contribution as an engineering combination of existing components (dual GCN, attention, gating, PPO) without a sharp articulation of the novel conceptual contribution, supporting the reviewer's positioning critique.

weakness: The generalization evaluation in Table 3 is a compact, selective summary of average/best gaps over a randomly sampled set of benchmark instances without per-instance detail, undermining the 'consistently generalizes' claim.
justification: Section 4.4.3/Table 3 as referenced provides only aggregated gap statistics without per-instance breakdowns in the main paper, which is a legitimate limitation supporting the reviewer's point.

weakness: Presentation quality issues: duplicated/inconsistent notation, undefined references like 'Eq.equation LABEL:eq:eq:d', inconsistent e definitions, and calling GENIS 'the proposed GENIS' when GENIS is a baseline not the paper's method.
justification: The paper text itself (line 208) mistakenly refers to 'Table 5 in the appendix gives the parameter settings of the proposed GENIS' despite GENIS being a baseline method (per line 258), confirming this labeling error exists in the paper.

weakness: Figure 1 does not map cleanly to a precise sequence of equations, and Figure 2 is restricted to CVRP50/inference budgets while supporting broader claims, showing a gap between visual exposition and experimental substantiation.
justification: Figure 2 is confirmed to cover only CVRP50 across T=5k/10k/20k (lines 279-283) while used to support a general variance/stability claim, and the paper does not provide an explicit equation-by-equation mapping of Figure 1's architecture blocks, supporting this critique.

weakness: The specification of TDMadDist's loss L'_r (Equation 9) is incomplete/truncated in the main paper, only stated informally in prose.
justification: The paper's Equation 9 text is indeed cut off mid-expression ('d_\theta(s_i, s_{i+1} + d_{\theta'}(s_{i+1}, s_r) - 12(9)))^2'), leaving the exact loss form unspecified beyond the prose description.

weakness: The MAD optimization objective (Equation 1) summing over S^2 is not well-defined for continuous state spaces, yet the paper claims a solution still exists there.
justification: The paper explicitly states for continuous S 'there still exists a solution... even though the states can no longer be enumerated' without reformulating the sum as an integral or measure, which is a genuine formal gap.

weakness: The closest prior baseline, Steccanella & Jonsson (2022), which MadDist is explicitly framed as an improvement of, is not included in the main experimental comparison (only QRL and the Hilbert method of Park et al. 2024b are compared).
justification: Section 6.1 explicitly positions MadDist as differing from Steccanella & Jonsson (2022) in two specific ways, but the Baselines paragraph in Section 7 only lists QRL and the Park et al. (2024b) Hilbert method, omitting this predecessor.

weakness: The proposed 'simple quasimetric' (Equation 3) is technically lightweight, and the paper overstates its distinctiveness/significance as a methodological contribution.
justification: This is a subjective judgment about how the contribution is 'pitched' without pointing to a specific misleading claim in the text; the paper does note in Appendix E that the ablation supports it, and simplicity is presented as a stated virtue, not concealed.

weakness: The main paper's broad superiority claims (e.g., 'outperforms QRL and Hilbert in all environments') are not fully verifiable from the main-paper figures alone since full results are deferred to the appendix.
justification: The paper transparently states in the main text that 'The full results produced in all environments... can be found in Appendix F,' which is standard practice and explicitly disclosed rather than hidden or overstated.

weakness: There are inconsistencies between the number of seeds reported: main text says five independent runs, but Figure 3's caption and Table 1's description reference three random seeds.
justification: The paper text states 'All reported results are means over five independent runs (random seeds)' in Section 7, while the Figure 3 caption states 'Shaded regions minimum and maximum values across three random seeds,' a direct textual inconsistency.

weakness: The fairness of baseline hyperparameter tuning (e.g., QRL) relative to the proposed methods is under-described, raising questions about whether comparisons are apples-to-apples.
justification: The main paper gives no detail on tuning budgets or validation protocol for baselines versus proposed methods in the visible text, so this is a legitimate, specific methodological gap.

weakness: The downstream planning experiment (Table 1) uses the true simulator with an MPC-style planner, so it evaluates the distance as a ranking heuristic under known dynamics rather than under realistic model uncertainty or true end-to-end control.
justification: The paper's main text presents Table 1 as demonstrating practical planning utility without qualifying that the planner has access to the true simulator, a real scope limitation on the strength of the claimed conclusions.

weakness: The 'ground-truth MAD' for PointMaze/OGBench environments is actually a discretized approximation (via Floyd-Warshall on a maze graph), not the exact continuous-control MAD, though the paper's phrasing suggests exact ground truth.
justification: The paper itself states the ground-truth MAD for PointMaze 'we use in our experiments to approximate the ground truth MAD, by computing the all pairs shortest path... over the maze graph,' confirming it is an approximation used somewhat loosely elsewhere as 'known' ground truth.

weakness: Presentation issues including inconsistent notation (d_theta vs d_phi) and informal explanation of TDMadDist's Bellman-style target make the method definitions hard to follow beyond the truncated Equation 9.
justification: Beyond the already-cited Equation 9 issue, this claim about notation inconsistency and 'reverse-engineering the intended target' is not backed by specific quoted instances of the alleged d_theta/d_phi mismatch or unclear passages.

weakness: The paper does not sufficiently analyze why TDMadDist underperforms MadDist and sometimes QRL, offering only a brief positive spin rather than a deeper investigation.
justification: The Discussion section only notes TDMadDist 'underperforms the MadDist and QRL algorithm' while highlighting its advantage over Hilbert, without any analysis of the cause of underperformance.

weakness: The literature positioning is somewhat selective, not clearly distinguishing the shortest-support reachability notion (MAD) from broader goal-conditioned metric surrogates, making some comparisons sound broader than they are.
justification: The reviewer admits 'this is not the main problem here' and provides no specific example of a related-work comparison that is mischaracterized, making the criticism unspecific and unsubstantiated.

weakness: The central knowledge transfer claim (title/abstract/intro) is not actually substantiated by the method, which contains no teacher-student distillation, frozen-teacher supervision, feature/logit matching, or layer-wise transfer mechanism—only language-specific BERT encoders used as front ends.
justification: Sections 3.1-3.4 and Algorithm 1 describe standard supervised training with BERT encoders as components; no distillation objective, teacher model, or transfer mechanism appears anywhere in the methodology.

weakness: The mathematical formulation is internally inconsistent about the antonym space: Section 3.2 states antonyms should be 'similar in an oppositional space' but the margin loss in Eq. 16b penalizes high similarity for antonym pairs, contradicting the conceptual description.
justification: Line 137 says antonyms 'should be similar in an oppositional space,' while the text at line 238 explicitly says 'for antonym pairs, similarity in antonym space should be below m_ant,' a direct contradiction confirmed in the paper.

weakness: The graph construction process in Section 3.3 is underspecified: threshold tau selection, whether the graph is recomputed per batch, how transitive edges are weighted/parameterized, whether edge weights feed into TransformerConv, and how isolated nodes and cross-lingual graphs are handled are all left undefined; additionally Eq. 10-11 conflate a single fused feature vector with a node-feature matrix required by the graph layer.
justification: Section 3.3 (lines 165-177) lists only high-level bullet points for edge construction without formal definitions, and Eq. 10 defines X^(0) as x_fused (a single vector per Eq. 9) while Eq. 11 requires a node-feature matrix for TransformerConv, confirming the notational gap.

weakness: The pooling/classification design is conceptually mismatched: global mean pooling over all graph nodes (Eq. 13) followed by a single prediction (Eq. 14) is inconsistent with per-pair binary classification, yet Eq. 15 defines BCE over N examples.
justification: Eq. 13-14 and Algorithm 1 line 11-12 compute one x_pool and one prediction per batch via global mean pooling, while Eq. 15's BCE sums over N examples, an unresolved mismatch present in the paper text.

weakness: The multilingual empirical evaluation is too weak to support the claims: Table 2 has no baseline comparisons for non-English languages, no variance/significance testing, only Bhav-Net's own numbers with dashes for all baselines in the Cross-Lingual Average columns.
justification: Table 2 shows dashes for all baseline rows under Precision/Recall/F1/Accuracy for cross-lingual results, and the paper itself admits 'direct baseline comparisons are unavailable for most languages due to lack of established benchmarks' (Table 2 caption, Section 4.4).

weakness: Table 2 does not clarify whether baseline numbers are taken directly from prior work, reproduced under the same split, or reimplemented with the same backbone, and Table 3's Bert vs Dual-encoder comparison does not isolate the graph transformer or margin loss contributions.
justification: The paper only states baselines are 'implemented with optimal hyperparameters as reported in their respective papers' (Section 4.2) without specifying reproduction protocol, and Table 3 only compares two variants without ablating the graph or margin components.

weakness: The paper promises Single-Space, No Graph, and No Contrastive ablation variants in Section 4.2 but never reports an actual ablation table; the '2-4% absolute F1' claim for the graph transformer in Section 5.2 has no supporting table.
justification: Section 4.2 lists the three ablation variants but no corresponding results table appears in Sections 4.4 or 5, and the graph-transformer improvement figure in Section 5.2 is stated without any cited table.

weakness: The multilingual dataset creation protocol lacks detail on extraction rules, deduplication, train/val/test split strategy, lexical overlap/leakage prevention, and annotation process, which is especially concerning for lexical relation classification prone to leakage.
justification: Section 4.1 only lists high-level principles ('Balanced Sampling,' 'Quality Filtering,' 'Cross-linguistic Consistency,' 'POS Distribution') without specifying split methodology, deduplication, or leakage controls.

weakness: The cross-lingual generalization/transfer claim in Section 5.1 (3-7% F1 improvement from high-resource initialization) is not backed by an explicit zero-shot/few-shot/transfer experimental protocol; the described setup is per-language training with language-specific encoders, not genuine transfer.
justification: Section 5.1 asserts transfer benefits but the Methodology (Algorithm 1, Section 3.1) only describes independent per-language training with separate encoders, with no described transfer/fine-tuning protocol matching the claim.

weakness: The related work positioning is incomplete and imprecise, including an unresolved placeholder citation ('The work of ? demonstrated...') and an overly broad claim that existing multilingual approaches treat all semantic relationships uniformly.
justification: Line 44 literally contains the broken citation 'The work of ? demonstrated that post-hoc specialization...' confirming this is a real defect in the paper, not a reviewer error.

weakness: The discussion's causal claim that performance variation stems 'primarily from embedding model quality rather than architectural limitations' is not supported by controlled experiments isolating encoder quality from confounding factors like dataset size and split difficulty.
justification: Section 5.2 makes this claim without presenting any controlled ablation varying only encoder quality, while Table 1 shows dataset sizes vary substantially by language, a confound the paper does not control for.

weakness: Figure 1 (Algorithm 1) shows only standard supervised optimization of parameters with BERT encoders in the loop, with no visible teacher-student transfer path or distilled objective, undermining the title's knowledge-transfer framing.
justification: Algorithm 1 (lines 205-225) shows a single model's parameters Θ being updated via BCE + margin loss with no teacher network, teacher logits, or distillation step present anywhere in the described procedure.

weakness: The central claim that minimizing entropy change 'preserves the full prediction distribution' is mathematically overstated, since entropy is a lossy scalar summary and many different distributions can share the same entropy.
justification: The paper repeatedly claims (abstract, intro, Sec 4.2, conclusion) that the entropy criterion 'minimizes the change of the global prediction distribution' and 'fully represent holistic predictions', but nowhere provides a mathematical argument connecting entropy preservation to distributional preservation; this is a legitimate rigor gap.

weakness: The importance score derivation is notationally inconsistent: Equation (4) defines the score as I_i(x), input-dependent, on the left-hand side, but the right-hand side is an average over the whole calibration set, so it should not be indexed by a single x.
justification: This is directly visible in the paper text: 'the final importance score, I_i(x) as $$\mathcal{I}_i(x) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{calib}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{calib}}...$$' (Eq. 4), which literally has the described inconsistency.

weakness: The argument that self-distillation has a critical zero-initial-gradient defect is asserted without a formal derivation or explicit objective showing where the zero gradient arises.
justification: Page 2 states 'the initial distillation loss is zero, leaving no gradient to guide the initial importance scoring' but the paper gives no formula or derivation to substantiate this claim anywhere in the text.

weakness: Empirical comparisons on Qwen models (Table 3) are only against SDMPrune, which is insufficient given the strong 'consistently outperforms existing pruning methods' claim made in the abstract/introduction.
justification: The paper itself admits: 'For brief, we focus on the comparative experiments with the previous best methods, SDMPrune,' confirming the narrower baseline set the reviewer describes.

weakness: The reported gains over SDMPrune are numerically modest (e.g., only 0.8/0.7 points in Table 1, and tiny JS-distance/Jaccard deltas in Table 7) and are reported without variance or repeated runs, undermining the strength of language like 'better preserves intrinsic knowledge.'
justification: Table 1 shows 58.2→59.0 (20%) and 55.6→56.3 (30%); Table 7 shows JS distance 0.243→0.241 and 0.362→0.353, Jaccard 0.439→0.445 and 0.588→0.595, all matching the reviewer's cited numbers, and no error bars or repeated-run statistics appear anywhere in the paper.

weakness: The headline results depend on LoRA fine-tuning recovery, which muddies attribution of gains to the pruning criterion itself; the no-fine-tuning ablation (Table 6) is shown on only one model family and is limited evidence.
justification: Table 6's ablation is run only on LLaMA-2-7B, and the main results in Tables 1-4 are all reported after LoRA fine-tuning per Section 5.1, so the causal-attribution concern is well grounded in the paper's actual experimental design.

weakness: Key implementation details for reproducibility are missing from the main text (e.g., how gradients are accumulated across tokens/sequences, whether entropy is computed at every token position, how padding/truncation is handled, whether scores are normalized across layers), and Algorithm 1 is too high-level to resolve these.
justification: Section 5.1 explicitly defers to 'Section A.1 of appendix' for hyperparameters, and Algorithm 1 and Eq. (3)/(4) do not specify per-token vs per-sequence entropy computation, padding handling, or cross-layer score normalization anywhere in the main text.

weakness: The MLP-only vs attention&MLP ablation in Table 8 does not normalize for equivalent FLOPs/parameter reduction or granularity differences, so it is not as decisive as the text claims for justifying the MLP-only design choice.
justification: Table 8 reports only zero-shot accuracy numbers for 'attn&mlp' vs 'mlp' conditions with no accompanying parameter-count or FLOPs-reduction figures to confirm the comparison is apples-to-apples.

weakness: The qualitative distribution visualizations (Figures 3-6) are claimed to 'visually confirm' the results, but the actual figures show mixed and not clearly persuasive evidence, oversold by the text.
justification: The paper's text asserts the figures 'confirm our method's superior fidelity' without qualification, while the reviewer's close visual inspection reports mixed/ambiguous evidence, a judgment call grounded in direct examination of the figures that the paper's own claims do not preempt.

weakness: The manuscript is repetitive, reusing slogans like 'modeling holistic predictions' and 'minimizing the change of the global prediction distribution' across multiple sections without deepening the justification, and contains minor typos/inconsistencies.
justification: These exact phrases appear repeated verbatim in the Abstract, Introduction, Related Work, Section 4.1/4.2, and Conclusion without additional formal support each time, matching the reviewer's specific textual observation.

weakness: The related work positioning does not adequately justify why entropy is the right scalar criterion compared to other label-free/distribution-aware alternatives (KL-based teacher-free surrogates, confidence margins, logit-energy, Fisher/Hessian approximations).
justification: The Related Work section only contrasts the entropy criterion against one-hot CE and self-distillation/SDMPrune, without discussing or comparing to KL surrogates, confidence margins, logit-energy criteria, or Fisher/Hessian-based approaches, supporting the reviewer's claim of a gap in the literature positioning.

weakness: The central methodological leap from pairwise weight cosines to mechanistic functionality is under-justified; the taxonomy in Table 1 assigns functional labels based on coarse thresholds while actual neuron contribution depends jointly on residual state distributions, feature magnitudes, and interactions not captured by weight cosines alone.
justification: The paper's method (Section 4) is purely weight-based and does not validate that the taxonomy corresponds to stable intervention-level behavior across datasets/contexts; this gap is real.

weakness: The threshold-based taxonomy (tau=0.5) is arbitrary and not stress-tested, with no sensitivity analysis in the main paper despite many neurons populating continuous clouds (Figure 2).
justification: The paper states 'we choose a threshold τ = ±0.5' with no principled derivation or sensitivity analysis presented in the main text.

weakness: The paper overstates the strength of cross-model evidence, using language like 'universal' while inconsistently stating 'nine different LLMs' in the Abstract/contributions and '12 LLMs' in Section 5.
justification: The abstract and contributions explicitly say 'nine different LLMs' while Section 5 says 'we apply our method to 12 LLMs' -- a genuine inconsistency, and the main-paper figures (1a, 1b, 2) indeed show only 9 models, one model, and one model respectively.

weakness: The ablation methodology does not use strong enough controls -- it only compares weakening neurons to random neurons from the same layers, not to matched neurons controlling for activation frequency, output norm, or cosine magnitude.
justification: Section 6.1 confirms the only baseline used is 'the same number of random neurons from the same layers,' with no matched-confound control described.

weakness: The choice of metrics (attribute rate and entropy) does not align tightly with the paper's mechanistic claims, and entropy reduction is interpreted as semantic 'sharpening' despite being a blunt, potentially non-semantic instrument.
justification: The paper itself flags in Appendix F.1 (referenced by reviewer) that the connection between attribute rate and the RW taxonomy is indirect, supporting this critique.

weakness: The claim that negative gate values are mechanistically important is not fully established, since zero-ablation is a nonlocal intervention and mean ablation in the appendix materially changes the picture.
justification: The paper relies mainly on zero-ablation conditional analysis in Section 6.2 for this claim, and the reviewer's point that this is a strong empirical claim built on a single intervention type is well-grounded.

weakness: The paper states that w_in is a row of W_out (a typo), undermining precision of weight semantics.
justification: The paper actually correctly states 'w_gate, w_in are each one of the d_MLP rows of W_gate, W_in' (line 73) -- w_in is stated as a row of W_in, not W_out; the reviewer misread the text.

weakness: The sign-preprocessing in Section 3.2 is not innocuous for interpretation, and the main text does not sufficiently discuss how much observed distributions depend on this convention.
justification: The paper defers the justification entirely to Appendix C and does not quantify in the main text how much this convention reshapes the reported distributions.

weakness: Section 4.2 speaks of 'closest prototypical case' without defining an explicit distance metric, so it's unclear whether classification is nearest-prototype or threshold-based.
justification: The paper explicitly states in Section 4.2 option (1): 'Classify neurons according to the closest prototypical case (we choose a threshold τ = ±0.5)' -- it is clearly stated to be threshold-based, which the reviewer overlooks.

weakness: The paper is weakly positioned relative to closely related prior work (Gurnee et al. 2024) and does not convincingly delineate what is genuinely new beyond adapting cosine analysis to gated neurons.
justification: The paper's own related work section (Section 2) concedes Gurnee et al. 2024 already compute input-output cosine similarities, though without interpretation, making the novelty-delineation critique fair.

weakness: Several conclusions rely on selective qualitative interpretation, leaping from mixed case-study findings to broad conceptual claims about weakening neurons.
justification: Section 8 itself admits the weakening neuron case study 'is much harder to interpret' and lacks obvious semantic relationship to its detected concept, supporting the concern about overgeneralizing from qualitative examples.

weakness: Presentation is uneven, with emphatic phrases like 'completely unexpected,' 'for the first time,' and 'universal' used despite descriptive, often single-model evidence in the intervention section.
justification: These exact phrases appear in the paper (Section 6, Section 9) while the ablation evidence is confined to a single model (OLMo-7B) as stated in Section 6.

weakness: Section 3.2 (Visual-Tactile Affordance) and the Conclusion describe a completely different paper (FEM-based soft-bubble membrane force estimation) that does not match TARS's stated visuo-tactile affordance framework using optical tactile sensors and point clouds.
justification: The paper text confirms this: Section 3.2 is entirely about membrane/FEM equations for a bubble sensor, and the Conclusion states 'We presented a finite element force estimation method for soft-bubble grippers with only three parameters...' which is unrelated to the TARS abstract/introduction content.

weakness: Mathematical presentation in Section 3.2 is underspecified/garbled: Eq. (3), (6), (7), (10), (11) have ambiguous notation, duplicate equation numbering for Eq. (7), and Eq. (4) mixes indices inconsistently.
justification: The paper text shows Eq 3 rendered as a run-on matrix without clear formatting, two separate items both essentially numbered/labeled (7) in the text (project equation and the later F_external-related expression), and Eq 4 does use sigma_j/sigma_i notation inconsistently with sigma_ii/sigma_jj elsewhere, matching the review's claim.

weakness: The core VTP loss function is announced ('The loss function for the VTP module is shown as follows:') but the actual formula is never given, only fragmented prose about the GMDM.
justification: The paper text in Section 3.3 indeed says the loss function is shown 'as follows' but the sentence transitions directly into descriptive prose about kernel functions and mixing coefficients without ever presenting a discrete loss equation.

weakness: Critical figures (Fig. 3, 4, 5) and tables (Tab. I, II, III) referenced throughout the text are missing from the paper, making the main empirical claims in Section 4.3 unverifiable.
justification: The provided paper text references these figures/tables multiple times (e.g., 'as shown in Tab. I', 'illustrated in Fig. 4') but none of them appear in the text; only Figures 1 and 2 are present.

weakness: Experimental results are described only narratively without success rates, standard deviations, seed counts, or protocol details, since Tab I-III are missing.
justification: Section 4.3 as given uses only qualitative language ('significant improvement', 'best overall performance') with no numeric values present in the text, consistent with the missing tables.

weakness: Baseline setup (RS, VA, PN+MLP) lacks implementation details needed to assess fairness (point count, encoder capacity, training budget, tactile info parity), and the end-to-end baseline is dismissed as non-convergent without diagnostics.
justification: Section 4.2 in the paper text gives only brief one-sentence descriptions of each baseline and states the end-to-end method 'was unable to achieve successful convergence' with no further quantitative trace, supporting the criticism.

weakness: The paper overstates novelty by claiming to be 'the first to apply these concepts to a robotic system using optical tactile sensors and external cameras' without clearly isolating what is new relative to cited robot synesthesia and affordance prior work.
justification: The Related Work section cites multiple prior works on point-cloud visual-tactile coordination and affordance (robotic synesthesia [18], affordance methods [24]-[27]) yet the paper's distinguishing contribution beyond combining known techniques is not clearly separated out in the text.

weakness: Presentation quality issues: broken section numbering, unusable placeholder Figure 2, missing spacing in 'visualtactile', and fragmented sentences in Section 3.3.
justification: The provided text shows Figure 2 rendered as an explicit placeholder ('A large empty rectangular box representing a placeholder for an image'), and Section 3.3 contains a fragmented, garbled loss-function passage, supporting these specific presentation complaints.

weakness: The claimed sim-to-real deployment story is not substantiated with a dedicated real-world evaluation section, concrete metrics, or visual evidence, despite being emphasized in the abstract/introduction.
justification: The paper text (main body provided) only mentions real-world experiments in passing ('we successfully conducted real-world experiments') without any dedicated results section, metrics, or figures for real-world tests.

weakness: There is a mismatch between the paper's stated ML contribution (affordance/policy learning) and its actual technical depth, which is concentrated in the unrelated FEM bubble-force derivation rather than in the affordance/policy learning pieces.
justification: This follows directly from the observed content imbalance: Section 3.2 is a lengthy multi-page FEM derivation while Section 3.3 (the actual policy/affordance learning method) is comparatively short and lacks a stated loss equation, as shown in the paper text.

weakness: The method is simple to the point that the paper overstates its conceptual contribution, and the novelty relative to existing test-time control methods is not convincingly established (mechanically still repeated prompting injected into the evolving context).
justification: The paper frames the approach as filling a 'largely unexplored' gap (Sec 1) while Algorithm 1 is indeed a repeated generate-inject-repeat prompting loop, so the reviewer's characterization is grounded in the actual mechanism described.

weakness: The central adaptivity claim is weakly justified because query complexity is never actually estimated; it is replaced by current generated length l_k, which is endogenous to the intervention itself, creating circularity.
justification: The paper itself states l_k 'serves as a complexity indicator' based only on a 'prior' correlation (Sec 3, Eq 1) and never validates that the adaptive schedule tracks true per-instance difficulty rather than just length, so the critique is well grounded in the text.

weakness: Several mathematical formulations (Eq 2 token slicing assuming exact tau_k tokens, Algorithm 1 line 8 l_k update using tau_k instead of actual generated length, Eq 3 real-valued position p with unspecified rounding) are underspecified or inconsistent with the implementation, given that generation can stop early (finish_reason check).
justification: Algorithm 1 line 4 uses max_token_len=tau_k (an upper bound) and line 10 checks finish_reason==Stop, confirming early stopping is possible, yet Eq 2 and line 8 treat tau_k as the exact generated length -- a genuine internal inconsistency in the paper's own formulas.

weakness: The ConciseHint-T training procedure is insufficiently specified: hint embedding length, frozen vs. trainable parameters, whether training traces are gold or model-generated, and training interval choice are not detailed, and the 'generalizes well to out-of-domain data' claim in Table 2 is stronger than the mixed accuracy results (e.g., GPQA-Diamond drop at gamma=1.0) support.
justification: The paper's description (Sec 3, page 5-6) omits hint token length, which parameters are frozen, and trace source, while Table 2 shows accuracy dropping from 39.39 to 35.05 on GPQA-Diamond at gamma=1.0, which is a real accuracy cost the 'generalize well' language downplays.

weakness: The empirical evaluation is incomplete for the paper's core claims: the main tables do not compare against a broader set of adaptive reasoning-budget or training-based compression methods, and ConciseHint-T is only evaluated on Qwen3-1.7B with one training source, making it hard to attribute gains to the mechanism vs. added supervision.
justification: Table 1 baselines are BeConcise, Prompt, Deer, and NoWait only, and Table 2 confirms ConciseHint-T results are reported only for Qwen3-1.7B trained on MixChain-Z-GSM8K, matching the reviewer's description.

weakness: The results tables show a more fragile accuracy story than the narrative admits, with specific examples of non-negligible accuracy drops (e.g., Qwen3-8B/GPQA-Diamond Prompt 57.58->55.56, DeepSeek-R1-14B/AIME24 Ori 63.00->61.00, Qwen3-4B/GPQA-Diamond BeConcise beating Ours(Ori) despite more tokens) and no standard deviations/confidence intervals despite small benchmark sizes like AIME24 (30 problems).
justification: All cited numbers match Table 1 exactly (57.58->55.56, 63.00->61.00, BeConcise 53.74 vs Ours(Ori) 52.73), and the paper indeed reports only point-estimate averages with no variance measures across Tables 1-5, while AIME24 is confirmed to have 30 problems in Sec 4.1.

weakness: The injection-position ablation (Table 4) is not fully convincing: 'At the head' achieves higher accuracy (58.95) and lower token usage (3798) than the dynamic strategy (55.56, 3880) on the reported token metric, so the main-paper evidence does not clearly justify Equation (3) as essential beyond a latency argument deferred to the appendix.
justification: These exact numbers appear in Table 4, and the paper's own defense of the dynamic rule rests on prefilling/latency costs discussed in the appendix (Sec A.2), not on the token-usage numbers shown in the main table, confirming the tension the reviewer identifies.

weakness: The paper does not adequately disentangle token savings caused by direct text insertion/context editing from genuine changes in model reasoning behavior, and the reduction in transition words (Table 5) is interpreted as removing redundancy without ruling out suppression of useful self-correction.
justification: The paper interprets Table 5's transition-word reduction solely as 'promoting efficient self-reflections' (Sec 4.4) without any error analysis distinguishing removed redundancy from removed correction steps, so the gap the reviewer identifies is real.

weakness: The exposition has sloppiness in terminology and calibration, e.g., conflating 'complexity-adaptive' with 'length-adaptive,' and the sweeping claim 'we find it always works well for various models and benchmarks' is not well supported given the limited grid and visible tradeoffs.
justification: The quoted claim appears verbatim on page 4 ('we find it always works well for various models and benchmarks'), and the paper does use 'complexity-adaptive' language throughout while the underlying mechanism is length-based, matching the reviewer's specific citations.

weakness: The main-paper evidence for real-world efficiency is thin because the main body reports mostly token counts while end-to-end latency evidence is deferred to the appendix, even though the method's repeated context edits mean latency is not trivially proportional to tokens.
justification: The paper itself states 'the detailed theoretical and empirical analysis for injection costs can be found at Section A.2' (Sec 3), confirming latency analysis is deferred to the appendix rather than presented in the main tables.

weakness: Assumption 3.1 is a strong uniform matching condition over arbitrary selections, and Lemma 3.2 only shows it holds for finite trajectories from individually stable iterates plus global Lipschitzness, narrower than the generality suggested in the introduction.
justification: The paper's own Lemma 3.2 proof only covers finite trajectories of individually δ-stable iterates with L-Lipschitz loss (lines 139-141), while contributions claim broad applicability to 'practically used optimization algorithms' (line 81), a real gap.

weakness: There is a mismatch between the generality of claims and actual guarantees; Corollary 3.3 only covers projected SGD with Lipschitz/smooth losses, but experiments use Adam/AdamW, with no theoretical justification of Assumption 3.1 for Adam.
justification: The paper explicitly proves stability only for projected SGD (Corollary 3.3, lines 149-151) yet Section 5 states 'trained with the ADAM optimizer' (line 241), confirming the theory-practice gap.

weakness: The core lemma (Lemma 3.4) and downstream results are only in expectation, which limits interpretation of worst-case bounds, and the paper only briefly acknowledges this in the conclusion.
justification: Lemma 3.4 and Theorems 4.3/4.4 all bound E[sup...] (lines 159, 211, 223), and the limitations section (line 307) mentions this only briefly as one bullet point.

weakness: Several mathematical details are underspecified/inconsistent: Definition 3.1 notation is imprecise, Assumption 3.1's ω' second argument is nonstandard, the 'without loss of generality' divisibility assumption in Theorems 4.3/4.4 is not really WLOG, and K_{n,alpha} is inconsistent between Theorem 4.4 and Lemma B.3.
justification: The paper text confirms the WLOG divisibility claims (lines 209, 221) and the K_{n,alpha} definition (line 223); these are real, checkable textual details the review specifically points to with page/location references.

weakness: The proof presentation around Lemma 3.4 in the appendix has inconsistent notation between different measures and set notations, making it hard to verify.
justification: This is a claim about appendix pages 18-19 which is not included in the provided paper text (appendix removed), but the reviewer gives specific claimed inconsistencies; since appendix isn't available to verify, treat as reviewer's specific technical observation not contradicted by available text.

weakness: The empirical estimation of the stability parameter is only a loose optimistic proxy for Assumption 3.1's quantity, undercutting claims that experiments 'strongly support Theorem 4.4'.
justification: The paper itself admits the estimation 'necessarily leads to an optimistic estimation of the stability parameter' (line 254) while still claiming results 'strongly support Theorem 4.4' (line 297), exactly as the review states.

weakness: Experimental validation is narrow: only two model-dataset pairs, no comparison against prior information-theoretic bounds, no ablation isolating stability vs. topological complexity contributions, and no sensitivity study on J, held-out set size, or trajectory subsampling.
justification: The paper's experiments section (lines 241-260) confirms only ViT/CIFAR-100 and GraphSAGE/MNISTSuperpixels are used with fixed J=50 and no such ablations or baseline comparisons are reported.

weakness: Table 1 does not support a 'tightness' narrative since bounds are roughly an order of magnitude larger than observed gaps, yet the paper calls them 'reasonable tight'.
justification: Table 1 (line 286) shows e.g. G_S=10.24 vs Bound=104.43, about 10x, and the paper text explicitly says 'reasonable tight' (line 295) despite this gap, confirming the reviewer's specific numeric point.

weakness: Figures 2 and 3 are correlational, with declining correlations at larger n (especially GraphSAGE), yet the text claims they 'strongly support Theorem 4.4', overstating what scatter plots show.
justification: Figure 3 shows r dropping from 0.92 to 0.28 as n increases (lines 272-276), while the paper claims 'our experimental results strongly support Theorem 4.4' (line 297), matching the reviewer's specific critique.

weakness: The paper's positioning against prior work is shallow regarding what is lost by removing the IT term, not clearly spelling out when the tradeoff (slower rate) is favorable.
justification: The paper's discussion of the tradeoff is brief, essentially one paragraph (lines 230-235) stating bounds 'result in a slower convergence rate' without detailed regime analysis, matching the reviewer's point about shallow treatment.

weakness: Presentation quality is uneven with several typos and notation issues (e.g., 'Due the dependence', 'enounced', 'particluar').
justification: These exact typos are verifiable in the paper text: 'Due the dependence' (line 31), 'enounced' (line 135); this is a legitimate, specific, non-vague presentation critique.

weakness: Equation (3) presents the belief transition b_{i+1}=f(b_i,q_i) as a deterministic function of (b_i,q_i), but since the private belief hat-b_i inside it depends on the realized signal s_i, the transition is actually stochastic; describing the planner's problem as an MDP with 'transition function defined by Equation (3)' is imprecise since an MDP needs a transition kernel.
justification: The paper's Equation (1) shows the private belief depends on the realized signal s_i, and Equation (3)/Section 3.2 indeed describes the process as an MDP with 'transition function defined by Equation (3)' without stating a kernel in the main text, confirming the notational gap the reviewer identifies.

weakness: Equation (1)'s posterior denominator for s_i=G, '1+2b_i q_i - b_i q_i', appears to be a typo/error inconsistent with the appendix derivation.
justification: The paper text as provided does show this exact denominator in Equation (1); the appendix is not included in the provided text to verify or refute the claimed inconsistency, but the specific quoted equation is accurately transcribed and the critique is a concrete, checkable mathematical claim about the main text.

weakness: The experimental evidence in Section 6 is too light to support the paper's broader robustness claims, lacking a main-text quantitative summary table (e.g., average deviation, variance across settings/seeds).
justification: Section 6.2 indeed relies on qualitative description ('remarkable structural similarity', 'deviation is often modest') and Figure 2a/2b are the only main-text quantitative artifacts; no summary table of means/variances across parameter settings appears in the main text.

weakness: The evaluation setup lacks key documented details (number of agent profiles, runs per setting, clipping/rounding of planner outputs, sampling temperature, how Figure 2c welfare was averaged), making it hard to assess robustness.
justification: Section 6 describes the three LLM roles and defers 'further detail on the experimental setup and prompting' to Appendix E without stating these specifics in the main text.

weakness: There is an unexplained model/evaluation mismatch: the theory defines delta in [0,1) but Table 1 (appendix) reportedly includes delta=1 among experimental parameters, with no explanation of what objective is used in that case.
justification: The main text (Section 3.2) explicitly restricts delta to [0,1) for the discounted MDP; the referenced Table 1 is in the appendix not included in the provided text, so the claim cannot be directly contradicted and is a specific, checkable technical observation.

weakness: The paper's positioning against nearby social-learning/persuasion work is under-differentiated, relying on the reader to infer what technical/proof novelty follows from moving to a dynamic per-agent precision choice.
justification: Section 2 (Online Persuasion and RL / Information Design) explicitly contrasts the paper's setting against prior work, stating the planner is not informationally advantaged, does not learn unknown parameters, and explaining sequential dependence arises from information externalities rather than online learning -- a fairly explicit statement of what breaks from prior assumptions.

weakness: The empirical claims (e.g., 'remarkable structural similarity', 'sophisticated strategic behavior') overreach what the qualitative figures actually establish, since the smoother LLM policy could be generic central-tendency bias rather than strategic adaptation.
justification: Section 6.2's claims are grounded mostly in visual comparison (Figure 2a) and post-hoc narrative explanation rather than a controlled ablation isolating strategic adaptation from generic LLM response bias, supporting the reviewer's caution.

weakness: The main paper lacks a clean apples-to-apples quantitative comparison between optimal non-myopic and myopic planners to support the claim that 'neglecting social learning substantially worsens outcomes.'
justification: Figure 2(c) is explicitly described as a 'Bar chart of Planner Expenditure and Social Welfare for Myopic and Long-term planners in Unaligned and Aligned settings,' and Section 6.3 explicitly states 'neglecting social learning (as in the myopic cases) substantially worsens outcomes' referencing this figure, i.e. the comparison the reviewer asks for is already present in the main text.

weakness: Key thresholds (d_A, t_A, t_1...t_5) are existential rather than constructive in the main text, and the public-belief dynamics would benefit from an explicit transition diagram or two-state expression instead of relegating this to the appendix.
justification: Theorems 3-5 in the main text indeed state 'there exist' thresholds without giving closed-form expressions, and Equation (3) is presented compactly with the stochastic detail deferred to Appendix B.2, supporting the critique.

weakness: The LLM-based validation only tests LLM agents against LLM planners/oracles rather than against human behavior or an external behavioral benchmark, limiting the strength of the empirical conclusions.
justification: The paper itself acknowledges this in the Conclusion: 'One limitation of our study is the dearth of human data... human data could be useful for verifying... the LLM simulators,' confirming the weakness is valid, even though self-acknowledged.

weakness: The robustness-related capacity bounds (Bounds 10-12) underlying the paper's headline practical claim are heuristic, not valid lower or upper bounds, undermining the strength of the main practical conclusion.
justification: The paper itself states in Section 2.5 that Bounds 10-12 are heuristics based on singular values, explicitly says 'despite Bounds 10 to 12 not being valid lower bounds' and shows in Figures 8/9 cases where the heuristic under- or over-estimates true capacity.

weakness: The terminology around 'bounds' is inconsistent and conflates exact counts, volume approximations, heuristics, and conservative lower bounds, creating a credibility problem (e.g. Bound 6 justified only empirically, Bound 13 called 'actual lower bound' but too conservative to support the narrative).
justification: The paper text confirms this mix: 'closely tracks Bound 5' language for Bound 6, and explicitly calls Bound 13 'extremely conservative and unrealistic' while relying more on the heuristic bounds for its narrative.

weakness: Several mathematical/notational details are sloppy, e.g., inconsistent dimensionality of the transformation operator M, an unproven heuristic derivation of the quantization reduction factor in Equation 6, and apparently corrupted formulas/intervals in Bounds 12 and 13.
justification: The paper confirms the heuristic, non-rigorous nature of the Section 2.5 derivations ('Our robustness bounds are heuristic rather than formal'), supporting the reviewer's specific textual/notational concerns about verifiability.

weakness: The empirical comparison is narrower than the paper's broad rhetoric about 'current models' underperforming, since the controlled experiments in Section 3 focus almost entirely on Video Seal and a scaled variant.
justification: Section 3's experiments (Figure 5, Table 1, Table 3) are all built around Video Seal/Chunky Seal, while the paper's abstract and conclusion make claims about 'modern methods' and 'current watermarking systems' broadly.

weakness: The single-gray-image, MSE-only experimental setup is used to overgeneralize and dismiss robustness, perceptual constraints, and data distribution as explanations for the capacity gap.
justification: Section 3.1/3.2 experiments are indeed a narrow special case (solid gray image, no augmentations), and the paper draws broad conclusions from them (e.g., 'cannot be attributed to factors such as data distribution, resolution, or augmentations'), matching the reviewer's concern about overgeneralization.

weakness: Chunky Seal's practical contribution is undercut by a much larger model size (90x embedder, 23x extractor) and mixed quality/robustness metrics, including LPIPS degradation from 0.0019 to 0.0085 and slightly worse robustness on rotation and JPEG.
justification: The paper's own Table 3 and Section 4 text confirm the 90x/23x scaling and the LPIPS numbers cited, supporting the reviewer's claim that the 'comparable' framing is somewhat generous.

weakness: The literature/related-work positioning is incomplete relative to the paper's broad claims about capacity ceilings and current practice, especially regarding recent high-capacity or geometrically robust watermarking methods.
justification: The main text relegates most related-work discussion to Appendix A with only a brief information-theoretic survey in Section 1, while the abstract/conclusion make sweeping claims about 'modern methods' broadly, supporting the critique of comparative empirical positioning.

weakness: The Section 2.6 dataset/distribution argument, which concludes data distribution has negligible effect on capacity (~0.05 bpp), is too speculative and relies on coarse upper-bounding logic not formally tied to blind decoding error.
justification: The paper's own analysis in Section 2.6 uses VQ-VAE/VQGAN-based estimation of 'possible covers' as a back-of-envelope argument, consistent with the reviewer's characterization of it as coarse and speculative.

weakness: Figures 1 and 4 visually juxtapose rigorous PSNR-only bounds with heuristic robustness bounds and practical models, risking an impression of stronger apples-to-apples comparison than is warranted, and Table 2's conservative bounds vary in looseness without sufficient discussion.
justification: Figure 4's caption itself states it uses 'the heuristic bounds (Bounds 10 to 12)' plotted alongside PSNR-only bounds on the same figure, supporting the concern that the distinct rigor levels are visually conflated.

weakness: Presentation quality in the theory-heavy sections is uneven, with mangled equations and inconsistent notation making derivations hard to verify.
justification: This restates the same notational issues already documented in Section 2.5 (mismatched operator dimensionality, unclear Bound 12/13 formulas), which the paper's own heuristic framing corroborates.

weakness: The novelty is narrower than the paper suggests — it is a fairly direct specialization of VFM/CatFlow to VQ-latents rather than a substantially new modeling principle.
justification: The paper itself cites CatFlow and VFM as directly prior categorical variational flow matching (Section 2.2) yet still claims Purrception 'firmly establishes... a novel, state-of-the-art approach' (Section 4.3), so the critique about overstated novelty is grounded in the text.

weakness: The mathematical presentation is too compressed; Equation 14's factorization of q_theta(c|z_t) over the latent grid (single variable vs. per-position) is left implicit in the main text.
justification: The main text equations (12)-(14) never state the per-position factorization explicitly; only the Figure 2 caption mentions 'for each patch,' so the formal objective as written is genuinely ambiguous about the grid factorization.

weakness: The sampling dynamics near t=1 are under-discussed despite the singular (1-t)^-1 factor in Eq. 13/Figure 6; no discussion of numerical stabilization near the endpoint.
justification: The paper only states that Euler integration with 100/250 steps is used (Section 4.1) with no mention of clipping, terminal offset, or endpoint stabilization anywhere in the main text or appendix excerpt provided.

weakness: The empirical scope is narrow relative to the breadth of claims — only ImageNet-1k 256x256 is evaluated, with no unconditional generation, other domains, or higher resolutions.
justification: The paper's own Limitations section admits 'its generalization to other datasets or higher resolutions needs validation,' confirming the single-benchmark scope the reviewer identifies.

weakness: Experimental comparisons are weaker than they could be — the convergence gains in Figure 3 are asserted rather than isolated via ablation (e.g., disentangling categorical supervision from classification-style targets), and baseline sampler settings may not be individually optimized.
justification: The paper indeed changes multiple factors between CFM/CFM-endpoint/DFM/Purrception and provides no ablation isolating the source of the convergence gain, and states only that all methods use Euler 100 steps 'for a fair comparison' without discussing per-baseline optimal settings (Section 4.1).

weakness: The final benchmark results (FID 3.88, behind DiT-XL/2 at 2.27 and SiT-XL/2 at 2.06) don't fully support the paper's stronger claims like 'state-of-the-art approach' and 'bridge the fidelity of continuous diffusion,' and Table 1 mixes methods with different tokenizers/training budgets.
justification: The paper's own Section 4.3 text uses exactly this 'novel, state-of-the-art' and 'bridges the fidelity' language while also conceding Purrception 'falls short' against DiT-XL/2 and SiT-XL/2, and Table 1 lists methods across autoregressive/diffusion/discrete families with varying tokenizers without normalizing for training duration.

weakness: Empirical evidence is thin relative to strong claims (two case studies plus vague 40-50 problem statement, no benchmark table, no failure analysis, no cross-model comparison, no quantitative success rate).
justification: Section 5 only offers qualitative bullets on '40-50 easier problems' with no table, numbers, or failure analysis, while the paper makes strong claims about research-level effectiveness in the abstract and intro.

weakness: Absence of a results table in Section 5 makes it impossible to assess coverage, robustness, or reproducibility.
justification: Section 5 is confirmed to contain only prose bullet points, no table listing problems, decomposition sizes, or outcomes.

weakness: The decomposition-generation method is underspecified (vague description in Step 2, and the prompt block shown in Section 4 is literally empty template text).
justification: Step 2 gives only a high-level description, and the paper explicitly shows a placeholder prompt with empty tags and even an unfilled editorial note '(** describe the structure of the prompt**)'.

weakness: The verification via grid search over C (1 to 10^4) is weaker than the 'rigorous verification' language suggests, and details like whether C is shared across subdomains are unspecified.
justification: Section 2 Step 4 confirms C is searched over a finite grid, and the paper does not specify whether C is shared across subdomains or how domain restrictions are normalized before calling Resolve.

weakness: The flagship proof for Equation (1) has a mathematical gap: the step e^{y/2}e^{y/2} >= xy is not justified without an omitted intermediate step.
justification: The proof as printed in Section 3 Case Study 1 indeed jumps from e^{y/2}e^{y/2} to >= xy without stating the intermediate inequality (e.g., e^{y/2}>=y), matching the reviewer's specific claim.

weakness: The series case's leading-order-term simplification rule is stated informally and not formally justified (no explicit conditions like positivity/monotonicity given for validity of replacing summand with ratio of leading terms).
justification: The paper states the heuristic 'summand << ratio of leading order terms' in Section 3 Case Study 2 without giving the formal conditions under which this holds, only mentioning 'enforcing positivity where required' in passing in Step 3.

weakness: The paper overclaims novelty ('No existing AI tools...', 'one of the first AI-powered tools...') without adequately differentiating from prior work; related work section is short and selective.
justification: The related work section (Section 6) only compares against AlphaGeometry, one Lean-tactics tool, and autoformalization broadly, which is a narrow set relative to the strong claims made in Sections 1 and 6.

weakness: The implementation section (Section 4) reads like a prototype note: prompt is omitted, Mathematica code is truncated/unclear, no algorithm box or pseudocode, no discussion of error handling.
justification: Section 4 as shown contains an empty prompt template and a truncated Mathematica snippet with '-' placeholders, with no pseudocode or discussion of fallback/error handling.

weakness: The main examples (Eq. 1 and the series) are too simple to establish 'research-level' capability, and full mechanically verified subgoals are not shown.
justification: Both worked examples in Section 3 are presented only via verbal/handwritten derivation, not via the actual Resolve outputs or subdomain formulas, supporting the claim that the demonstrated rigor is thin relative to the 'research-level' framing.

weakness: Numerous unfinished/placeholder passages and formatting issues (e.g., '(** describe the structure of the prompt**)', empty prompt skeleton, reference placeholder 'insert-hash-or-date') reduce credibility.
justification: These placeholders are directly present in the paper text in Sections 2, 4, and the references list, confirming the reviewer's specific citations.

weakness: The paper's language ('rigorously verified', 'assured that the estimate is indeed true') overstates the trust model given that Mathematica's Resolve does not produce independently verifiable proof objects.
justification: The paper itself acknowledges in Sections 1 and 7 that Resolve does not emit externally verifiable proof objects and there is 'an element of trust involved', yet elsewhere uses stronger assurance language, supporting the reviewer's critique of terminology inconsistency.

weakness: The theoretical bridge from BRAC to DOAL (Proposition 1) is weaker than the paper's framing suggests: DOAL's target (Eq 17, gradient evaluated at data action a) differs from the BRAC target in Prop 1 (Eq 14, gradient evaluated at policy output π_θ(s)), so Prop 1 doesn't formally establish BRAC-DOAL equivalence; the notation in Eq 13 is also malformed.
justification: Directly verifiable: Eq 14 evaluates the Q-gradient at a'=π_θ(s) while Eq 17 evaluates it at the data action a, a genuine mismatch. The paper's own footnote 1 concedes 'we are not claiming the two objectives are equivalent,' but the review's point that the framing still leans too heavily on this as formal justification is a fair, specific critique.

weakness: Proposition 2 / the trust-region interpretation mixes first-moment and second-moment norm constraints inconsistently across the stated condition, the practical implementation paragraph, and Equation (17).
justification: Confirmed in the paper text: the stated condition uses E[||g||_2]=δ (line about 'expected squared magnitude' worded but using ||g||_2, not squared), the practical paragraph switches to E[||∇Q||_2^2], and Eq (17) reverts to the first-moment (non-squared) normalization — a genuine mathematical inconsistency.

weakness: The empirical gains are modest, inconsistent, and often concentrated in one or two tasks rather than showing a robust advantage across the OGBench/D4RL results.
justification: The paper itself states in Section 5.1 that OGBench gains are 'due to one or two tasks that has significant gains... otherwise, their performance is very similar,' and Table 1 shows DOAL variants often failing to beat baselines on D4RL, directly supporting this weakness.

weakness: The experimental/hyperparameter-selection protocol raises fairness concerns: hyperparameters chosen on one model family (e.g., n_sample on TrigFlow, δ on DTrigFlow) are shared across other methods without a clear held-out validation split, raising risk that reported gains partly reflect test-time tuning.
justification: The paper explicitly states IQL-shared hyperparameters were chosen this way and that per-task δ, n_sample, α_critic are tuned (Table 5/Appendix G referenced), with no described held-out validation protocol distinct from the reported benchmark scores.

weakness: The computational-efficiency accounting in Figure 2/Section 5.2 treats all forward/backward calls as roughly equal cost and is too optimistic about memory/parallelism (e.g., claiming MaxQ sampling 'has no impact' if it fits memory).
justification: This is a direct quote from the paper ('MaxQ sampling runs many samples in parallel, so as long as it fits to memory, it has no impact'), and the paper does treat all calls as equal cost in its total-calls-vs-runtime regression, supporting the critique.

weakness: Several equations and algorithm specifications are underspecified or inconsistent (e.g., generic BCLoss in Eq 10 not formally bridged to policy-native diffusion/flow losses, α claimed unimportant in Appendix F.3 but retained in Eq 16, malformed Eqs 22-23, and a0 vs a^target mismatch in the diffusion forward process).
justification: Verifiable examples exist in the visible text: Eq (10) uses a generic BCLoss while later diffusion/flow losses (Eqs 3, 6) are policy-specific and not formally bridged; Eq (16) retains α as stated, matching the review's concrete critique.

weakness: The strongest empirical story is arguably the MaxQ n_sample tuning rather than DOAL itself, since much of the baseline improvement over prior work (e.g., IFQL vs IQL*) comes from this tuning rather than the DOAL target-learning mechanism.
justification: The paper explicitly frames n_sample as 'a crucial hyper-parameter' and Section 5.1 shows large baseline improvements from n_sample tuning alone (IFQL over IQL*), supporting the review's point about a competing contribution narrative.

weakness: Figure 3 and Figure 4 do not fully support the stronger claims made in the text: Figure 3 shows task-dependent, sometimes drifting gradient-norm trajectories rather than universal stability, and Figure 4 highlights that DOAL was not compared against the best point in its own nested family (δ=0 excluded from tuning).
justification: The paper's Figure 3 caption/description shows varying absolute levels across tasks (puzzle-4x4 much higher and fluctuating) and the paper explicitly states δ=0 is excluded from tuning 'to explicitly show that first order gradient-based policy extraction might not always work,' confirming this critique.

weakness: The paper's positioning relative to prior Q-guided diffusion/flow policy extraction work is not sharp enough about when DOAL should be preferred.
justification: Section 6.2 lists many related Q-guidance and MaxQ-sampling methods but the main text does not give explicit criteria for when DOAL is preferable, supporting this specific, non-generic critique.

weakness: Presentation quality is below expectations: duplicated text, inconsistent task naming, typos (e.g., 'BARC objective' for BRAC), and notation slippage throughout.
justification: Both cited examples are directly present in the paper text: the duplicated 'Empirically, in all, we tested over three different Q-value Empirically...' sentence in the introduction, and 'While the BARC objective is almost necessary' in Section 2, confirming the typo.

weakness: The paper's core supervision still relies heavily on oracle or oracle-like verification (Eq. 7 r_dis and Eq. 9 r_refine both require r_oracle), which undercuts the broader claim of training critics 'without stronger labeling', and the summarization experiment swapping in a learned reward model reinforces that the method is verifier-dependent rather than supervision-free.
justification: Equations 7 and 9 in the paper explicitly depend on r_oracle, and the abstract/intro frame the contribution as developing critics 'without relying on stronger labeling or an oracle reward function during testing,' which the reviewer correctly notes is a narrower achievement than the framing suggests.

weakness: The RL objective specification is sloppy: Equation 2's SFT loss lacks a negative sign for the log-likelihood, there is a D_SFT vs D_SFI symbol inconsistency, Equation 9 samples critiques from the Stage-I policy instead of the Stage-II policy which is claimed to be a non-harmless error affecting the policy-gradient interpretation, and the KL term is ambiguous about whether it is token-level or sequence-level.
justification: The paper's actual Equation 9 samples c from π_φ^Stage-II(·|x,y), not π_φ^Stage-I as the reviewer claims -- the central technical claim underlying this weakness (that sampling is done under the wrong policy, changing the gradient interpretation) misreads the paper's own equation.

weakness: The extraction function f(x,y,c), central to Stage I's discrimination reward, is underspecified -- it is unclear how the model's judgment is parsed from the critique, how disagreements between step-level and final-answer judgments are resolved, or how malformed outputs are handled.
justification: The paper introduces f(x,y,c) in Algorithm 1 and Equation 7 as 'the critique model's judgment of the correctness of the original response' but never gives a precise definition, parsing procedure, or handling of malformed/ambiguous outputs in the main text.

weakness: Empirical gains may be entangled with extra compute and pipeline structure (two RL stages vs single-phase baselines), and the paper does not provide a compute-matched comparison to isolate whether gains come from the discriminability/helpfulness factorization or simply more optimization budget.
justification: The paper trains Critique-RL through Stage I + Stage II (500 steps each per Section 5.1) against baselines with a single RL phase, and no compute-matched ablation controlling for total updates/tokens is presented in Table 1, 2, or 3.

weakness: The evaluation remains narrow relative to the paper's framing toward general scalable oversight -- the main paper is overwhelmingly centered on verifiable mathematical reasoning, and the only open-ended experiment (summarization) is moved to the appendix.
justification: Datasets used (MATH, GSM8K, AQuA, SVAMP, TheoremQA) are all math/reasoning tasks, and the paper itself states the summarization/CNN-DailyMail experiment is presented 'in Appendix G,' confirming it is outside the main paper despite the intro/conclusion's broader scalable-oversight framing.

weakness: The baseline set (SFT, STaR, Retroformer, CTRL) is decent but not fully convincing for the specific claim of training better critics, since several recent lines of work on stronger critic construction and multi-agent/deliberate stepwise critique generation are not compared, and STaR is described as a somewhat awkward comparator.
justification: The paper's baseline list in Section 5.1 is limited to these four methods with no comparison to multi-agent or deliberate stepwise critique-generation approaches, so the point about limited baseline coverage for the critique-training claim is grounded in what's actually compared.

weakness: Acc@Dis, defined as a binary agreement metric between critic judgment and true correctness, is too coarse an interpretation of discriminability since it collapses richer step-level assessment and could be gamed by a correct final verdict paired with poor local reasoning.
justification: Section 3.3 defines Acc@Dis strictly as whether 'the correctness assessed by the critic aligns with the true correctness of the original response,' a binary metric, even though Figure 2 shows the critic also produces step-level judgments that this metric does not evaluate.

weakness: Several writing/notation issues reduce confidence, including a typo ('accessed' vs 'assessed') in Section 3.3, dataset symbol inconsistency in Equation 2, and a parameter inconsistency where the main text states beta1=0.2 for Stage II while Appendix Table 13 discusses different beta1/beta2 values.
justification: Section 5.1 confirms 'In Stage II, β1 is set to 0.2,' and Section 3.3's metric description uses the word 'accessed' where 'assessed' was clearly intended, supporting the reviewer's specific textual observations.

weakness: The compute-efficiency claim is suggestive rather than established, since the comparison bundles multiple operations (response-critique-refinement) into one 'sample' without normalizing by actual generated tokens or wall-clock cost against direct response sampling.
justification: Section 6 describes the inference-scaling comparison purely in terms of sample counts (K vs 3K sampling) without any token-count or wall-clock normalization, so the claim of 'compute-efficiency' is not fully substantiated as stated.

weakness: The main theoretical guarantees (Theorems 1 and 3) rely on assumptions much stronger than the practical setting — orthonormal representations, uniform state distribution, and symmetric P^{π_z} — which is misaligned with the deep visual-control domains used in experiments, yet the paper still uses this theory to motivate claims like 'sound approach for zero-shot policy evaluation'.
justification: Confirmed: Theorem 1 explicitly lists assumptions (A1) φ⊤φ=ψ⊤ψ=I, (A2) uniform state distribution, (A3) symmetric P^{π_z}, and the conclusion admits 'formal guarantees rely on an assumption of symmetry' as future work, supporting the critique of an unaddressed theory-practice gap.

weakness: Theorem 2's non-collapse guarantee assumes a continuous-time relaxation where predictors are optimized to stationarity at every step before representation updates (two-timescale), whereas Algorithm 1 updates all components jointly via SGD/Adam with target networks and EMA, so the theorem covers a different dynamical system than what is actually trained.
justification: Confirmed by the paper's own statement of Theorem 2 ('at each step t, the optimal predictors ... are first computed and then a gradient step ... is taken') versus Algorithm 1's simultaneous SGD updates with EMA target networks.

weakness: There is mathematical sloppiness/notation drift: the predictor T_φ's argument order is inconsistent between Section 3.1/3.3, e.g. π_z(φ(s))=argmax_a T_φ(φ(s),a,z)^T z is followed almost immediately by T_φ(φ(s), z, a) ≈ F^{π_z}_ψ(s,a) with swapped argument order.
justification: Verified directly in the paper text (Section 3.3): the predictor is written as T_φ(φ(s), a, z) in one sentence and then as T_φ(φ(s), z, a) two sentences later, confirming the inconsistency the reviewer flags.

weakness: The 'zero-shot' framing is rhetorically stronger than the actual protocol: at test time the method still requires a reward-labeled inference dataset D_rwd and a linear regression fit to obtain z_r, which is not really 'any reward function' in an unrestricted sense.
justification: The paper's own Section 3.3 confirms this mechanism (closed-form linear regression on D_rwd to get z_r), and the reviewer accurately notes the paper only partially discusses this limitation via Theorem 4 without spelling it out in the empirical discussion.

weakness: Empirical gains are less decisive than the narrative suggests, e.g., TD-JEPA is slightly below BYOL-γ* on OGBench_RGB (41.34 vs 41.58), ties HILP on OGBench average, and badly trails FB on antmaze-me (20.20 vs 51.60).
justification: All cited numbers are directly verifiable in Table 1 of the paper, confirming the mixed picture the reviewer describes even though the paper's phrasing 'matches or outperforms' is technically accurate.

weakness: The analysis of why TD-JEPA helps is confounded by many moving parts (TD objective, separate encoders, asymmetric training, target networks, orthonormal regularization, actor rule), and Figure 3 does not fully isolate which component contributes what, with the symmetric-variant ablation showing only modest gaps.
justification: The paper's own ablation (Figure 3 right) reports that the symmetric variant 'performs comparatively rather well,' supporting the reviewer's observation that the asymmetric formulation's benefit is not sharply isolated from the other design choices.

weakness: Figure 2's probability-of-improvement summary is too aggregated to diagnose where the method is stronger, and the paper should add more main-text decomposition by domain type or dataset coverage rather than requiring the reader to reconstruct the story from Table 1.
justification: The paper already provides Table 1 with full per-domain breakdowns, Figure 2 aggregate statistics, and per-domain discussion in the text (e.g., explicit comparisons to FB/HILP and BYOL-γ* by suite); asking for yet more main-text decomposition is not necessary given the extensive breakdown already provided.

weakness: Theorem 4's exposition is overly compressed, hiding the constant c (which the appendix reveals as S/(1-γ)^2) in the main text, blunting the interpretability of the bound.
justification: The paper's main-text Theorem 4 indeed states the bound 'for some c' without specifying its value/dependence on S and γ, which is a legitimate presentation critique.

weakness: There is a mismatch between the theoretical motivation for symmetric training of ψ in Section 3.2 and the later admission (in Related Work) that the practical TD-JEPA objective is not bi-directional like BYOL-γ, with these layers not clearly separated in the main text.
justification: Confirmed: Section 3.2/footnote 2 discusses using two forward-in-time losses, and the Related Work section explicitly states 'its practical objective is not bi-directional ... it only implements forward TD prediction,' supporting the reviewer's observation of an under-clarified distinction.

weakness: The technical contribution feels narrow / closer to feature grafting than a substantial methodological advance (frozen AIDE backbone, one added handcrafted feature stream via concatenation).
justification: The paper itself describes exactly this integration strategy (Section 3.3): freeze Patchwise/Semantic encoders, add a cuboidal-partitioning feature vector through one FC+GELU layer, then concatenate before the existing Discriminator MLP, so the critique of limited methodological depth is grounded in the actual design.

weakness: The method description is underspecified: the exact pixel feature p_i, the cut search space/tie-breaking rules, the meaning of 'greatest potential gain' at each step, and what happens when N=1024 exceeds feasible splits are not specified.
justification: The paper indeed only says p_i is 'e.g., RGB values' (Eq. 1), never states the candidate-cut search procedure, tie-breaking, or resizing/stopping behavior for N=1024, so these are genuine reproducibility gaps.

weakness: Equation (3) is sloppy/notation-overloaded, using the same symbol for the per-split gain and the cumulative normalized feature, creating ambiguity.
justification: The paper actually distinguishes the two: the per-split gain is denoted \hat{g}_j while the cumulative normalized feature is denoted \tilde{g}_i in Equation (3), so the claimed notation collision does not exist as described.

weakness: The empirical comparison protocol is not fully convincing because baseline numbers are pulled from different published papers rather than a uniform, controlled re-evaluation.
justification: Section 4.1 explicitly states 'the specific baselines used vary by benchmark, as we rely on the comparison results published in the original papers,' confirming this is a real limitation of the evaluation protocol.

weakness: There is a major inconsistency between Section 4.5's claim of 91.85% mean (second-best) on AIGCDetect and Table 2, which the reviewer reads as showing 95.58 for 'Ours' and higher means (97.05, 98.43) for AIDE and PatchCraft.
justification: The reviewer misread the table: the 'Mean' column in Table 2 is the last column (91.85 for Ours, 93.02 for AIDE, 89.85 for PatchCraft), while 95.58/97.05/98.43 are the SDXL column values, not the means; the text and table are actually consistent.

weakness: There is no ablation isolating the source of improvement (raw vs. projected structural vector, sensitivity to N, alternative pixel representations, frozen-head vs. joint finetuning, or comparison to simpler partitioning baselines).
justification: The paper reports no such ablations anywhere in Section 4, so it is impossible from the paper to tell whether gains come from the specific hierarchical structural signal or merely from adding another feature stream.

weakness: The qualitative evidence (Figures 1 and 3) is a cherry-picked single example and one-sided (only shows successes), without quantitative localization validation or failure-case examples despite the paper admitting degradation exists in some subsets.
justification: Figure 1 presents one example and Figure 3 only shows cases where the model succeeded and AIDE failed; the paper never shows the reverse cases even though Section 4.8 acknowledges performance decreases on certain subsets.

weakness: The paper has multiple presentation/consistency problems, including the AIGCDetect mean mismatch and Table 2 containing duplicate 'StyleGAN' columns, unexplained names like 'Adide,' 'MediPentary,' and an unexplained 'SOTA' column.
justification: Table 2 as printed in the paper has columns ProGAN, StyleGAN, BigGAN, CycleGAN, StarGAN, CurGAN, StyleGAN2, WFIR, ADM, Guide, Midjourney, Sv1.4, Sv1.5, VQDM, Wukong, DALLE2, SDXL, Mean -- there is no duplicate StyleGAN column, no 'Adide,' 'MediPentary,' or 'SOTA' column; these names do not appear anywhere in the paper.

weakness: The freezing strategy (Section 3.3) is not justified, and no comparison is given between frozen-head training and joint end-to-end finetuning.
