justification: Section 2.3.3 explicitly states experts construct test cases 'specifically designed to fail the various incorrect solutions we had collected' and the review team 'writes various incorrect and inefficient solutions to verify comprehensiveness,' confirming the same solution pool drives both construction and evaluation with no held-out split described.

weakness: The paper's 'first benchmark' claim is overreaching given its own related work cites other benchmarks that also collect problems from premier competitions (USACO Bench, LLM-Pros, OJBench, ICPCEval).
justification: Section 4.2 lists these prior works but the paper still claims to be 'the first benchmark to comprehensively collect latest problems from premier competitions around the world,' an overreach the paper itself partially concedes only by scope/recency, not exclusivity.

weakness: The paper never empirically compares model performance on existing benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench) versus AetherCode to quantify the claimed overstatement of proficiency, relying only on qualitative argument.
justification: The Introduction cites prior benchmarks' reported Pass@1 numbers (e.g., >90% on MBPP/HumanEval) qualitatively but never runs AetherCode's own evaluated models on those benchmarks for a direct paired comparison.

weakness: Difficulty classification methodology is described inconsistently (four levels vs. three roughly-equal categories) with no explicit numeric thresholds, and Figure 2 counts are not actually roughly equal.
justification: Section 2.2 says 'divided into four levels' then later 'we divide the dataset into three roughly equal categories: Easy, Medium, and Hard,' and Figure 2 shows Easy=159 vs Hard=132, a real inconsistency with no explicit solve-rate thresholds given.

weakness: Severe class imbalance across the 10 algorithmic categories (e.g., Basic=225 vs Tree=24) undermines reliability of per-category Pass@1 rankings, and the 144 sub-tags average too few problems each for meaningful evaluation.
justification: Figure 2 and Table 2 confirm the imbalance (Tree=24, Geo=36 vs Basic=225), and the paper itself only briefly acknowledges category difficulty variation without quantifying uncertainty for small categories.

weakness: Failure analysis in Section 3.3 is shallow, reporting approximate percentages without per-category breakdowns linking error types to problem categories.
justification: Section 3.3 gives only aggregate percentages ('approximately 70% to 80%') and qualitative anecdotes (GLM-4.5 language errors) without any table cross-referencing error type by algorithmic category as in Table 4.

weakness: The conclusion uses vague phrasing like 'small fraction of problems' instead of citing the concrete metrics, and does not include a human baseline to substantiate the claimed human-LLM gap.
justification: Section 5 indeed says 'even the most advanced models today can only solve a small fraction of problems' without restating the 35.5%/3.8% figures, and no explicit human contestant score baseline is given anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: Related work Section 4.1 is descriptive/list-like rather than explicitly comparative to AetherCode.
justification: Section 4.1 does provide the contribution's context (its focus is basic/SWE benchmarks, distinct from code reasoning) and Section 4.2 explicitly contrasts AetherCode against every cited benchmark; demanding a rigid per-paragraph comparative template for 4.1 is an excessive stylistic demand not necessary for the paper to be sound.

weakness: Excessive descriptive detail about OI/ICPC competition formats in Section 2.1 is irrelevant to benchmark construction and should be condensed.
justification: This is a subjective style/space-allocation preference rather than a substantive flaw; the competition format details establish provenance and scope relevant to a benchmark paper, and trimming them is a nice-to-have polish request, not a genuine weakness.

weakness: The paper omits the decoder architecture, training objective/loss function, and training algorithm, making reproducibility difficult.
justification: Section 4 (Methodology) only briefly says 'a decoder' is used without specifying its architecture, and there is no training objective, loss function, or optimization algorithm described anywhere in the paper text provided.

weakness: No standard deviation, confidence intervals, or multi-seed runs are reported for any experiment, so statistical significance of the claimed improvements cannot be assessed.
justification: All results tables (Table 1-6) report single point estimates (Obj./Gap/Time) with no variance measures anywhere in the paper.

weakness: Mathematical inconsistency between Definition 1 (W1,W2 in R^{k×k}) and the construction in Eq. (4) (W1,W2 in R^{2k×k}), with the approximation bound left unformalized.
justification: Definition 1 explicitly states X∈R^{n×k}, W1,W2∈R^{k×k}, while Eq. (4) defines W1=[I_k|0]^T, W2=[0|I_k]^T ∈ R^{2k×k} acting on X∈R^{n×2k} — a genuine dimensional mismatch in the paper text.

weakness: SVD reconstruction quality claims (85%/93%/97%) are presented without defining 'matrix information' or reporting variance across instances.
justification: The paper states 'The top 10 singular values could capture around 85% of the matrix information...' without ever defining the retention metric or giving any variance/statistics across instances.

weakness: Real-world experiments reuse GCN/MatNet baseline results from the RRNCO paper without controlled re-evaluation under identical training protocols.
justification: The paper itself states: 'we directly reuse the GCN and MatNet results reported in their paper, excluding other baselines due to incompatible settings,' confirming the cross-paper comparison concern is valid.

weakness: Missing runtime parity information for baselines: RADAR's training time is reported but not for MatNet, ICAM, ReLD, ELG, etc.
justification: Section 5.1 reports RADAR's training time (39.31h/54.74h) but the results tables only show inference time for baselines, never training time, so a training-cost comparison is indeed absent from the main text.

weakness: Sinkhorn normalization analysis is incomplete: the paper does not discuss doubly-stochastic vs row-stochastic attention rationale, gradient stability through Sinkhorn iterations, or how iteration count T affects convergence/sparsity.
justification: The paper already includes a Sinkhorn-vs-softmax comparison in Appendix D.5 and an iteration-count (T) sensitivity study in Appendix D.7 (Section 6.2), which the review overlooks when claiming these analyses are entirely missing; only the gradient-stability point is genuinely unaddressed.

weakness: The theoretical energy reduction formula in Table 1's caption, (E_sparse - E_dense)/E_sparse × 100%, is mathematically wrong (would yield negative values in the expected savings case) and E_s in Eq.1 is not defined relative to E_MAC/E_AC, and 'total spikes' is ambiguous between neuron-level and synapse-level counting.
justification: The paper's Table 1 caption literally states reduction = (E_sparse - E_dense)/E_sparse × 100%, which is inverted from what would produce the positive percentages reported, and Eq.1 leaves E_s and 'total spikes' undefined in terms of the MAC/AC costs and neuron vs synapse counting given earlier.

weakness: The paper overclaims that sparse ANNs 'universally' achieve 'much higher accuracy' than dense ANNs, which is contradicted by VGG-16 and ViT-B results where sparse ANNs underperform dense ones.
justification: The quoted sentence ('sparse ANNs can achieve a much higher accuracy than dense ANNs') appears in Section 3.1 specifically about MLP results; for VGG-16/ViT-B the paper explicitly and separately states sparse ANNs have 'similar accuracies' to dense ones, never claiming 'much higher' there, so citing VGG-16/ViT-B numbers as contradicting a claim the paper never made about those architectures is a scope misreading.

weakness: No variance, standard deviation, or statistical significance is reported for any accuracy or energy result across the grid search, making it impossible to know whether small accuracy differences (e.g., ±0.2-0.6 points) are systematic or noise.
justification: Table 1 and Figure 2 report only single-point accuracy/energy values with no mention of seeds, std, or significance testing anywhere in the Methods or Results sections.

weakness: The time-lag analysis establishes only correlation between firing-rate saturation and accuracy saturation and between sparsity and lag magnitude, yet the paper presents it as a potential causal mechanism for the accuracy-energy trade-off without ruling out confounders.
justification: No experiment in the paper manipulates time lag independently of sparsity level (e.g., varying membrane time constants at fixed sparsity), so the mechanistic link asserted in Section 3.3/Discussion is not established, only observed as an association.

weakness: Critical CHT reproducibility details are omitted from the main text: the fraction of weights removed per iteration, the specific link-prediction rule used for growth, the update frequency of topology evolution, and how CHT-Conv adapts CHT to convolutional layers.
justification: Section 2.1.1 only qualitatively describes the remove/percolate/regrow steps and defers the actual quantitative mechanism to external citations (Zhang et al. 2024b/2025, Hanning et al. 2025) rather than specifying removal fraction, growth rule, or update cadence in the paper itself.

weakness: The ViT-B training protocol (prune a pretrained dense network to 70% sparsity, then fine-tune with CHT) is fundamentally different from the from-scratch DST protocol used for MLP/VGG-16, confounding cross-architecture comparisons, yet this is only disclosed in a footnote rather than the main text.
justification: Footnote 1 on page 3 explicitly states ViT-B uses a 'hybrid structural-functional re-training pipeline' via pruning + CHT fine-tuning, distinct from the from-scratch CHT training used for MLP and VGG-16, and this distinction is not discussed in the main body when interpreting ViT-B's accuracy degradation.

weakness: The Discussion's claim that the accuracy-energy trade-off 'is not obtainable through either ANN-to-SNN conversion or dynamic sparse training alone' is an unfalsifiable exclusivity claim, since the paper never compares against alternative baselines like post-conversion pruning of dense SNNs or directly-trained sparse SNNs.
justification: The Discussion section makes this exclusivity statement without any experiment comparing against post-conversion pruning or direct sparse SNN training baselines within the main results (only STBP and pruned-ANN comparisons are mentioned as being in the Appendix, not addressing the exact exclusivity claim).

weakness: The abstract's headline '99% energy reduction' figure only reflects the MLP setting, while VGG-16 achieves only 31-47% and ViT-B achieves 58.87%, so the abstract inflates the best-case result relative to more practical architectures.
justification: The abstract states 'reduce theoretical energy consumption by up to 99%' without qualifying that this applies only to the 99%-sparse MLP, while Table 1 shows VGG-16 in the 31-47% range and ViT-B at 58.87%, which are the more practically relevant CNN/Transformer architectures.

weakness: The novelty claims ('for the first time', 'have never been studied') cannot be verified because external literature search was unavailable during the review, so novelty is deferred for manual verification.
justification: This is not a critique of the paper itself but an admission of a limitation in the review process; the paper already hedges its novelty claims with 'to the best of our knowledge' phrasing, and the reviewer offers no concrete evidence from the paper or elsewhere that the novelty claim is false.

weakness: Absence of empirical validation: the paper is purely theoretical with no experiments, simulations, or numerical illustration of the claimed improvements.
justification: The paper contains no experimental or simulation section; all results (Theorems 6-14, Tables 1-2) are purely theoretical with no numerical instantiation.

weakness: Computational practicality of Algorithm 1's minimax optimization over Φ and Π is not addressed, and no computational complexity analysis is given.
justification: The paper's Algorithm 1 (Section 4) presents the minimax problem in Eq. (3) abstractly with no discussion of tractability or computational complexity of solving it.

weakness: Assumption 3 severely limits applicability, failing to capture hybrid low-rank MDPs with unknown reward features, and Assumption 4's reliance on known linear reward features further restricts scope.
justification: The paper itself acknowledges exactly this in Section 3.2: 'Assumption 3... does not capture all learnable hybrid MDPs... if the transition space is partitioned according to Assumption 3 for hybrid low-rank MDPs with unknown reward feature, then log|Φ| will scale polynomially.'

weakness: High-probability guarantees are incomplete: only expected regret bounds are given for the hybrid setting, and it's unclear if high-probability bounds are achievable there.
justification: The paper states in Section 5.1: 'we can achieve same results... with high-probability if we replace... This variant, however, cannot handle the hybrid setting,' confirming this gap is real and unresolved.

weakness: Key technical details (proofs, estimation procedures, comparison tables) are deferred to Appendices A, B, C, F, H, I, J, and since the appendix was not provided, the reader cannot verify the claimed bounds, which is a substantial barrier to evaluation.
justification: The missing appendix is an artifact of this review pipeline ('the appendix is removed from the provided manuscript' per the review itself), not a defect of the paper; theory papers routinely place detailed proofs in appendices, and faulting the paper for a review-tooling limitation is an invalid criticism of the work itself.

weakness: Writing clarity issues: several grammatically awkward or incomplete sentences (e.g., 'For simplicity, we |Π| is finite' has a missing verb), and heavy unglossed use of acronyms (DEC, E2D, AIR, DMSO, Dig-DEC).
justification: The paper text on page 2 literally reads 'For simplicity, we $|\Pi|$ is finite,' confirming the grammatical error, and the paper indeed uses many acronyms without a consolidated glossary.

weakness: Limited baseline comparison undermines SOTA claims: only 2 external baselines (GradABM, EiNNs) on 2 locations (US and Massachusetts), with missing entries and EiNNs beating HG-DCM in 3/8 settings.
justification: Table 1 confirms only US and Massachusetts are compared, with dashes for missing GradABM/EiNNs results, and EiNNs indeed outperforms HG-DCM in several cells (e.g., US 4-week, MA 6-week/8-week).

weakness: Unexplained Mean MAE anomaly at the 4-week setting in Table 2, where HG-DCM's mean MAE spikes far above 2-week and 6-week values while median MAE improves monotonically, and the paper does not discuss this.
justification: Table 2 shows Mean MAE of 18602.6 (2wk), 110452.4 (4wk), 7112.5 (6wk), 4643.1 (8wk) for HG-DCM, and the text (Section 3.2.2) never mentions or explains this spike.

weakness: The core assumption that biologically distinct pandemics (SARS, Ebola, Dengue, Influenza) share universal macroscopic dynamics is insufficiently defended, resting on a single citation without evidence.
justification: The paper's justification for cross-disease universality (Section 1, citing Viboud et al.) is a brief assertion without empirical support or discussion of biological differences between vector-borne, contact-based, and respiratory diseases.

weakness: The loss function has unaddressed mathematical/indexing ambiguities: MAPE term divides by C_ij which can be zero, and the beta weighting in Eq. 5 is not explained.
justification: Section 2.2's Data Preparation only addresses negative counts being set to zero, not zero cumulative case denominators in the MAPE term, and the paper never states how beta in Eq. 5 is chosen.

weakness: Empirical validation is single-disease (only COVID-19) and does not truly test generalization to a novel pathogen, since the model trains on historical diseases plus early COVID data and tests on later COVID data from the same outbreak.
justification: Section 3.1.2 confirms only COVID-19 is used for the forecasting evaluation, and no held-out-disease generalization test is reported.

weakness: Missing reproducibility details for the constructed dataset: vague inclusion criteria ('more than 100'), no dataset size statistics, and no described train/val/test splitting strategy.
justification: Section 3.1.1 gives only a qualitative description of inclusion criteria and never reports counts of locations/time series per pandemic or an explicit split methodology.

weakness: Overclaiming in novelty framing ('first study', 'new paradigm') that cannot be verified without external literature search.
justification: The reviewer explicitly states this claim is 'deferred' and unverifiable in this run, meaning the criticism is not actually grounded in a checked contradiction with the paper or literature, making it an unsupported assertion rather than a verified weakness.

weakness: The Limitations section is too narrow, omitting issues like testing/reporting bias, dataset imbalance, single-disease evaluation, real-time updating, and spatial generalization.
justification: Section 4 (Limitation) only discusses data granularity/interpolation and exclusion of mortality data, and does not mention the listed omissions.

weakness: The parameter inference section contains a repeated phrase error and an unsupported claim that HG-DCM's estimates are 'realistic' without known ground-truth parameters.
justification: Section 3.2.3 does contain the duplicated phrase 'median day of action, median day of action' and asserts 'realistic' estimates without providing ground-truth parameter values for comparison.

weakness: BN removal is presented as a key architectural insight but lacks an ablation experiment (with-BN vs without-BN) to empirically validate the claim.
justification: Section 2.1 justifies BN removal only via reasoning about cross-pandemic batch statistics instability, with no reported with-BN comparison experiment anywhere in the results.

weakness: The core KL estimator derivation from Eq(2)+(3) to Eq(4) skips critical algebraic steps in the main text, making it hard to verify the integrand's correctness.
justification: The paper text indeed presents Eq(4) immediately after invoking Dynkin's formula without showing the intermediate algebraic expansion, only referring the reader to the appendix for the full derivation.

weakness: The theoretical error bound (Eq 7) depends on undefined constants C1*, C2, and the D|χ| scaling factor could be very large in practice, which is not discussed.
justification: The main text only vaguely states 'mild assumptions on the boundedness of the score functions (constants C1, C2)' without specifying norms or domains, and does not discuss when the D|χ| scaling makes the bound vacuous.

weakness: Novelty claims such as 'unique' and 'outperforms alternatives relying on the embedding trick' cannot be verified because the reviewer's own retrieval tool was disabled during this review run.
justification: This is not a flaw in the paper at all but a limitation of the reviewer's own process (no external literature access); the paper does compare against embedding-based competitors like MINDE within its own experiments, so this criticism is invalid as a critique of the paper.

weakness: Several important experimental details (backbone architecture, training modifications, hyperparameters) are deferred to the appendix rather than described in the main text.
justification: The main text repeatedly says 'see Appendix C.1' for backbone details and 'we slightly modify the training strategy... check Appendix C.2 for details' without specifying architecture or hyperparameters in the main text.

weakness: The text summarization reference MI derivation (256 to 303 nats) is a coarse approximation that should be labeled as a rough estimate rather than treated as ground truth.
justification: The paper already explicitly frames this as 'an order-of-magnitude estimate' and states 'we cannot establish an exact ground truth for these experiments,' so the reviewer's request is already satisfied by the text.

weakness: The conclusion lacks any explicit discussion of limitations of INFO-SEDD despite the method having clear failure modes.
justification: The conclusion section only discusses strengths and future extensions (Generator Matching, mixed continuous/discrete data) with no limitations paragraph.

weakness: The claim that INFO-SEDD is 'an invaluable tool for motif discovery' is an overclaim based on a single known motif in one species without a controlled experiment for the robustness-to-correlated-motifs claim.
justification: The paper demonstrates motif discovery only on the TATA-box in Arabidopsis thaliana and asserts robustness to correlated motifs via reasoning rather than a controlled experiment, matching the reviewer's specific claim.

weakness: Eq (1) has a circular definition where the diagonal correction term references the same reverse-transition-matrix entries being defined.
justification: The diagonal term sums the already-defined off-diagonal reverse entries (the first term in Eq 1 for b≠a), which is the standard convention of defining diagonal entries as negative row sums of off-diagonal entries; there is no actual circularity.

weakness: The distillation loss (Eqs. 5-9) is adopted from Primus et al. 2024's DCASE 2024 Task 8 system without stating what, if anything, is modified, undermining the novelty claim of contribution C1.
justification: The paper itself states in Section 2.2 that it 'adopted a distillation loss approach from the top-ranked DCASE 2024 Task 8 system (Primus et al., 2024)' and never specifies a delta from that prior formulation.

weakness: No statistical significance, variance, or confidence intervals are reported for any results in Table 2, despite very small deltas between configurations.
justification: Table 2 reports only single-point mAP/R@k numbers with no standard deviation or repeated-run statistics anywhere in the paper.

weakness: Unequal batch sizes across backbones (64 for PaSST, 24 for EAT, 16 for BEATs) confound the comparison of backbone performance, since InfoNCE loss strength depends on batch size (more negatives).
justification: Section 3.4 explicitly states these batch sizes were set 'due to computational resource constraints,' and the paper draws a backbone comparison ('PaSST consistently outperformed...') without controlling for this confound.

weakness: The claimed 'reproducible' LLM-based augmentation pipeline (contribution C2) actually depends on the proprietary, non-deterministic GPT-4o API, contradicting the reproducibility claim.
justification: The abstract/intro claims a 'Reproducible LLM-based augmentation pipeline,' yet Section 2.4 uses GPT-4o and the Limitations paragraph itself admits 'reliance on proprietary LLMs for augmentation' as a limitation -- a direct internal tension the review correctly flags.

weakness: Cluster guidance (SID 4/5) shows mixed or negative gains versus SID 3 for PaSST, undercutting the conclusion's claim that clustering 'contributed to additional performance gains.'
justification: Table 2 shows PaSST mAP@16 falling from 46.41 (SID3) to 46.39 (SID4), and the paper's own abstract concedes 'cluster guidance yields mixed gains across backbones,' which is in tension with the Conclusion's unqualified positive framing.

weakness: The paper has no Related Work section and the introduction does not establish a concrete research gap or critique of prior work, making novelty hard to assess.
justification: Section 1 is a single short paragraph listing contributions with no discussion of prior methods or gaps, and no Related Work section appears anywhere in the paper text.

weakness: Potential data contamination: AudioCaps train/val/test splits were merged for pretraining and, unlike WavCaps, no deduplication against CLOTHO evaluation data is mentioned for AudioCaps despite both being derived from AudioSet.
justification: Section 3.1 explicitly describes deduplicating WavCaps against Clotho evaluation subsets but says nothing about a similar check for AudioCaps, which is merged wholesale for pretraining.

weakness: The 50,000 LLM-mix synthetic captions generated via GPT-4o have no reported quality verification (human eval, filtering, or alignment scoring), risking label noise.
justification: Section 2.4 describes generating the mixed captions via GPT-4o but does not mention any quality control step, and results for augmentation (SID2 vs SID3) are indeed inconsistent across backbones as the review notes.

weakness: The conclusion is generic, uses filler language ('drawing inspiration from state-of-the-art methodologies'), and the limitations paragraph is too terse to be actionable.
justification: This criticism does not identify a concrete factual flaw beyond restating W5's point about overclaiming; calling language 'filler' or a paragraph 'too terse' without specifying what content should be added is a subjective, non-specific critique.

weakness: CLIP/Tiny-ImageNet results show KL+L0 combination performs substantially worse than L0-only or KL-only, contradicting the paper's generality claims of a 'plug-and-play solution for existing models and various data modalities'.
justification: Table 4 shows KL+L0 PGD accuracy 26.50% vs L0-only 53.31% at eps=2/255, while the abstract/intro claim broad generality; the paper's own explanation is speculative and unverified.

weakness: The TP/FN definitions in Experiment 1 are unconventional and conflate correct classification with attack detection, potentially inflating precision/recall.
justification: The paper's own confusion-matrix definitions (lines 186-191) count (â,ŷ)=(0,y*) as TP and (â,ŷ)=(0,-y*) as FP, which indeed departs from standard detection TP/FP definitions as described.

weakness: Theorem 1's threshold Γ_i(ε) is never instantiated, and the procedure for splitting test data into 'Theorem-Compliant' vs 'Non-Compliant' is not described.
justification: The paper states Γ_i(ε) is 'some threshold' (Theorem 1 statement) without defining its functional form, and Experiment 1 only says samples are partitioned by 'sufficient inter-class prototype separation' without specifying the decision rule.

weakness: No variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for any experimental results across Tables 1-4.
justification: All reported numbers in Tables 1-4 are single point estimates with no seeds, std, or CI mentioned anywhere in the experimental setup section.

weakness: The choice of forward KL(c||p) over reverse KL(p||c) or symmetric JS divergence is never justified or empirically compared.
justification: Eq. (1) defines only the forward KL with no discussion of directionality, and the ablation study (Experiment 2) never varies the KL direction.

weakness: The L0 metric's threshold τ·μ(c,p) creates a circular dependency since μ depends on the perturbation magnitude itself, undermining the fixed-τ theoretical proof.
justification: Eq. (2) defines the L0 threshold relative to μ(c,p), which itself scales with perturbation size, while the proof sketch (Prop. 4) relies on finding an adjustable τ 'for any given adversarial perturbation,' whereas the implementation fixes τ=0.75.

weakness: The BCE-based fine-tuning loss optimizes absolute similarity rather than the margin between correct and nearest-incorrect prototype distances needed for Theorem 1's separation assumption.
justification: Eq. 5-6 defines a pairwise BCE loss on similarity scores with no explicit margin term, while Theorem 1 (A4, coordinate gap condition) requires sufficient class separation that BCE alone doesn't guarantee.

weakness: The non-standard 50/50 test/validation split of the development sets reduces comparability with the broader literature using standard CIFAR-10/Tiny-ImageNet splits.
justification: Section 4.1 explicitly states 'we randomly split the development sets into two equal halves to serve as the test and validation sets,' confirming the non-standard split with no discussion of its effect on comparability.

weakness: The paper lacks comparison against established detection baselines (feature squeezing, LID, Mahalanobis, NIC, MagNet) under the same experimental protocol.
justification: The related work section discusses these methods only conceptually (Section 2) but no experiment in Section 4 empirically compares KOALA's detection accuracy against them.

weakness: The proof sketch has unresolved gaps that cannot be verified because Appendix B was not available in the provided manuscript excerpt.
justification: The paper explicitly states 'A complete proof of Theorem 1 is provided in the appendix B,' so the gap is due to the reviewer's own lack of access to supplementary material rather than an actual deficiency of the paper.

weakness: Theorem 1's unbiasedness claim for the DDC-clipped gradient estimate is under-justified: SPSA already carries O(epsilon^2) bias, clipping adds truncation bias unless C→infinity, and Eq. 8's substitution of E[||∇||]^2 by (∇L)^2 assumes unbiasedness of the unclipped estimate without justification.
justification: The paper's Theorem 1 and Eq. 8 derivation (visible in the main text) do make this substitution without addressing the inherent SPSA finite-difference bias, which is a legitimate mathematical gap not addressed in the shown text.

weakness: The upper-bound fine-tuning baseline uses SGD rather than AdamW (per footnote 2) due to compute budget, creating a mismatch since the headline 18x memory reduction is computed against AdamW while performance comparisons use the weaker SGD upper bound.
justification: Footnote 2 explicitly confirms fine-tuning experiments use SGD due to limited compute, while Figure 1's memory savings figure is measured against AdamW (16-bit), confirming the asymmetry.

weakness: No experimental comparison is provided against prior ZO+quantization methods (ZO-signSGD line: Feng et al. 2024, Zhou et al. 2025, Bar & Giryes 2025) despite the paper claiming QZO is 'inherently more efficient and flexible' than them.
justification: The Related Work section discusses these methods and asserts QZO's superiority in efficiency/flexibility, but no table in the paper includes empirical comparison against them.

weakness: The QZO vs MeZO comparison conflates three variables simultaneously (weight precision, trainable parameter count, and optimization scope), making it hard to isolate which factor drives the observed performance differences.
justification: Table 1 and Table 2 show QZO differs from MeZO in bit-width, parameter count, and update scope all at once, with no ablation isolating individual factors.

weakness: Table 3 (2-bit results) only compares QZO against Zero-Shot-Q, omitting 16-bit zero-shot, MeZO on 16-bit, and QZO at 4-bit on the same model, making it hard to assess how much performance is sacrificed for the extreme 2-bit compression.
justification: Table 3 as shown in the paper text contains only Zero-Shot-Q and QZO rows, confirming the missing baselines the reviewer identifies.

weakness: The paper's framing that QZO performs 'on par with MeZO' is overstated, since Table 1 shows some large gaps (e.g., CB: 69.6 vs 91.1 for Llama-3-8B, a 21.5-point difference).
justification: The 69.6 vs 91.1 CB numbers for Llama-3-8B appear directly in Table 1, substantiating that the 'on par' characterization glosses over a large task-specific gap.

weakness: The conclusion introduces the new Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large experiment with only a qualitative claim ('visually closer to the ground truth') and no quantitative metrics (e.g., FID/CLIP) reported in the visible text.
justification: The paper explicitly directs readers to Appendix F for 'results and discussions,' which is standard practice for summarizing supplementary experiments in a conclusion; briefly mentioning an appendix-detailed result is not an inherent flaw.

weakness: All results in Tables 1 and 3 are single-point estimates without variance, confidence intervals, or multi-seed reporting, despite ZO methods being known for high gradient variance.
justification: No standard deviations, error bars, or seed counts appear anywhere in the results tables or text shown, and the paper itself notes ZO's high gradient variance as a known issue (Section 3.2.2), making this a legitimate rigor gap.

weakness: Notation inconsistency: quantized weights are denoted as bar-theta in Definition 3.3/Eq.5 but switch to tilde-theta in Algorithm 1 without explanation.
justification: Definition 3.3 and Eq. 5 use \bar{\theta} while Algorithm 1's Require line and updates use \tilde{\theta}, confirming the inconsistency.

weakness: The Related Work section on LLM Quantization is catalog-style, listing methods sequentially without comparing their assumptions/limitations against QZO.
justification: This is a generic stylistic complaint about related-work organization that could apply to nearly any paper's related work section, without pointing to a specific missing comparison that affects the paper's technical claims.

weakness: The introduction's statement that activation memory is 'mostly affected by the size of mini-batch' is an oversimplification, ignoring sequence length, hidden dimension, and layer count, and omitting gradient checkpointing as a mitigation.
justification: The paper's Introduction (Section 1) does state activations 'are mostly affected by the size of mini-batch' without mentioning sequence length or model depth, matching the reviewer's specific textual citation.

weakness: Experimental validation is insufficient: only two datasets, one model type, no variance/statistical significance reporting, no multiclass/d>1 experiments, adversarial distribution construction not described, limited baseline comparison.
justification: Section 5 confirms only two regression datasets (Bike Sharing, California Housing), a single 2-layer MLP, Table 1 reports only mean utilities with no variance, and no experiments with d>1 despite the paper motivating H-calibration partly via high-dimensional intractability of full calibration.

weakness: Linear utility assumption (Assumption 2.1) restricts practical scope, especially for risk-averse high-stakes domains, and the paper does not quantify how limiting this is.
justification: The paper explicitly states in Section 2 and the Conclusion that nonlinear/risk-averse utilities 'fall outside our framework' with only a brief one-sentence acknowledgment and no quantitative discussion of the restriction's impact.

weakness: Theorem 3.1 lacks a formal citation or justification (e.g., compactness/convexity conditions, Sion's minimax theorem) for the saddle-point existence claim.
justification: The theorem statement and surrounding text assert a saddle point exists but do not cite a specific minimax theorem or explicitly verify compactness/convexity conditions for the infinite-dimensional policy space.

weakness: Proposition 4.4's self-orthogonality claim assumes population-level first-order stationarity, but does not caveat that finite-sample/SGD training only approximately satisfies this, potentially overstating precision.
justification: Proposition 4.4 is stated exactly at the population level, and the experiments section only vaguely says the learned forecaster 'approximately satisfies' the calibration condition without a formal finite-sample caveat tied to the proposition.

weakness: Decision calibration's practicality (sample complexity, achievability) is asserted in the Conclusion without empirical demonstration or quantitative sample-complexity analysis; experiments use self-orthogonality instead of decision calibration.
justification: The Conclusion states decision calibration is 'a natural requirement' but Section 5 experiments only use the self-orthogonality condition, not decision calibration, and no sample-complexity numbers are given in the main text.

weakness: Related work (Section 1.2) is organized as a paper-by-paper narrative rather than a thematic taxonomy, making comparison axes harder to locate.
justification: Section 1.2 is indeed structured as three narrative paragraphs discussing individual papers/clusters rather than organized by explicit comparison axes, matching the criticism.

weakness: The framework assumes a finite action set A throughout, and the Conclusion only mentions the linear utility assumption as a limitation, not the finite-action restriction.
justification: The Conclusion explicitly states both assumptions together: 'their utility functions u(a,v) are linear in v and A is finite; these are standard assumptions in the calibration literature' — so the paper does mention the finite-A limitation, contradicting the reviewer's claim that only linearity is noted.

weakness: The abstract/Theorem 1 claim of a sqrt(L_max) improvement over existing studies is ambiguous because it doesn't explain that prior works used different demand-characteristic parameters not directly comparable.
justification: The paper's Table 1 caption explicitly states 'we list the regret bounds for each reference by replacing the demand characteristic parameters used in each paper with our indicator L_max' and footnote 2 lists the exact correspondence (1/gamma, 1/mu, D, etc.) for each reference, so the reparameterization is already disclosed.

weakness: Theorem 3 (OGD-based algorithm) requires prior knowledge of P_T despite the paper's claim of working 'without knowing L_max and P_T a priori'.
justification: The paper itself states for Theorem 3: 'To obtain the optimal regret order, we must know P_T a priori... which is sometimes difficult to determine in advance,' confirming this genuine limitation of the OGD instantiation relative to the headline claim, which the reviewer correctly notes is under-emphasized.

weakness: Theorem 2's general assumptions (regret decomposition L^alpha R(T), switching cost O(L^-beta)) are not explicitly instantiated with concrete alpha, beta values for the OGD/SOGD base learners.
justification: Theorems 3 and 4 state final regret bounds directly without walking through the alpha/beta parameter mapping from Theorem 2, leaving the connection between the general framework and concrete algorithms implicit in the main text.

weakness: The L_max definitional condition is extremely strong/restrictive (worst-case over all items and intervals) and the paper doesn't adequately discuss how restrictive it is in practice.
justification: The paper explicitly discusses this: it notes that L_max=o(T) 'mildly constrains the duration of periods with small demand,' that sublinear regret is impossible when L_max=Omega(T), and that L_max 'does not primarily constrain the fluctuations in demand,' plus Remark 3 gives a probabilistic relaxation and worked example.

weakness: The doubling-trick logic in Algorithm 2 (parameter sequence 2,4,8,... vs. Theorem 2's use of R_{2Lmax,T}) is not explicitly derived/explained.
justification: The reviewer themselves acknowledge this is 'standard for doubling tricks,' so demanding an explicit derivation of a well-known standard technique is an excessive ask rather than a substantive flaw.

weakness: The argument in Section 1 for why standard two-layer meta-algorithms fail in OIO conflates issues and doesn't clearly connect the carryover-violation concern to the algorithm architecture.
justification: The paper explicitly makes this connection: 'A meta-algorithm's decision y_t might be larger than the output y_t^a of a base learner a. With a small demand, x_{t+1} can exceed y_t^a... this inconsistency prevents us from obtaining a theoretical guarantee for the two-layer structure,' directly linking the mechanism to the architectural failure.

weakness: The Related Work OCO paragraph omits reference to the matching Omega(sqrt((1+P_T)T)) lower bound from Zhang et al. (2018b), which is relevant to the optimality discussion in Section 5.
justification: Checking Section 2's OCO paragraph, it only mentions Zhang et al. (2018b)'s upper bound (Ader achieving O(sqrt((1+P_T)T))) without citing the matching lower bound, which only appears later in Section 5; this is a legitimate, specific organizational gap.

weakness: The Conclusion is too brief and lacks a structured summary of proven results, using informal language like 'we believe'.
justification: Demanding an enumerated, precisely-worded summary of results in the conclusion of a theory paper is a stylistic preference rather than a substantive flaw; the conclusion already states the main contribution and two concrete limitations.

weakness: Algorithm 1 is mislabeled as an 'algorithm' when it actually describes the environment's behavior/problem setup rather than a decision rule.
justification: Algorithm 1 is already explicitly titled 'Setting of online inventory optimization,' which is precisely the rename the reviewer suggests, so the criticism overlooks the paper's existing labeling.

weakness: No variance, standard deviation, or statistical significance testing is reported for any experimental results across Tables 1-3, making it impossible to assess whether reported gains are genuine or due to random variation.
justification: The paper's tables (1, 2, 3) report only single point-estimate numbers for H@1/H@5/MRR with no error bars, std, or significance tests mentioned anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: The test-time reasoning (TTR) module relies on a 72B-parameter MLLM (Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct) but the paper discloses no inference time, GPU memory, or per-query computational cost, and provides no ablation with a smaller MLLM.
justification: Section 3.1 states the model choice but nowhere in the visible text is compute cost, latency, or a smaller-model ablation discussed.

weakness: Assumption 1, which underlies the greedy attribute selection/consensus estimation, is presented without empirical validation and could fail under attribute redundancy.
justification: The paper only provides a proof for Theorem 1 in Appendix E; Assumption 1 itself is stated as a working assumption with no empirical verification in the visible sections.

weakness: The conclusion makes an unsupported speculative claim and the paper lacks a dedicated limitations section.
justification: The conclusion text literally states RULE 'might remarkably enrich the learning paradigm,' and no limitations section is present anywhere in the paper body.

weakness: The paper has no dedicated Related Work section; citations are scattered through the Introduction without systematic categorization.
justification: Confirmed by inspecting the paper structure: Introduction, Method, Experiments, Conclusion — no Related Work section exists.

weakness: Novelty claims (e.g., 'one of the first methods to enhance test-time robustness for MMEA') cannot be verified because external literature retrieval was unavailable in this review run.
justification: This is a caveat about the reviewer's own tool limitations during the automated review process, not a substantive critique grounded in the paper's content, so it does not identify an actual flaw in the paper.

weakness: Eq. 11 and Eq. 13 define losses via Dirichlet integrals without providing closed-form solutions, making the method hard to implement without consulting external references.
justification: The visible main text presents Eq. 11 and Eq. 13 with integral/KL forms and defers detail via a citation to Sensoy et al. (2018), without giving the closed-form expansion in the main text.

weakness: The uncertainty u_i has a narrow dynamic range (claimed ~[0.27, 0.73]) due to the tanh function in Eq. 2, reducing discriminative power.
justification: u_i = Ñ/Q_i is an aggregate over all Ñ candidate entities (Eq. 3), not a value directly bounded by the tanh/exp range of a single pairwise evidence term as the reviewer's derivation implies, so the specific numeric bound claim misreads the formula.

weakness: The linear reliability combination with γ=0.5 may be dominated by one signal since consensus is unbounded while uncertainty is bounded; sensitivity analysis for γ should be in the main text.
justification: The paper explicitly states in Section 2.2 that γ is 'fixed as 0.5 for simplicity, see Appendix G.10 for more choices,' meaning a γ sensitivity analysis already exists, contradicting the reviewer's claim that it is missing.

weakness: There is a circular dependency in the problem formulation since y_ij^m depends on y_ij and h_i^m, which are themselves unknown, and the paper does not explicitly address this.
justification: The paper's entire method (Section 2.2) is designed precisely to estimate reliability from observable similarities without requiring the true unknown h_i^m/y_ij labels, which already resolves the circularity the reviewer describes.

weakness: Single-run evaluation without variance reporting undermines statistical reliability of model comparisons (small gaps like GPT-5 vs Deepseek-Chat-V3.1 could be noise).
justification: The paper explicitly states results come from 'conducting single runs due to cost' (Section 5) with no confidence intervals or repeated trials reported anywhere in Table 2.

weakness: Causal attribution in the memory grafting experiment is confounded by context-length effects rather than communication ability.
justification: The paper attributes GPT-5's improvement to a 'deficiency in its interactive communication abilities' but never runs a self-grafting/length-matched control condition to rule out the shorter-context explanation.

weakness: The 'Interaction Test-Time Scaling Law' is overstated given that only Claude-3.7-Sonnet clearly exhibits the pattern while other models and the a-Interact setting do not.
justification: The paper itself notes only that 'Claude-3.7-Sonnet exhibits clear scaling behavior' among the four tested models, and the Figure 4 caption states a-Interact performance 'remains relatively flat or slightly decreases,' yet the paper still labels this a 'Law.'

weakness: The conclusion's claim of a gap in 'strategic interaction skills' introduces an undefined, unoperationalized construct.
justification: The term 'strategic interaction skills' appears only in the conclusion and is never defined or measured anywhere in the paper's methodology or metrics section.

weakness: The claim that ambiguous queries are 'unsolvable without clarification yet fully reconstructable once clarifications are provided' is not empirically verified in the main text.
justification: The main text asserts this via 'Quality control ensures' without presenting a zero-shot/no-clarification experiment to substantiate it; details are deferred to an unavailable appendix.

weakness: The human-alignment correlation difference (r=0.84 vs r=0.61) is not directly tested for statistical significance between the two correlations.
justification: The paper reports separate p-values for each correlation (p=0.02 vs p=0.14) but never performs a direct comparison (e.g., Fisher z-test) between the two coefficients.

weakness: Several key components (AST-based LOC retrieval, AMB/LOC boundary, debugging budget accounting, reward penalty formula, 2x budget multiplier justification) are underspecified in the main text, creating reproducibility risk.
justification: The main text repeatedly defers these details to appendices (e.g., 'detailed in Appendix N', 'details can be found in Figure 3') without giving sufficient specification for independent reimplementation from the main text alone.

weakness: The paper lacks a sharp delineation of what is inherited from LiveSQLBench versus what BIRD-INTERACT newly contributes.
justification: Section 3.1 lists LiveSQLBench's advantages and states the paper's contribution is 'to convert this static benchmark into a dynamic, interactive setting' in prose, but no explicit component-by-component attribution table is provided.

weakness: Notation is inconsistent in the formalization (S_0 vs S, undefined subscript r in U_r, ambiguous concatenation operator).
justification: Equation (1) defines S_0 and U_r, but subsequent text refers to plain 'S' (e.g., 'for S to generate SQL solutions'), and the subscript r in U_r is never explained anywhere in the paper.

weakness: The introduction's paragraph structure weakens narrative impact by front-loading citations and burying the key technical novelty.
justification: This is a subjective stylistic complaint about prose structure with no concrete factual error identified in the paper; it reflects the reviewer's personal preference for restructuring rather than a substantive flaw.

weakness: Regret experiment compares mGISS pruning against brute-force over all nodes without a baseline controlling for arm-count reduction (e.g., random subset of same size), so improvement could be an artifact of fewer arms rather than mGISS's node selection.
justification: The paper's Figure 3 experiment only compares mGISS vs brute-force with no equal-arm-count control baseline reported anywhere in Section 6.

weakness: Regret computation uses an estimated optimal arm ("the arm that most runs concluded to be the best") which is circular since it is derived from the same algorithm being evaluated.
justification: Footnote 11 explicitly confirms the paper defines the best arm this way, which is a legitimate methodological concern not addressed in the paper.

weakness: Target-node selection is biased toward nodes with most ancestors in both random and real-world pruning experiments, favoring cases with more aggressive pruning and not representative of arbitrary target nodes.
justification: The paper states in Section 6 and footnote 8 that Y is chosen as "the node with the most ancestors," and does not report pruning rates for other node choices.

weakness: Random-graph experiments report only point estimates (e.g., 17%, 29%, 62%, 77%) without variance, standard deviation, or confidence intervals across the 1000 generated graphs per configuration.
justification: The main text (Section 6) reports only mean retention fractions with no error bars or spread statistics for the random-graph experiments.

weakness: The novelty claim of being "the first" full characterization cannot be verified because external literature retrieval was disabled during the review.
justification: This is a limitation of the reviewer's own process, not a flaw in the paper; the paper already discusses and distinguishes its novelty from cited related works (Lee & Bareinboim 2018/2019/2020, Sen et al. 2017, etc.) in Sections 1 and 7.

weakness: No guidance is given on how a practitioner should choose the conditioning set Z_X, since the only constraint is An(X)\{X} ⊆ Z_X ⊆ V\De(X), leaving significant freedom that may affect the mGISS guarantee.
justification: The paper explicitly states in Section 2 that "the precise conditioning set Z_X for each X is pre-determined by the specific problem or application, or by the practitioner," making the choice of Z_X out of scope by design, and Theorem 13/Proposition 4 make clear the mGISS characterization holds regardless of the specific observable Z_X chosen.

weakness: Table 4 contains a duplicate row (ESGM=✓,Lc=✓,DDPO=✓ appears twice) with contradictory metric values (FID=37.98 vs 24.92, YOLOScore=47.74 vs 58.99, mAP50=53.21 vs 54.44), undermining trust in the ablation.
justification: The paper's Table 4 indeed lists two identical-configuration rows (last two rows, both ✓✓✓) with different reported values, and the text gives no explanation distinguishing them.

weakness: No variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for any experiment, making claimed improvements hard to assess as reliable.
justification: Tables 1-4 and the appendix references contain only single point estimates with no std/CI/significance testing mentioned anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: The DDPO reward function (Eq. 9) is written as KNN(x0, x0), which computes a distance from a point to itself and is always zero, making the diversity term non-functional as stated.
justification: Eq. 9 in the paper literally reads r(x0,c) = KNN(x0,x0) - ω KL(x0,x0'), matching the reviewer's quoted equation and creating the flagged inconsistency.

weakness: The mix-feature linear schedule and stop-gradient strategy in Eq. 3 lack empirical justification or ablation for the choice of schedule.
justification: The paper only states the linear schedule and cites SimSiam for stop-gradient without providing any ablation comparing schedule choices (constant/cosine/learned), so the criticism is well-grounded.

weakness: The third listed contribution (C3) is merely a summary of experimental results rather than a technical contribution.
justification: The third bullet in Section 1's contribution list reads 'Extensive experiments demonstrate that OF-Diff generates high-fidelity...' which is indeed a results statement, not a new technical contribution.

weakness: The abstract has a grammatical error ('in the remote sensing') and makes an unqualified SOTA claim without specifying comparison scope, and the mAP gain numbers are stated without clarifying they come from downstream detection rather than direct image-quality evaluation.
justification: The abstract sentence exactly matches the quoted grammatical issue, and the mAP percentages are presented in the abstract without stating they derive from the downstream detection augmentation experiment.

weakness: ESGM's mask pool construction and sampling selection mechanism are underspecified (pool size, per-category distribution, selection method, handling of unseen categories).
justification: Section 3.3 only states 'it selects enhanced shapes from a lightweight mask pool collected during or after training. In our experiments, we use masks generated during training' without specifying pool size, selection mechanism, or category distribution.

weakness: The caption vs. no-caption trade-off discussed in Section 4.5 is not resolved; the paper never clarifies whether main result tables (1-3) use the caption or no-caption variant.
justification: Section 4.4 states ablations use no-caption, and Section 4.5 discusses the trade-off, but the visible text of Section 4.1-4.3 does not specify which variant is used for Tables 1-3's main results.

weakness: The shape fidelity metric based on Canny edge maps conflates texture/contrast sensitivity with true object silhouette/shape, undermining the 'Object Fidelity' framing.
justification: Section 4.3 confirms the shape metrics are computed via cv2.Canny edge detection on cropped/resized patches, which is indeed sensitive to texture and contrast gradients beyond pure silhouette, a legitimate methodological concern.

weakness: The conclusion lacks an explicit discussion of limitations (e.g., reliance on training-set mask pool, computational cost, rare-category failure cases, unresolved caption trade-off).
justification: Section 5 (Conclusion) only claims 'effectiveness and superiority' and does not mention any limitations, confirming the reviewer's observation.

weakness: Theorem 1's variance inequality (Eq. 6) has the variance subscripts and estimator names swapped relative to the definitions given just above it, so the inequality as literally stated does not match the intended claim that VeriFree has lower variance.
justification: The paper defines G_Verifier(x,y*,z,y) (depends on y) and G_VeriFree(x,y*,z) (no y), but then Eq. 6 writes Var_z[G_Verifier(x,y*,z)] <= Var_{z,y}[G_VeriFree(x,y*,z,y)], reversing which estimator carries the y-dependence -- an internal inconsistency in the theorem statement.

weakness: No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests are reported for the benchmark comparisons, despite some margins being small or reversed (e.g., GPQA 4B: VeriFree 42% vs Verifier 45%).
justification: Tables 1 and 2 and Fig. 1 report only point-estimate accuracies with no variance/CI/significance information anywhere in the experimental section.

weakness: The claim that VeriFree's faster convergence is caused by reduced gradient variance is asserted without any direct empirical variance measurement.
justification: The paper states 'We attribute this improved learning efficiency to reduced gradient variance' (Sec 3.2) but reports no gradient-variance metrics, only downstream accuracy curves.

weakness: The unique-correct-answer assumption underlying the equivalence to RLVR is not quantitatively validated against the actual WebData training set, and the equivalence-class ablation is confounded by using an 8B model to generate the extended answer set for a 1.7B student model.
justification: Sec 2.2 states the assumption but the paper never measures how often it holds in WebData, and the equivalence-class experiment in Sec 3.3 explicitly uses a Qwen3-8B-derived model to generate additional correct answers before fine-tuning a 1.7B model, introducing a scale/teacher-student confound the paper does not address.

weakness: Removing KL regularization is justified only by citing two prior works rather than by the paper's own ablation at the model scales/training budgets used in this paper.
justification: Sec 3.1 states 'We do not employ KL regularization... as recent studies suggest...' citing Liu et al. 2025c and Hu et al. 2025, with no ablation of KL removal conducted within this paper's own setup.

weakness: Dataset curation (filtering to answers under seven tokens, LLM-based quality filtering) may bias the training distribution toward short-answer factual questions, and the 'non-math' subset used in the transfer experiment is not verified to be free of mathematical content.
justification: Sec 3.1 describes the filtering criteria but the paper provides no analysis of resulting distributional bias, and the transfer experiment in Fig. 5 does not report any verification that math content was fully excluded.

weakness: The paper uses promotional/unsubstantiated language such as 'results are striking,' 'neat way of optimizing,' and 'effectiveness and robustness,' which the review flags as a weakness.
justification: This is a stylistic/wording nitpick rather than a substantive flaw in the paper's methodology or results; it does not identify a concrete factual error or missing content, matching the Vague Critique / Generic comment pattern of criticizing tone without grounding in a specific technical deficiency.

weakness: The final gradient estimator (Eq. 7) applies the RLOO baseline only to the reasoning term (A_i) but uses the raw reward (R_i) for the reference-answer term, and this asymmetry is not explained or ablated.
justification: Eq. 7 in the paper indeed shows A_i (RLOO-baselined) multiplying the reasoning-term gradient and R_i (raw probability) multiplying the reference-answer-term gradient, with no textual justification or ablation of a symmetric alternative provided.

weakness: The claim that the '>' character does not appear in standard tokenizer vocabularies is stated too generally without specifying it is tokenizer-specific (e.g., to Qwen3).
justification: Sec 2.4 makes the general claim 'the pattern ">" does not appear in standard tokenizer vocabularies' without qualifying it to the specific Qwen3 tokenizer used in experiments, so the generalization is unverified for other tokenizers.

weakness: LoLoRA HPCA performs essentially identically to LoRA-FA (EVA) across GLUE, GSM8K, and TinyLlama ablations, and never achieves the best score on any GLUE task, undermining the paper's central claim that online local updates improve over frozen-A methods.
justification: Tables 1-2 show LoLoRA HPCA is never bolded (best) on any GLUE task; Table 3 shows LoLoRA HPCA and LoRA-FA (EVA) both at 0.829 accuracy on GSM8K; Tables 5-6 show near-identical perplexities between LoRA-FA(EVA) and LoLoRA HPCA/AE variants.

weakness: The GSM8K evaluation reports the best checkpoint across every-0.2-epoch testing rather than final-checkpoint accuracy, which can inflate/bias results toward higher-variance methods.
justification: Section 5.2 explicitly states: "The model was tested on GSM8K every 0.2 epoch during fine-tuning, and the best result is reported for each method," confirming this protocol choice.

weakness: The theoretical framework (Section 4) relies on strong assumptions (i.i.d. Gaussian ΔW0, isolated stationary submodule targets, linear squared-error regression) that limit its practical relevance to actual non-stationary, non-linear LLM fine-tuning dynamics.
justification: Assumption 4.1 explicitly posits i.i.d. Gaussian entries for ΔW0, Definition 4.2 treats submodules as having a stationary local target, and the conclusion itself admits "each submodule isolated with stationary targets... is not strictly the case in multilayer architecture."

weakness: The paper reports only mean±std across experiments without any statistical significance tests, despite many reported differences between methods falling within the reported standard deviations.
justification: Tables 1-6 report only ± standard deviation/error values (e.g., RTE: LoRA-FA uniform 86.4±1.1 vs LoLoRA HPCA 84.6±1.6) with no paired significance test reported anywhere in the provided text.

weakness: Algorithm 1 uses abstract interfaces (LocalRule, Opt_loc) without providing the concrete HPCA/SNL update equation or clarifying update frequency and stability, limiting reproducibility.
justification: Algorithm 1 (lines 106-118) only shows abstract calls like g_A^loc <- LocalRule(A,z,u) and Opt_loc.step(A); the specific SNL update rule and stability considerations are not spelled out in the main text (deferred to unavailable Appendix B).

weakness: The conclusion introduces a new, unvalidated future application (MLA projection blocks) that was never discussed or tested in the paper, reading as speculative and unfocused.
justification: The conclusion's final sentence about "projection blocks in efficient attention variants like MLA" appears nowhere else in the paper and is not evaluated experimentally.

weakness: Related Work (Section 2) is organized as a sequential list of prior work rather than a comparative analysis positioning LoLoRA against EVA/LoRA-FA on axes like memory-accuracy trade-off or assumption strength.
justification: Section 2 as written is a sequence of paragraphs each describing a cluster of prior work without any comparison table or explicit axis-based positioning of LoLoRA.

weakness: Definition 3.1 contains a typo: it lists "W_q, W_k, W_o, or W_o" for attention submodules, duplicating W_o and omitting W_v.
justification: The paper text literally reads: "W can be either W_q, W_k, W_o, or W_o in an attention layer," confirming the duplicate/typo exactly as described.

weakness: The claimed 13-20% memory savings are relative to LoRA's activation memory only, and shrink to a much smaller relative saving in the multimodal LLaVA setting where vision tokens dominate sequence length.
justification: Table 4 shows LoLoRA HPCA extra memory of 24.1GB vs LoRA (uniform) 24.6GB, a small saving compared to the 13% (30GB->26GB) seen in the GSM8K setting, and the paper itself notes "memory gains are not that prominent due to the short textual part... in comparison to image tokens."

weakness: Energy efficiency claims are entirely unvalidated (no energy consumption, power, latency, or FLOP measurements).
justification: The paper repeatedly motivates the work with 'low power consumption' and energy efficiency for edge deployment, but reports only accuracy/perplexity, never any energy, power, latency, or spike-count/FLOP measurement anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: Theoretical guarantees are weaker than claimed: Lipschitz continuity assumption is unverified/questionable for discontinuous quantized operations, Lipschitz constants are never bounded, and exact equivalence in Theorem 2 is acknowledged as rarely achievable with no bound on the approximation error.
justification: The paper's own Remark 1 admits exact equivalence 'may not be perfectly achieved in practice' and uses only ≈ without quantifying the approximation error, and Assumption 1's Lipschitz constants ρ^k are never estimated or bounded in the given text.

weakness: Missing statistical significance and variance reporting across Tables 2-4 (single-point numbers, no seeds/CI).
justification: All tables in the paper report single deterministic accuracy/PPL values with no mention of multiple seeds, standard deviation, or significance testing.

weakness: Critical implementation details for nonlinear operations are missing, delegated to You et al. (2024) without summarizing approximations; calibration hyperparameters (optimizer, LR, steps, dataset size) not specified in main text.
justification: Section 3.2.3 states nonlinear operations are handled via 'spiking-compatible operations proposed in You et al. (2024)' with only 'Additional implementation details are provided in the Appendix,' and Section 3.4 gives the calibration objective without any optimizer/LR/steps details in the visible main text.

weakness: Performance degrades consistently as T increases, which the paper attributes to unevenness error without deeper analysis of why calibration cannot compensate.
justification: Table 2 shows monotonic accuracy decline with increasing T even after calibration, and the paper's explanation is a single sentence ('we attribute this phenomenon to the growing unevenness error') without further analysis, matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: Figure 3 is misleading because it uses incompatible dual axes (log scale vs linear scale with negative values) for an MSE quantity that should be non-negative.
justification: The paper's own figure caption/description confirms a dual-axis plot with the right axis ranging from -8 to 2 for what is described as MSE loss, which is inconsistent since MSE cannot be negative.

weakness: Overclaiming in conclusion/contributions: 'substantial improvements in accuracy' actually only reflects recovery from degraded uncalibrated SNN, not improvement over the quantized baseline, which the calibrated SNN mostly underperforms.
justification: Table 2 shows the calibrated 'Ours' results at T>1 are consistently below the quantized PrefixQuant/Baseline W6A6 numbers, so 'substantial improvements' in the conclusion overstates results relative to the quantized baseline, though it is arguably true relative to uncalibrated conversion.

weakness: Related work section (2.2) reads as a catalog without a comparison table on axes relevant to LLMs (retraining requirement, neuron type, scale, time steps).
justification: Requesting a dedicated comparison table in the related work section is a stylistic/presentation preference beyond what is necessary to support the paper's claims; the paper already provides Table 1 comparing conventional vs. their method on similar axes.

weakness: PPL anomaly in Table 3 (group_size=64 gives 9.17, an outlier vs. 6.89-7.39 for other settings) is unexplained and raises reproducibility concerns.
justification: Table 3 as given in the paper does show PPL of 9.17 for group size 64 while all neighboring group sizes are in the 6.89-7.20 range, and the paper provides no discussion or explanation of this discrepancy.

weakness: Reproducibility statement is a placeholder ('source code will be publicly released after publication') that does not aid reviewers.
justification: The Reproducibility Statement section in the paper contains exactly this placeholder sentence with no further detail, pseudo-code, or hyperparameter specification.

weakness: Insufficient environment specification for reproducibility (action scales, control frequency, physics timestep, observation noise, termination conditions, and the 34-dim task specification encoding undefined).
justification: The paper states 'Exact details of the reward functions are provided in Appendix A.2' and 'we provide additional details in Appendix A', and the reproducibility statement says code for the simulator/task-suite/algorithms is attached in supplemental materials; the reviewer did not check the appendix which was excluded from the provided text, so claiming these are 'omitted' from the paper overall is unsupported without checking there.

weakness: Introduction lacks a clear problem-gap-solution narrative and conflates motivations.
justification: This is a subjective structural/stylistic critique with no concrete example of confusion caused; the introduction does state a clear gap (existing benchmarks focus on learning from human data / lack open-ended exploration) followed by the BuilderBench solution, so this is a vague, generic critique.

weakness: Claim-evidence misalignment: attributing algorithm failure on 3-cube tasks to 'inherent difficulty' without ablations/failure analysis to rule out poor algorithm choice or reward design.
justification: The paper text at Section 7 does state 'it primarily underscores the inherent difficulty of the task setup itself' without providing ablation or diagnostic experiments distinguishing this from algorithm/reward issues, matching the described gap.

weakness: Missing comparative analysis with Minecraft: dismissed in one sentence without addressing Minecraft's advantages (community, task diversity, proven agent research).
justification: The paper's related work section indeed gives Minecraft only a brief comparison ('While based on similar block-building foundations... we believe BuilderBench is better suited... due to speed and task-suite'), without discussing Minecraft's community/proven agents like Voyager, supporting this critique, though the paper does note Appendix C has more discussion, which the reviewer could have flagged rather than treating as fully absent.

weakness: LLM evaluation protocol too narrow (only open-loop text planning, binary success without granular error analysis) to support the broad conclusion that current models can't achieve the needed reasoning.
justification: The paper's Section 7.1 explicitly only tests open-loop high-level plans with X/success only, and does state a fairly broad conclusion ('highlights how solving our tasks requires non-obvious reasoning... beyond what current models can achieve through scaling alone'), supporting this critique of overreach given the narrow eval design.

weakness: Abstract uses informal language ('mimicry and sharpening' undefined) and rhetorical question adds no factual content.
justification: This is a stylistic nitpick treating informal/rhetorical phrasing as a flaw; such stylistic choices are not a substantive weakness of the paper's content.

weakness: Contribution bullet list mixes conceptual and engineering claims without distinguishing them.
justification: This criticizes organizational style without explaining why mixing benchmark design and engineering contributions in one bullet list is actually problematic or misleading.

weakness: Speed claim (10-100x) lacks comparative benchmark methodology details (hardware, measurement methodology, task configurations).
justification: The main text only states the speedup claim with a pointer to 'see Appendix B for a speed test' but the main body itself gives no methodology, so within the provided text this critique about the main claim lacking detail is reasonably grounded, though Appendix B may address it.

weakness: Conclusion makes unsupported/speculative claims about future extensibility ('should be easy' to add stochasticity, partial observability, multi-agent).
justification: The paper's Limitations section states 'we expect extending BuilderBench to incorporate these settings should be easy' with no supporting evidence or argument, matching the critique.

weakness: Citation typo: 'Kaeling, 1993' should likely be 'Kaelbling, 1993'.
justification: The paper text at line 179 indeed cites '(Kaeling, 1993)' which appears to be a misspelling of Kaelbling, a legitimate minor citation error.

weakness: No comparative baselines or benchmark evaluation against standard jailbreak methods (HarmBench, AdvBench, GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN); the paper's claim that no existing method generalizes across all evaluated models is asserted without evidence.
justification: The Discussion section explicitly states 'it is unlikely that a meaningful benchmark can be established' and asserts superiority over existing methods without citing any comparative evidence, confirming the gap.

weakness: The #ASA metric is lenient (counts success if at least one unsafe output among 10), overstating the headline '90/100' result, and no confidence intervals or variance statistics are reported.
justification: Section 3.1 defines #ASA exactly this way, and no variance/CI statistics accompany the reported #ASA or #Avg UPA numbers anywhere in the results.

weakness: The paper lacks a testable mechanistic hypothesis for why the attack works, relying on vague language like 'confusing the model's internal value alignment' without operationalizing or testing it.
justification: The paper repeatedly uses this phrase (Introduction, Conclusion) and the Conclusion admits 'it remains an open question why the strategy is so effective,' confirming no operationalized mechanism is tested.

weakness: Exclusion of resistant models (o1/o3) from the main evaluation and the decision not to test GPT-5 selectively removes counterexamples, biasing the claimed universality upward.
justification: Section 3.2 confirms o1/o3 resisted the original attack and were only tested with a modified prompt for over-refusal, and GPT-5 was skipped as 'not very essential' — exactly the confound described.

weakness: Insufficient reproducibility documentation: exact prompt not given as copy-ready text, and temperature/sampling/API details are not reported.
justification: While Fig. 3/4 show substantial prompt structure, no temperature, sampling parameters, or API version details are given anywhere in the paper, supporting the reproducibility gap.

weakness: The paper contains overclaims and unsupported strong language (e.g., 'existing jailbreak attacks seem less necessary', 'veritaserum that universally bypasses even the most robust guardrails', 'all their built-in guardrails collapse').
justification: These exact phrases appear verbatim in the Abstract, Conclusion, and Discussion sections and go beyond what the single-prompt-configuration evidence supports.

weakness: The 'meta-prompt' concept is under-defined and not distinguished from related prompting concepts in the literature.
justification: The paper only briefly states 'the prompt...effectively functions as a meta-prompt' (Section 2) without a formal definition or comparison to related prompting paradigms.

weakness: Ablation studies (operator R and B) lack statistical rigor and model coverage, testing only 2-3 models with no confidence intervals or significance tests.
justification: Table 1 tests only 3 models (Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok 4, GPT 4.1) and Table 2 only 2 models (Gemini 2.5-flash-lite, Qwen3-235B), with no statistical testing reported anywhere in Section 3.3.

weakness: The topic-distribution analysis (Section 3.5) poses a deep question about the source of topic imbalance but leaves it unanswered.
justification: The paper itself asks 'Do they represent the models' internal reasoning reflections, the frequency of such content in their pre-training corpora, or the actual real-world unsafe material?' and provides no follow-up analysis toward answering it.

weakness: Inconsistent narrative framing in the Introduction, oscillating between motivating the attack and reviewing related work without clearly establishing the research gap, with the contribution statement embedded rather than listed separately.
justification: This is a subjective stylistic complaint about narrative flow without pointing to any specific missing or incorrect content; it does not identify a concrete scientific flaw.

weakness: The abstract/introduction claim EGG-SR 'consistently enhances' performance, but Table 1 shows counterexamples (e.g., EGG-DRL noisy (4,4,6): 5.09 vs DRL 2.46; EGG-MCTS noisy (3,2,2): 0.012 vs MCTS 0.007) that are not discussed.
justification: Table 1 in the paper does show DRL 2.46 underlined (better than EGG-DRL 5.09) and MCTS 0.007 underlined (better than EGG-MCTS 0.012) for these exact settings, while the abstract states 'EGG-SR consistently enhances' and the introduction states 'EGG consistently improves performance across diverse frameworks' without qualifying these failure cases.

weakness: The LLM experiments compare EGG-LLM's own runs against previously published LLM-SR numbers rather than reproducing the baseline under identical conditions, introducing uncontrolled variance.
justification: The paper explicitly states 'The result of LLM-SR directly uses the reported result in Shojaee et al. (2025),' confirming the baseline was not re-run under matched conditions.

weakness: The theoretical contribution (Theorem 3.1) is heavily dependent on the existing Laurent & Maillard (2020) framework, with the novelty being the observation that EGG-MCTS fits their graph-merging analysis, which the paper does not clearly demarcate.
justification: The proof sketch itself states 'Laurent & Maillard (2020) analyze MCTS on a graph obtained by merging identical tree nodes... Our final results follow their regret analysis on the unrolled tree,' confirming the paper leans on this prior framework without a clear main-text delineation of what is new versus inherited.

weakness: The EGG-DRL gradient estimator (Eq. 4) raises unresolved technical questions about unbiasedness of the log-sum gradient and the undefined baseline b'.
justification: The main text only provides a one-sentence proof sketch for unbiasedness ('unbiasedness can be obtained by expanding the definitions') without derivation, and b' is introduced in Eq. (4) without any definition or estimation guidance in the main text, supporting the reviewer's concern.

weakness: The experiments section is missing statistical rigor: no standard deviations/confidence intervals for Table 1 NMSE values, no stated number of trials/seeds, and no discussion of whether baselines received equal compute budget.
justification: Table 1 in the main text reports only median NMSE with no variance measure, and the main text experimental description does not state number of seeds/trials or compute-budget parity between EGG variants and baselines.

weakness: The paper has overclaiming and writing quality issues, e.g., 'consistently enhances' contradicting Table 1, unstated 'mild theoretical assumptions,' a grammatical error ('using EGG than without'), and an unjustified 'orthogonal to existing approaches' claim.
justification: All quoted phrases appear verbatim in the paper (abstract, introduction, related work), and the paper does not enumerate the 'mild theoretical assumptions' referenced nor justify the 'orthogonal' claim in the related work section.

weakness: No statistical significance or variance reporting (std, CI, multiple seeds) across main results; some margins (e.g., 50% compression TR@1 55.1 vs 54.9) could be within noise.
justification: The paper reports only single-run point estimates in Tables 1-5 with no mention of seeds, std, or significance tests anywhere in the text.

weakness: Contributions C1 and C2 are overlapping/restated versions of the same claim, and C3 is merely an experimental outcome rather than a conceptual contribution.
